Latest Update: Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in New York City

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit.
  • As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood.
  • In many ways, this transition is happening outside of me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit. It is a small but enduring presence, tended to around the clock, its care passed from one person to the next so that the light never goes out. I’ve often thought about how much of life is like this, how we are constantly passing the torch from one version of ourselves to another.

As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood. I was becoming someone different from the girl I had been, carrying parts of her with me but beginning to understand the world through a newly introduced lens. Now, years later, I find myself at another such transition: I am becoming a different version of a woman, one I am still getting to know.

In many ways, this transition is happening outside of me. Thirteen years ago, I moved away from my family in Mumbai and the home where Diwali had always been celebrated. For all those years, the rituals continued, even as I participated in them from thousands of miles away, mostly over video calls. Back in Mumbai, Diwali meant a house full of family and friends, kitchens bustling with cooking and frying, and the warm glow of diyas illuminating the mandir. I was no longer physically there, but I remained part of it. This year, for the first time, I hosted my parents for Diwali in the home I’ve built for myself in New York City.

In a recent development, it felt cataclysmic, or at least I was making it feel that way in my head. As I welcomed a different version of myself, I was also taking on a newly introduced role within my family. I was no longer simply the daughter returning to their house for Diwali; I was the one opening my home, preparing the food, tending to the rituals, and making space for the people who first taught me what this celebration means. There is perhaps no greater joy than watching the people I love receive and experience care. And yet, this was a responsibility I had chosen to take on, and one that felt particularly daunting as the eldest daughter. I wanted to get it right.

Sources indicate that for me, that care has always found its way to the table. Food is how my family celebrates, how we mark occasions, and, perhaps most importantly, how we look after one another. So naturally, much of my energy went into planning the meal. Despite my best efforts, my dad promptly assigned himself the task of making the goat kari—apparently, even after 13 years away, some things hadn’t changed. We headed to our local butcher in Brooklyn to buy fresh goat meat, and almost immediately, his attention turned to the spice tolerance of my guests.

In a recent development, “How much spice can your friends tolerate?” he kept asking me. “Should I keep it at a level six? But our level six might be their level ten. What do I do?” he lamented. “Relax, they’ll be able to handle it! Just make it our level five,” I told him.

According to recent reports, I gave in and handed over part of the kitchen to my mother, too. She took charge of the paneer, cooking generous chunks in a luscious onion-tomato gravy and making the chapatis. Selfishly, I didn’t mind relinquishing that responsibility: This would be my one chance for the year to eat chapatis fresh off the tava, puffed up and piping hot, and made by my mother.

Industry observers note that as the days drew closer, I found myself loosening my grip on the aims I’d made. My parents had their own ideas about what needed to be cooked, and while I was initially resistant to them taking over (any immigrant will tell you how hard it is to get our parents to just relax!), I was learning that hosting didn’t necessarily mean doing everything myself. It also meant making room for everyone to contribute and allowing upcoming rituals to form.

Industry observers note that the evening began with freshly fried moong vadas. My mother, of course, insisted on frying them for everyone, right before serving. Made from soaked and ground mung lentils, these little fritters are crisp and golden on the outside, with a soft, almost creamy interior. They have a naturally earthy, nutty flavor from the lentils, sharpened with green chiles, ginger, and spices.

Moong vadas are best eaten immediately, still hot out of the oil, with a tangy green chutney. The scene reminded me of Diwalis back in Mumbai, when the vadas rarely even made it to the serving platter: Everyone would gather around the kitchen, waiting for the next batch to come out of the kadai, reaching for them before they had a chance to cool. I saw the same thing happening in my kitchen in Upcoming York.

It has been revealed that in the meantime, my friends Leanne and Christina took charge of the tamarind margaritas, my ode to the soft, sweet-tart tamarind candies I grew up savoring as a kid. The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

Industry observers note that the table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as rapidly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

In a recent development, at the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

Sources indicate that for dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

Sources indicate that as I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in Latest York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Half a can of pumpkin leftover pumpkin may not be enough for another pie, but you can definitely put it to use in other fall recipes.

In a recent development, our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Fall baking has a way of leaving you with awkward amounts of leftover canned pumpkin. So many recipes call for half a can or some other quantity that leaves you wondering what exactly you’re supposed to do with the rest. You put the open can of Libby’s pumpkin puree in the refrigerator with every intention of using it, yet a few days later, there it is, still waiting for you to come up with a plan. It’s not as though you can make half a pumpkin pie.

In a recent development, fortunately, you don’t need much pumpkin to make something wonderful. In fact, one of the best things I’ve made with leftover pumpkin requires less than a cup, a handful of pantry staples and very little effort. It’s the sort of recipe that makes having leftover pumpkin feel less like a nuisance and more like a stroke of good luck.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

In a recent development, these are a little different from the dense, chewy blondies you might be accustomed to. They have golden edges and a wonderfully soft, almost cakey center, thanks in part to the pumpkin puree. Brown sugar gives them their rich, buttery sweetness, while cinnamon and pumpkin pie spice make them taste unmistakably like fall. The recipe lists the chocolate chips as optional, though I’d argue strongly in favor of including them. Chocolate and pumpkin are excellent together, and the little pockets of melted chocolate are delicious against all those warm spices.

In a recent development, the pumpkin blondies also almost suspiciously easy to make. Everything comes together in one bowl, using ingredients you probably already have on hand. There’s no frosting to fuss with, no dough to chill and no pie crust to negotiate. Just spread the batter into a 9-inch pan and bake it for 25 to 30 minutes. You’ll have a dozen soft, spiced bars that are equally at home on a Thanksgiving dessert table as they are next to your morning coffee.

Sources indicate that best of all, the recipe calls for just 1/2 cup of canned pumpkin. That’s a particularly convenient amount when you’ve got the remains of another baking project taking up residence in the refrigerator. And if you have a full cup left, making a double batch seems like a perfectly reasonable course of action.

And there’s no reason to limit pumpkin to sweet recipes. A few spoonfuls can add body and richness to soups, pasta dishes and risotto, especially when paired with sage, garlic and Parmesan. Just be sure you’re using plain pumpkin puree rather than pumpkin pie filling, which already contains sugar and spices and isn’t as versatile.

If you’re not quite ready to commit to another pumpkin project, you can always freeze your leftover pumpkin puree. That way, the next time a recipe calls for an odd amount of pumpkin, you’ll have some on hand.

#42742. ZWO Seestar S30 Plus review

ZWO Seestar S30 Plus review

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2204 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There's much to enjoy about the Seestar S30 Plus.
  • Editing controls could be a little more responsive.
  • Sources indicate that why you can trust Live Science Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best ones for you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There's much to enjoy about the Seestar S30 Plus. The image quality is great, it's easy to use, and it's compact and lightweight enough to take it anywhere. It's not quite as good as the more expensive S30 Pro, but it's a nice middle-ground option between the S30 and the S30 Pro that gives you a lot of features for the money.

Seestar app is reliable and easy to navigate.

All-in-one workflow from shooting to sharing.

2K image quality is better than we expected.

Lightweight and easy to travel with.

Editing controls could be a little more responsive.

Not suitable for smaller planetary nebulas.

Sources indicate that why you can trust Live Science Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best ones for you. Find out more about how we test.

Industry observers note that ZWO has just released the newest member of its smart telescope range: the Seestar S30 Plus. This all-in-one smart telescope is designed for beginners and hobbyists who want an affordable way into astrophotography that won't leave you scratching your head, and lets you capture, process and share your images in one simple workflow. It sits between the Seestar S30 and S30 Pro, and is priced at $499 for its release.

Recent findings suggest that with 2K image quality, a light pollution filter and a user-friendly interface, it's a smart telescope that anyone can enjoy, regardless of your experience level, and regardless of whether you're shooting from your city balcony or a dark sky site. Like the other models, it uses dual cameras to capture a wide range of subjects, including deep-sky objects with the telephoto camera, and constellations, star trails and the Milky Way with the wide-angle camera. It's lightweight and easy to travel with, and it even comes with a separate solar filter for solar imaging and eclipse time-lapses.

We got our hands on an advance copy to test ahead of its release, so we put it through its paces on several different celestial subjects.

Industry observers note that the Seestar S30 Plus is one of the smallest, most compact smart telescopes on the market, weighing just 3.63 pounds (1.65 kg) and measuring 8.3 x 5.5 x 3.2 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm). Its sleek, matte white design looks identical to the other Seestar models (we compared it to our S30 Pro), except for the branding on the unit itself.

It comes in a padded soft carry case and includes a small tripod (although we always prefer to use our own), a solar filter, a 40-inch (1 meter) USB-A to USB-C charging cable, a removable shoulder strap for the carry case, and a quick-start guide. With its accessories and case, the whole setup weighs 4.89 pounds (2.22 kg).

According to recent reports, on the unit itself, you'll find just one button, which powers it on, plus the USB-C port on the side. Super simple, although we'd have liked the USB-C port to be covered to prevent moisture or dust from getting in.

Industry observers note that the set-up process couldn't be easier. When you turn the telescope on, you'll hear a double beep and see the power button light up alongside the red dots on the black screen to indicate the battery level. Four dots mean the battery is full. The telescope will tell you when it's ready to connect, at which point you can sync it up to the app on your smartphone or tablet. To turn it off, you just select "Shutdown" in the app, which closes the arm and turns the unit off.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, it also features an anti-dew heater, which we've found works quite well in mild to moderate humidity. On a couple of our shoots, we noticed a tiny bit of condensation forming on the unit when the humidity was higher, so we wouldn't feel confident leaving it unsupervised for long periods on a particularly dewy evening. (We used the Clear Outside app to monitor the humidity levels.).

According to recent reports, the Seestar App is user-friendly and easy to navigate, with just the right amount of controls: you have plenty of options to choose from but it doesn’t become overwhelming. The main Seestar page is where you'll likely spend most of your time, as this is where you can search for celestial objects to shoot, access your album, strategy a shoot and read up on what objects Seestar recommends based on your time and location.

Industry observers note that the Stargazing section is where you can select or search for the subject you want to shoot. You can use the search function to find a specific target or browse Tonight's Best, and you can also search through different types of subjects like galaxies, nebulas, clusters and more. From here, you can also select planets, track comets and photograph constellations using the wide camera.

Click on a subject and the app will display information about it, including its current altitude and coordinates, which help determine what time is best to shoot that particular object. It automatically applies the appropriate filters and settings, but you can override these if you want to.

It has been revealed that there's very little to complain about when it comes to using the app. It has lots of information for beginners, so you don't need a ton of knowledge about the night sky, and everything is fairly self-explanatory. There were a couple of occasions when it failed to calibrate itself (for example, when we tried to locate the Pleiades, which had just risen above a tree), and other times when we chose a new target and it slewed the long way round instead of only having to move slightly. But otherwise, the app worked well.

Sources indicate that the AI Enhance section has some good editing tools to bring out the best from your photos. You can reduce the stars, adjust the brightness, contrast, saturation and RGB curves, apply denoise and eliminate any satellite trails — although we'd love a dehaze slider to bring out some of the fainter nebulosity of certain objects. The sliders could do with being a little more responsive, especially the RGB curves, but overall, it does a pretty good job of editing your pictures to get a pleasing result.

We had about 10 days to test our review unit before its release on November 10, so we could only capture as much as the weather permitted in that time. All our tests were conducted from our backyard in a Bortle 4 region, and captured before moonrise to eliminate as much light pollution as possible. Due to these time constraints, we aimed to capture our images for a total of 60 minutes each, although we'd ideally have aimed for longer in some cases.

According to recent reports, nov. 16, 2026: Lunar, solar and Heart Nebula images and information added.

Now for the fun part — the images. The Seestar S30 Plus has a focal length of 160mm, which is advantageous for capturing large subjects like the Andromeda Galaxy, the North America Nebula and the Pleiades. Large emission nebulas are where it really shines; however, the focal length is too short to capture smaller apparent objects.

For this review, we aimed to capture as many different types of objects as possible. All our images were edited in the Seestar app with, in some cases, a few minor tweaks in Lightroom. You also have the option to download the individual files to your computer to process them yourself in dedicated astrophotography software, which is advantageous if you're a more experienced user.

Industry observers note that everyone's favorite star cluster, the Pleiades, was one of the first targets we wanted to capture. We could see the faint blue nebulosity after as little as 15 minutes of integration time, and it only improved over time. After 60 minutes, we had a really nice image and could easily bring out the blue haze via the editing tools in the app. However, we got a much more impressive result after tweaking our image a little further in Lightroom, bringing out even more haze and reflective dust.

The Andromeda Galaxy is a perfect target for the Seestar S30 Plus. It takes up a large portion of the frame, and with long integration times, it can reveal beautiful details in the faint outer arms. We shot for around an hour in our tests due to weather and time constraints, but we still got an impressive image. As we approached 60 minutes, there was a lot of cloud cover, and we noticed it struggling to stack images toward the end of the session, so we stopped the integration at 57 minutes.

Andromeda is certainly going to be the most impressive galaxy for the Seestar visually, as most others will appear smaller in the frame and will need longer integration, so make sure you have a clear, dark night for it.

Sources indicate that large emission nebulas are where the Seestar S30 Plus thrives, and the North America Nebula is a great target. It covers the whole field of view, and the red hydrogen gas easily comes to the forefront of the image.

Industry observers note that the Eastern Veil Nebula and Heart Nebula are also lovely targets for the Seestar S30 Plus. In the Eastern Veil Nebula in particular, you can bring out the beautiful red and turquoise hues in as little as 15 minutes, but longer integration times will yield brighter, more colorful results.

It has been revealed that planetary nebulas are where you will see the limitations of the Seestar's 160mm focal length. Most planetary nebulas have a very small apparent size — we've previously captured the Dumbbell Nebula and Cocoon Nebula with our S30 Pro, and they were a tiny dot in the middle of the screen. We tried the Helix Nebula, and even though it's one of the largest apparent planetary nebulas, it's still fairly small on the Seestar S30 Plus. You can still get a decent image of it, but if you want to focus on imaging planetary nebulas, you'll need a bigger scope. Because it was very low in the sky and there was some interfering cloud, we stopped integration at 27 minutes.

In a recent development, solar and lunar imaging is easier than ever thanks to the Seestar S30 Plus. The included solar filter is easy to attach to the front of the telescope (and should be used for every solar session). Solar mode is ideal for viewing sunspots and creating a timelapse of a solar eclipse — we captured the total solar eclipse with our S30 Pro back in the summer. Similarly, lunar imaging gives you the option to capture images, video and timelapses of the moon, and we were impressed with the detail we got on a crescent moon, particularly at 2x. On both solar and lunar modes, you can shoot at 1x, 2x and 4x.

Recent findings suggest that the Seestar S30 Plus is an affordable entry point into deep-sky astrophotography without the confusing settings and expensive setup. It's ideal for beginners, although more experienced users will likely want to upgrade to the superior image quality and extra features of the S30 Pro.

Still, for under $500, we can't complain. Not only is the Seestar S30 Plus easy to navigate and use, but it teaches you about space in a fun and interactive way, and you don't need to spend hours stacking individual frames on your computer to process — although you still can do that if you want more control over your editing.

If you want better image quality.

Sources indicate that if you can stretch your budget, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade. It produces 4K images and offers more pro-level features.

Read our full Seestar S30 Pro review.

If you want a longer focal length.

To see deeper into space, the Seestar S50 Pro has a longer focal length of 260mm and a larger 50mm aperture, making it better for smaller apparent objects.

Read our full Seestar S50 Pro review.

If you want a more traditional telescope.

If the imaging aspect doesn't interest you, the Celestron StarSense Explorer range of telescopes connects to your phone to guide you around the sky, but you observe the cosmos through an eyepiece instead of capturing it on your phone.

Read our full Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 70AZ review.

Kimberley Lane, E-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, reviewing camera gear from Sony, Canon, OM System and more. With over 6 years of photography experience, her skills span across landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in a number of national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan. She has also contributed to our sister site Space.com and Tech Radar, and she regularly uses binoculars and telescopes to stargaze in the dark skies of South Wales.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Even in an election cycle marked by surprises and upsets, Capitol Hill observers will spot some familiar faces (identical twins notwithstanding) among this year’s midterm winners.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, here at a Oct. 20 campaign event near Ohio University in Athens, won his comeback bid Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Even in an election cycle marked by surprises and upsets, Capitol Hill observers will spot some familiar faces (identical twins notwithstanding) among this year’s midterm winners.

At least seven former members won comeback bids Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that the winners included alumni who dusted themselves off after election losses just two years ago. But other winners haven’t been in office in nearly two decades, their service predating the addition of a women’s restroom in the House (more recent than you may guess).

Here’s how these former members did on election night:.

Carl lost a primary to fellow Republican Rep. Barry Moore in 2024 after a upcoming map placed them in the same district. But with Moore running for the Senate in 2026, Carl had an easier path back to his old seat, which was redrawn again this year. He defeated his Democratic opponent Tuesday by 18 points.

It has been nearly two decades since Solis last served in Congress. She left in 2009 to serve as President Barack Obama’s first Labor secretary. Solis was in her sixth term as a Los Angeles county supervisor when she revealed a bid for Congress after California voters approved a map that created five Democratic pickup opportunities.

Solis faced limited resistance on her path to victory in the 38th District, especially after Democratic Rep. Linda T. Sánchez opted to run for the redrawn 41st District.

Bean is making her way back to the House after losing her suburban Chicagoland seat in the conservative tea party wave of 2010.

Sources indicate that A decade-and-a-half later, she won an eight-way primary for the 8th District seat Democrat Raja Krishnamoorthi vacated for an unsuccessful Senate bid. Winning the nomination all but guaranteed Bean a November victory in the deep-blue seat.

One of the cycle’s biggest comeback stories was in the Buckeye State, where Sherrod Brown was mounting a bid two years after Republican Bernie Moreno had unseated him. Positioning himself as an opponent of data centers, Brown defeated appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in a special election for the remainder of now Vice President JD Vance’s term. He could take office as early as December but would have to run again in 2028 if he wants another full term.

First elected in 2018, Allred left Congress two years ago after an unsuccessful Senate campaign against Republican incumbent Ted Cruz. After briefly launching a second Senate bid, Allred switched to a redrawn open House seat and won his primary over Rep. Julie Elizabeth Johnson, his successor in the chamber. Allred had no trouble winning his general election Tuesday for a fourth House term.

McAdams served one term in Congress representing a battleground Utah seat, before being unseated by Republican Burgess Owens in 2020. But after a state judge approved a latest congressional map that created a heavily Democratic seat anchored in Salt Lake City, McAdams jumped into the race. He comfortably won his primary over more progressive opponents and stomped his way to a second term on Tuesday.

Once a high-ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee, Luria lost her Hampton Roads seat in 2022 to Republican Jen Kiggans.

But a week after Virginia Democrats posted strong showings in the commonwealth’s 2025 off-year elections, Luria launched her House comeback bid and went on to oust Kiggans on Tuesday.

Former House Intelligence Chairman Mike Rogers left the House after the 2014 elections and made his first Senate bid 10 years later. He lost to Democrat Elissa Slotkin but sought the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters the following year.

In a recent development, rogers tried to take advantage of Democratic divisions between primary winner Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens, even winning a late endorsement from the congresswoman. But it was not enough to stop El-Sayed on Tuesday.

Republican John E. Sununu served three terms in the House and one in the Senate before losing to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen in 2008. With Shaheen retiring, Sununu attempted a comeback but ended up losing decisively to Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas.

Perriello won an upset victory in a Charlottesville-anchored district in 2008 before losing reelection in the tea party wave two years later. He rolled out a comeback bid this cycle for the current version of the seat, but the Republican incumbent, John McGuire, narrowly prevailed.

Two years after losing her at-large House seat to Republican Nick Begich, Peltola chose to challenge Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The race was rocked by late revelations by The Latest York Times that top aides to Peltola’s campaign were closely involved in recruiting a second candidate named Dan Sullivan into the race to peel votes from the incumbent. As of Wednesday afternoon, Peltola was clinging to a narrow lead as votes were counted.

A Chef’s Guide to Eating and Drinking in Santo Domingo

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, on a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo.
  • According to recent reports, on the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge.
  • Bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, on a Friday night in July, Nidia Evangelista walked with her arms crossed over the Puente Flotante toward East Santo Domingo. Six lanes of traffic jockeyed inches from her left shoulder, while the black waters of the Río Ozama coursed below. “Oh my God, Oli, what are we doing?” she stated. “Nobody does this.” Evangelista is the communications manager for Santo Domingo’s most intriguing restaurant, Casarré. Her boss, Swiss Dominican chef Olivier Bur, was leading Evangelista, photographer Clay Williams, and me beyond the fortified walls of the Zona Colonial, where few travel on foot.

According to recent reports, on the other side, we turned a corner and found hundreds gathered around a dance floor in the undercroft of a bigger bridge. Live bachata drowned out the traffic overhead. Bur procured a major bottle of Presidente and plastic cups from a vendor, poured, and raised a “Salud!”.

Bur normally walks (or bikes) everywhere. Moving slowly, he’s learned the textures of the city. Still, for the next six days, he took Williams and me to his most beloved restaurants by car. We visited a string of chimi stands where hawkers compete for clientele through the night; a chicharrón spot where couples dance shoeless on the cool tile floor; and a cafeteria where boys shuffle stewed eggplant, beets, and goat to bus drivers en route. Places like these are the “infrastructure for life,” Bur said. “Thirty years ago, there was nothing else.”.

Over the last couple of decades, however, another dining scene has sprouted. Dominican chefs have returned from kitchens in Mexico, Japan, or Switzerland to explore the forgotten and sometimes shunned ingredients of their (or their parents’) homes. They served us conch, cassava, breadfruit, and djon-djon mushrooms in sashimis, foams, tostones, and surprising dessert creams. The dishes were fresh and exciting, but local and global traditions have always mingled—as such, the cuisine is not “New Dominican,” it’s simply “Dominican,” fully expressed.

Calle Andrés Julio Aybar 13+1 829 545 7503.

It has been revealed that the Piantini neighborhood was once verdant and sleepy, according to Bur. Now it’s a bustling business district. Most of the remaining vegetation decorates the façades of restaurants, like Ajualä’s. Brushed palm thatch and a bushy barba de Fidel (Fidel’s beard) tree greet you at the tall aged-steel door.

It has been revealed that venezuelan chef Saverio Stassi is a leader among the culinary new guard. His treatment of local ingredients is virtuosic. He confits guinea hen in cocoa butter and tops breadfruit tostones with local yellowfin and Cambita avocado; and over two days, his team bathes the succulent goat from the northwest—where they famously graze on wild oregano, self-infusing their meat—in Seville orange juice before roasting it in a barbacoa pit.

Calle Max Henríquez Ureña 14+1 809 547 3592.

Chef Erik Malmsten has cooked at his parents’ cabaret in Gothenburg, Sweden, at Aquavit in New York, and at Bocuse d’Or competitions around the world. But to take his career to the next level, he returned to his mother’s homeland to open a Nordic-Japanese restaurant.

Sources indicate that “You’ll see, it’s really good,” Bur told us. The meal starts with “lobster chicharrón,” with a reduced crustacean bisque, fried into airy orange sheets of bubbly crackling and served with tōgarashi Kewpie. Then, a parade of sashimi, like king fish, served with brown butter soy emulsion, ikura, and lemon zest. It ends with Dominican chocolates, molded, painted, and plated to look like koi fish on a synchronized swim.

Calle Caonabo 35+1 809 584 9481.

Sources indicate that if, like me, you come from a pizza region, you might not be inclined to use one of your Santo Domingo meal slots on a pie. But I urge you: Make time for Casa Gazcue. Spanish Dominican chef Francis Pena’s 48-hour-fermented crust comes blistered and sometimes covered in honeyed sesame seeds. Iterations are variously laden with spicy Dominican oxtail, chimi sandwich sauce, pistachio, and jamón ibérico, but you don’t have to choose: For groups, he serves a rosca (a round with an open middle) of six sections arranged like floral pizza petals.

Calle Pablo Casals+1 809 562 6060.

Industry observers note that in 1954, the Bonarelli family opened the legendary Italian restaurant Vesuvio. For decades, it was the place—the only place—to go out for a formal sit-down meal around here. Vesuvio closed over 20 years ago, but the founder’s grandson, Giancarlo Bonarelli, now runs Bottega Fratelli in a sleek modern building in Naco (Piantini’s equally upscale neighbor).

Industry observers note that you’ll notice a great variety of beet dishes in the Dominican Republic. Farmers harvest them year-round in the cool, pine-forested Costanza Valley. Try them here, roasted and served with blue cheese, chèvre, candied nuts, and honey. Also try a carpaccio of king mackerel, caught off the eastern coast, or any of the risottos, an emblem of the family’s enduring Italian culinary influence.

Calle del Seminario #57+1 809 565 1621.

Recent findings suggest that hideyoshi Tateyama’s parents opened Samurai in 1990. The restaurant joined Vesuvio, along with one or two others in that era’s small restaurant scene. It still stands out today among the many dozens.

Recent findings suggest that be sure to order the guatapaná con coco. A tried-and-true combo of shrimp and coconut imbued with native guatapaná leaf, tobiko, sesame seed, and scallion—it’s been on the menu for two decades. Also, don’t miss the chance to sample a sashimi of the meter-long “calamar diamante” from the Samaná region. It’s simply brightened with lemon zest. Meals are capped with a green tea amaro. Once a month, Tateyama personally runs a chef’s-choice omakase service.

Avenida Independencia 312+1 809 682 1433.

On the day we visited Villar Hermanos, lines formed around the block for each of two buffets. Women balanced towers of takeout containers tightly wrapped in plastic. It was the World Cup Final, and people were rushing to get some of the city’s best comfort food to their coffee tables. “This is the place to come for all the Dominican classics,” Bur told us.

We found a large table under the sprawling canopy of a banyan tree and ordered mofongo. It was moist, punctuated with crisp chicharrón crackling. The sancocho, the classic Domincan stew thick with potato and yuca starch, assumed extra body when alternating spoonfuls of broth and rice. While I didn’t have my coveted mangú and tres golpes (salami, queso frito, and eggs), I would trade my house and car to live next door and eat breakfast there every morning under the filtered sun.

Avenida San Vicente de Paúl, Santo Domingo Este 11504+1 809 244 8906.

On Avenida San Vicente de Paúl in East Santo Domingo, scooters zip down the busy street all through the night, many popping over a curb into the Plaza Del Chimi. The “plaza” is a stretch of  10 to 15 “chimi” sandwich stalls outfitted with griddles and prep stations heaped with roasted pork shoulders. Dealers quickly slice the meat, lay it on the griddle, flip it onto a squishy pan de agua roll, and top it with cabbage, tomato, and tangy pink sauce before sliding it into your mitts. The stalls are open till 6 a.m. When they run out of beer, a man runs bottles from a cooler at his house and serves them in paper bags.

Avenida Independencia KM 8+1 809 532 2580.

Across from a shopping mall on Avenida Indepencia, about a dozen cars cram into five parking spaces for the lunch or late-night staple pica pollo. Behind a crowded serving station, a woman slides eight pounds of chicken into a hotel pan, and the picking begins. Six sets of tongs compete for room, like bird beaks, snapping the chicken into styrofoam containers before barely holding them shut with strained rubber bands. Another eight pounds comes out less than two minutes later.

Industry observers note that pica pollo is one of the lasting influences of Chinese immigrants in Santo Domingo. Usually cooks marinate it in bitter orange, garlic, and oregano before coating it in flour and spice (in this case we detected Chinese five-spice) and deep-frying it to golden brown.

Avenida Cayetano Germosén+1 809 286 2141.

At Parque Mirador Sur, teens and whole families perch along concrete walls and hilltops eating fried yuca and succulent mojo-dipped chicharrón with long toothpicks. It comes from the crowded, steel-barred serving window across the street: Chicharrones Light de la Cayetano.

Among all the chicharrón we ate in the city (there was a lot), theirs stood out. There’s a small covered seating area where you can order beer to share. Bachata plays loud over a hanging speaker. Women take turns kicking off their heels to do the four-step shimmy with their jevos (boyfriends).

Calle Ciriaco Ramirez 70+1 809 689 5544.

It has been revealed that the Colmado, Bur notes, “is essential to Dominican life. Everything happens there.” For 70 years, Colmado La Venganza has anchored a prominent corner in the Don Bosco neighborhood. It’s hosted thousands of late-night domino games and sports viewing parties. We were there during the World Cup.

At the entrance, a man with a crisp-edged haircut, major sunglasses, and a pressed floral shirt parked his shoe on a milk crate while a boy polished it with a rag. Inside, groups spanning all ages gathered at high-tops and around the bar. Folks shared triple-stacked ham, pickle, and cheese sandwiches, pressed, cubed, and spiked with toothpicks: the “sándwich especial.” Leaving the bar, chef Raniel Cruz (part of our party) texted his mom in Montreal. She responded: “Wait, you’re at Venganza? I used to drink there.”.

Calle Luperón 52+1 849 460 5600.

One couldn’t understand the Dominican Republic’s vast culinary splendor in a lifetime, but if you had just one night to try, you’d want to dine at Casarré. Every Tuesday, the team takes excursions. We accompanied them to meet the countryside cooks, who wrap guáyiga root masa in leaves from the almond trees on Najayo beach and bake it in coal-covered pots. We visited a produce market, where vendors passed fruit samples, like little red “frutas milagrosas” that, when chewed beforehand, make bitter limes taste like sweet limeade.

In a recent development, at night, in a candlelit, contemplative room in the Zona Colonial, Bur and his team showcase their findings in a series of sublime, thoughtful dishes. On our visit, they presented djon-djon mushrooms from the Haitian borderlands in a sweet, guáyiga-thickened foam and in the broth of a citrusy okra and fish soup. Chef Isabella Sánchez explained: “The broth is murky, like the current state of the Río Ozama. It represents the negative aspects of our water—contamination and conflict—and the beautiful: the fish, the beaches, and our grandmother’s tea.”.

Avenida Lope de Vega 44+1 809 816 7200.

It has been revealed that smoke from an open Uruguayan-style parrilla floats in the soft light over two stories. Our waiter remarked, “We want this to feel like a Sunday asado.” Indeed, the smoke, the char, and the Malbec are there. This asado, though, also has Negronis smoked tableside and poured from a glass goose. As we awaited a perfect aged rib eye, we enjoyed paper-thin beef carpaccio with foie, and a paella-esque rice with soft leeks, cilantro, and pork trotters.

Recommendations on where to dine, shop, and stay, wherever you’re headed next.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

It takes just 25 minutes to make chicken broccoli Alfredo by combining veggies and meat in a creamy garlic and Parmesan sauce.

I love dishes that make it feel like you’re treating the family to a dinner at a restaurant, and anything with Alfredo definitely falls into that category. And yet, even though the cream sauce in this chicken broccoli Alfredo is made from scratch, it’s actually totally doable at home. (Plus there’s no need to dress up to go out to eat—you can enjoy this meal in your pajamas if you want to!).

In a recent development, there are a lot of ways to adapt this chicken Alfredo recipe using up other ingredients you might have on hand. Make it with chicken breasts as written, or swap in chicken thighs or leftover rotisserie chicken instead. Use fresh broccoli or pull those frozen florets from the freezer. Spice up the Parmesan sauce with a little extra cayenne pepper, or add a swirl of herby pesto.

Recent findings suggest that cook the fettuccine according to the package directions for al dente. Add the broccoli florets to the water for the last five minutes of cooking.

Editor’s Tip: Here’s what al dente actually means, and how to achieve it in your fettuccine and other pastas.

In a recent development, meanwhile, in a large skillet, cook the chicken and chopped onion in butter until the chicken is no longer pink. Add the minced garlic, salt and cayenne pepper, and cook for one minute longer. Stir in the flour until it’s blended with the other ingredients.

It has been revealed that gradually add the half-and-half, thawed peas and Parmesan cheese to the skillet. Bring the mixture to a boil. Cook and stir the sauce for one to two minutes or until it’s thickened.

Drain the fettuccine and broccoli, and toss them with the chicken mixture. Serve the chicken broccoli Alfredo while it’s hot.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

Once the chicken broccoli Alfredo cools, transfer it to a sealed food storage container. Store it in the refrigerator for up to four days.

It has been revealed that yes, you can prepare this dish up to three days ahead of time. Gently reheat the chicken broccoli Alfredo in a covered skillet on the stove.

The creamy sauce in this Alfredo recipe may separate and turn watery when frozen and then thawed. To protect the texture, it’s best not to freeze chicken broccoli Alfredo.

ELLIE CROWLEY FOR TASTE OF HOME.

It has been revealed that yes, you can substitute cubed chicken thighs for the chicken breast. Cook the thighs in butter until the internal temperature reaches 170°F.

In a recent development, save a little time by using meat from a cooked rotisserie chicken. Cube or shred the breast meat—or a combination of breast and dark meat. Add the chicken to the sauce near the end of cooking time to warm it through.

Yes, frozen broccoli can be substituted for fresh. Add the frozen florets to the pasta water a couple of minutes before the end of cooking time to blanch them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this pasta is the easiest way to cram an entire head of cabbage into one comforting dinner. The secret? Cooking it in butter over a long, relaxed period of time until it softens into a decadent, caramelized tangle. Paired with spaghetti, heavy cream, and some Dijon mustard and lemon zest to brighten everything up, this dish is a celebration of how versatile cabbage can be. Feel free to top your bowl with lots of fresh dill, or leave it unadorned with nothing more than an extra sprinkle of cheese.

More vegetarian pasta recipes here.

It has been revealed that cook 12 oz. spaghetti in a large pot of boiling generously salted water, stirring occasionally, until very al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid. Set aside.

In a recent development, melt 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pot over high heat. Add 1 large head of green cabbage (about 3 lb.), cored, thinly sliced, and 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring often, until cabbage is very tender and browned in spots, 18–25 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup), 1½ cups heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and reserved pasta to cabbage and toss to coat. If sauce is too thick, add pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time, tossing constantly, until glossy. Taste pasta and season with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with finely chopped dill if desired.

#42732. Meet the history-makers of the 120th Congress

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

Meet the history-makers of the 120th Congress

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1384 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that democrat Annie Andrews, here addressing supporters at her election night party in Charleston, S.C., on Tuesday, is the first woman elected to the Senate from South Carolina.
  • The incoming freshman class of the 120th Congress includes several people who scored historic wins in their states and the nation at large.
  • Among them were women breaking glass ceilings in the Senate and trailblazers for Native American representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that democrat Annie Andrews, here addressing supporters at her election night party in Charleston, S.C., on Tuesday, is the first woman elected to the Senate from South Carolina. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

The incoming freshman class of the 120th Congress includes several people who scored historic wins in their states and the nation at large.

Among them were women breaking glass ceilings in the Senate and trailblazers for Native American representation. Beyond Washington, a handful of nominees pulled off milestone victories in gubernatorial elections, including four Black candidates. Congress is also poised to witness history next year with Upcoming York Democrat Hakeem Jeffries expected to become the first Black speaker.

Here are some of the candidates who made history on election night, both in Congress and in the governor's mansions:.

Alfonso, the son-in-law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, is the first Gen Z Republican elected to Congress with his victory in Wisconsin’s open 7th District, a seat his father-in-law once held.

Andrews, a pediatrician, becomes the first woman elected to the Senate from South Carolina after defeating appointed Republican incumbent Darline Graham, the first female senator from the Palmetto State.

According to recent reports, with her victory in Newly introduced York’s 13th District, Avila Chevalier becomes the first Muslim person elected to Congress from the Empire State. She succeeds Democratic Rep. Adriano Espaillat, whom she defeated in the primary.

Benitez-Thompson, a former majority leader of the Nevada State Assembly, is the first Democrat elected to represent the state’s 2nd District since its creation after the 1980 census.

According to recent reports, with his victory over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, Colom, a district attorney, will be Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. He will also be the Magnolia State’s first Black senator elected directly by voters.

In a recent development, conely, a Navy veteran, unseats Republican Rep. Mike Lawler to become the first openly gay woman elected to Congress from New York.

Dandiya, the daughter of Indian immigrants, becomes the first South Asian American elected to Congress from Florida with her victory in the redrawn 22nd District. She is also one of the first adherents of Jainism to be elected to Congress, along with Arizona's Amish Shah (see below).

With his victory over Republican Mike Rogers, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, becomes the first Muslim person elected to the Senate.

Industry observers note that A member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, Flanagan becomes the first Native American woman elected to the Senate with her victory over Republican Michele Tafoya. The outgoing Minnesota lieutenant governor is also the first Native American to represent the state in Congress.

Ford, a state senator, unseated Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz to become the first openly gay person elected to Congress from Indiana.

Recent findings suggest that hamawy, a former Army surgeon who emigrated from Egypt to the U.S. as an infant, is the first Muslim person elected to Congress from Fresh Jersey, with his victory in the state’s 12th District.

Killin, an Army veteran and onetime chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff, is the first Democrat elected to represent Colorado’s 5th District since its creation after the 1970 census.

Kiros, who upset Rep. Diana DeGette in the Democratic primary for Colorado’s 1st District, easily won the general election to become the first Black woman elected to Congress from the Centennial State. Kiros, who was born in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and emigrated to the U.S. as an infant, is also the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress.

Koh, the son of a Korean American father and a Lebanese American mother, is the first Asian American elected to Congress from Massachusetts. The former Biden administration alumnus will succeed Democrat Seth Moulton in the state’s 6th District.

Letlow, the first Republican woman elected to the House from Louisiana, earns the same distinction in the Senate with her victory over Democrat Jamie Davis in the open-seat race to succeed GOP Sen. Bill Cassidy.

In a recent development, limtiaco will be the first Chamorro woman to represent Guam in Congress after she unseated Republican Del. James C. Moylan. She previously was the first woman to serve as U.S. attorney for the Districts of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands.

McCann, a state senator, defeated Republican Rep. Bill Huizenga to become the first Native American elected to Congress from Michigan. McCann is a member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation.

Moss, the president pro tempore of the Michigan Senate, keeps Rep. Haley Stevens’ 11th District in Democratic hands, becoming the first openly gay person elected to Congress from Michigan.

The grandson of a Mexican immigrant, Ojeda, who defeated National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, is the first Latino elected to Congress from North Carolina.

By defeating former Sen. John E. Sununu, Pappas, a fourth-term congressman, becomes the first openly gay man elected to the Senate.

The daughter of immigrants from Chile and Cuba, Powell is the first Latino person elected to Congress from Nebraska after flipping the state’s 2nd District. She is also the first Democratic woman elected to Congress from Nebraska.

It has been revealed that unofficial returns show Sarauw winning the open-seat race to succeed outgoing Del. Stacey Plaskett, making her the first openly gay person elected to Congress from the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Recent findings suggest that the son of Indian immigrants, Shah is the first South Asian American elected to Congress from Arizona. The former state legislator is also one of the first adherents of Jainism to be elected to Congress, along with Florida’s Pia Dandiya.

It has been revealed that A citizen of the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo Nation, Valdez is the first Native American elected to Congress from New York. The New York State assemblywoman will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez.

Wiener, a state senator who succeeds former Speaker Nancy Pelosi in California’s 11th District, is the first openly gay person elected to represent San Francisco in Congress.

Industry observers note that with her victory over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, Acton becomes the first woman elected governor of Ohio. Republican Nancy Hollister briefly served as the state’s top executive in the late 1990s but was never elected governor.

In a recent development, the son of Mexican immigrants, Becerra, a former congressman and Health and Human Services secretary, is the first Latino to be elected governor of California. He is the state’s second Latino governor after Romualdo Pacheco, who was never elected to the role but briefly succeeded an incumbent in 1875.

Blackburn, Tennessee’s first female senator, will soon become the Volunteer State’s first female governor after her victory over Democrat Jerri Green.

#42731. Breaking: Red-Wine-Braised Short Ribs

📅 16 Aug 2011 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (785 w)
📖 Baca

Breaking: Red-Wine-Braised Short Ribs

📅 16 Aug 2011 | ⏱️ 4 min read (785 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These red-wine-braised short ribs have fans.
  • It has been revealed that flavor builds in layers: The bone-in beef is browned, then the onions, carrots, and celery cook in its drippings.
  • Even better: You can make the ribs a day ahead, leaving little to do before dinner but reheat them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These red-wine-braised short ribs have fans. “This has been my go-to recipe for short ribs for as long as I can remember,” states one commenter. “It never fails.” It’s the kind of special-occasion dish you make once and return to forever.

It has been revealed that flavor builds in layers: The bone-in beef is browned, then the onions, carrots, and celery cook in its drippings. A full bottle of dry red wine reduces by half before the broth goes in; a whole head of garlic and plenty of fresh herbs round out the braise. After that, a few hours in the oven turn the meat fall-off-the-bone tender.

Even better: You can make the ribs a day ahead, leaving little to do before dinner but reheat them. Serve over mashed potatoes, soft polenta, or wide egg noodles to soak up every drop of the rich sauce.

What kind of short ribs should I buy?

It has been revealed that look for meaty, bone-in English-cut short ribs, with a single rib bone beneath each piece of meat. Ask your butcher to cut them crosswise into 2" lengths—you’re not expected to saw through the bones at home. Avoid the thin strips sold for grilling.

What’s the best wine for braised short ribs?

It has been revealed that choose a dry red wine you’d enjoy drinking. Cabernet Sauvignon is the recipe’s first choice, but Merlot or a Rhône-style red also fits the bill. There’s no need to splurge; save your special bottle for the table.

Drawbridge Cabernet Sauvignon 2024.

Do I have to strain the vegetables?

Sources indicate that for the smooth sauce intended here, yes. The vegetables flavor the braising liquid, and straining removes them along with the herb stems, bay leaves, and garlic skins.

For a more rustic approach, pluck out the herbs and garlic skins (leave the cloves behind) and use an immersion blender to purée the cooked vegetables into the sauce.

How do I know when short ribs are done?

Recent findings suggest that start checking after 2 hours in the oven. A fork should slide into the meat easily, and a gentle twist should pull it apart. If the meat still resists, keep braising. The listed cooking time is a guide, not a hard stop.

Can I make these short ribs ahead, and how should I reheat them?

According to recent reports, yes. Finish cooking the ribs and strain the sauce, then refrigerate the ribs with their sauce in shallow containers within 2 hours of cooking. The next day, lift off the hardened fat. Transfer the ribs and sauce to an ovenproof pot or baking dish, cover, and reheat in a 350° oven until hot throughout—the meat should reach 165° in the center.

Save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app.

Try this recipe with this expert pick from the Bon Appétit Wine Shop.

Staub Enameled Cast Iron Round Dutch Oven 7-Qt.

Preheat oven to 350°. Season 5 lb. bone-in beef short ribs, cut crosswise into 2" pieces by your butcher, with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Working in 2 batches, cook short ribs, turning occasionally, until browned on all sides, about 8 minutes per batch. Transfer to a plate. Pour off all but 3 Tbsp. drippings from pot.

Cook 3 medium onions, chopped, 3 medium carrots, peeled, chopped, and 2 celery stalks, chopped, in same pot over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onions are browned, about 5 minutes. Add 3 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and 1 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until combined and deep red, 2–3 minutes.

Sources indicate that stir in one 750-ml bottle dry red wine (preferably Cabernet Sauvignon), then add short ribs along with any juices that have accumulated on the plate. Bring to a boil; reduce heat to medium and simmer until wine is reduced by half, about 25 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, halved crosswise, 10 sprigs parsley, 8 sprigs thyme, 4 sprigs oregano, 2 sprigs rosemary, and 2 fresh or dried bay leaves; stir in 4 cups low-sodium beef broth. Bring to a boil, cover, and transfer pot to oven. Braise until short ribs are tender, 2–2½ hours.

Uncover pot and transfer short ribs to a platter. Strain sauce through a fine-mesh sieve into a heatproof measuring glass; spoon fat from surface and discard. Season sauce with salt and pepper. Arrange ribs in shallow bowls, over mashed potatoes if desired, and spoon sauce over.

#42729. Alexis Nikole Nelson, aka the Black Forager, Makes Nature Her Buffet

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1990 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Saveur ↗ Open Full Page

Alexis Nikole Nelson, aka the Black Forager, Makes Nature Her Buffet

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people.
  • According to recent reports, alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community.
  • Nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is Amused Bouche, SAVEUR’s food questionnaire that explores the culinary curiosities of some of our favorite people. This interview series will dive deep into their food routines, including dinner party strategies, cherished cookbooks, and the memorable bites they’d hop on a flight for.

According to recent reports, alexis Nicole Nelson’s life mantra is simple: “Don’t put things in your face hole unless you know what they are!” This mostly applies to foraging wild foods, something she has been doing since she was a kid with her mom and has since turned into a flourishing career and community. She has showcased her adventures and recipes as @blackforager since 2018 (with millions of curious followers across Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube) and now in her debut cookbook, Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! This comprehensive guide to finding and cooking with ingredients from your backyard or nearby forests and fields is organized by season and anchored by Nelson’s vibrant personality and boundless energy, encouraging readers to get out of their comfort zones and educate themselves on edible plants hiding in plain sight.

Nelson’s journey to becoming the Black Forager started with an interest in vegetarianism as a 5-year-old, which, at the time, was discouraged by her family. “You have to finish growing first!” Nelson recalls her mom saying. Nelson ate meat products to keep from wasting food her parents prepared until she was 12, when she decided to start packing her own lunches. “It was a lot of undressed Boca burgers and French fries. It was a bleak time,” she admits with a laugh. She went fully vegan at 24 and hasn’t looked back.

I am not a very outdoorsy person, but I was captivated by the whimsical way Nelson goes about foraging and sharing online, and even more so after chatting with her on a recent Zoom call. When I asked for easy gateway foraging ideas, she immediately suggested field garlic or onion grass: “I am a biased party, because that is the first forageable that my mom taught me. Once you notice it, you see it everywhere, and it has a foolproof test, which is the smell test. If you break it and it doesn’t very fragrantly smell of onions and garlic, you have the wrong plant. Easy, easy!” She recommended looking for little purple flowers or round pink spiky balls, and on my next walk with my dogs, I spotted some. I haven’t picked and cooked with any yet, but now I’m on the lookout (and smell-out) for this abundant allium and initiative on pairing it with the maitake bacon recipe from her book. Nelson suggested making a “BLT-adjacent sandwich with whatever mild greens are in season, a slice of tomato, and maitake bacon on toasty sourdough.”.

According to recent reports, whether you’re a foraging beginner or an expert, Nelson’s edition of Amused Bouche will be equally eye-opening and mouthwatering. Read on for her adventures and misadventures in the fields and in her home kitchen.

If you could only eat one thing 24/7/365, what would it be?

Recent findings suggest that I love a tofu scramble and mixing in whatever is in season, and I bring home mushrooms, greens, and aromatics. In the springtime, it’ll be ramp leaves and oyster mushrooms. In the summer, it’s chanterelle and bicolor bolete with some nodding onion flowers from my front yard. As we move into winter, I’m thankful that we get enoki mushrooms pretty consistently all throughout the season in the woods. I do a combo of firm silken and super-firm tofu because I want the best of both worlds. Eggs don’t just have one texture; the whites and yolks are different, and I always want to try to get as close to eggs as I can with my tofu textures. I’m perpetually on a search for a forageable legume that I can make my own tofu with. One of my friends, Jesse Akozbek (@feralforaging), makes tofu with black walnuts.

What’s the first thing you learned how to cook?

The first thing that I remember cooking is baking cakes with my dad—usually just a basic frosted vanilla cake. My mom used to be a cool head-honcho character at Procter & Gamble, and she would be gone for two or three weeks at a time for work. We’d bake the cake the night before [she got back], frost it, and then just before she came home, we’d leave the cake out and hide.

How about your latest kitchen adventure?

I broke out my food mill because I went a little overboard harvesting cornelian cherries with my fiancé this year. They’re fun to harvest, and we brought a step stool to reach more and ended up going home with a couple gallons of fruit. It’s all fun and games until you see them all on the counter and realize they’re gonna go bad so I gotta figure out what I’m doing with all of this. I thought of doing a glacé cornelian cherry like I’ve done with chestnuts before, but the water content of the cherries is so high that when I simmered them in a sugar syrup, they just disintegrated and disappeared. I tried to stir it carefully, but it all just turned into goo. I fished them out with my little spider, put them in my food mill, and ground it. They have massive ol’ pits on the inside, and I am not trying to eat any of those. It was an applesauce consistency in the end, but like what if applesauce had dreams? What if applesauce was the star of a Studio Ghibli movie? I made cornelian cherry shortcakes with it, and my fiancé was like, “So I’ve had three…” and we realized that when you eat a lot of fruit and fiber at once, you remember it later. I also saved the flavored syrup that was created after straining out all of the goopy fruits, and I am saving it specifically for making Shirley Temples!

What’s your treat-yourself splurge?

My favorite way to treat myself is getting dinner with my fiancé at Agni, an amazing Bengali American fusion restaurant here in Columbus, led by my friend, chef Avishar Barua! They have these french fries that take three days to make, and I—no joke—dream about them sometimes.

What’s your most cherished cookbook?

In a recent development, marie Viljoen’s Forage, Harvest, Feast is the cookbook that highlighted me as a recent college graduate that foraging, the weird thing I’ve been doing since childhood, could become such elevated cuisine. It’s absolutely stunning, and she is a recipe and photography genius—she does it all! I remember checking that book out from the library for the first time and my jaw dropping at how she used foraged foods in ways I had never even let myself consider. She gets shouted out in my cookbook because I used a few of her recipes as a jumping-off point then over time I started changing things to make them my own. A decade later, it becomes something different but still has the heart of that original recipe, like my milkweed nectar is definitely the child of her milkweed cordial! Her book was eye-opening for me even before I knew this was what I was going to end up making my career, back when it was something I just did because I loved it and I was a poor recent grad. A really great way to spruce up a 59-cent pack of ramen is wild greens and mushrooms!

Is there a cooking disaster that made you swear off a dish forever?

Recent findings suggest that I keep doing this thing where I start fermenting drinks and then travel, which is dumb. Don’t do that! My most explosive ferment was actually not mine, it was a gift from fellow foraging friend Gabrielle Cerberville (@chaoticforager). She very kindly brought me a bottle of her wild plum wine, and I did not put it straight into the fridge because I was not using my noggin. Three days later, I went to open it to pair with dinner, and it was like my world was in slow motion and it was just a geyser everywhere! Wine on the ceiling, wine on the walls, a lot of wine on the floor, a lot of wine on me. I cleaned it up sadly, shooing my pets away. No drunk pets! I also had a milkweed cordial explode, which meant I had to scrub sticky pink off every single thing in the refrigerator. Do not recommend it.

Which nostalgic foods from childhood bring you the most comfort?

Sources indicate that I grew up in the Cincinnati area, so there will be a soft spot in my heart for Cincinnati chili forever. It’s just ingrained within me. Thankfully Skyline has vegan rice and beans using the same spices that you can also put onto pasta like a wild Ohioan. That will always taste like a Friday evening with my dad, because my mom is from Newly introduced England and famously hates Cincinnati chili. I think calling it a chili was maybe its biggest downfall—when you learn about the history behind it and how it’s actually the child of a Greek meat sauce, suddenly the spice palette makes so much more sense. I think people would be so much cooler with that, but everyone’s expecting Tex-Mex chili, and that is not what you are signing up for!

When you’re playing dinner party DJ, what’s spinning?

There was a podcast I was obsessed with called The Dinner Party Download a decade ago, and I named my playlist after that. It has been evolving throughout the past 10 years and has Mitski, which I know feels sad for a dinner party but it’s mellow, some alt-J, Bill Withers, The Contours. A lot of Motown-era music, like The Supremes, Stevie Wonder, The Four Tops, Staple Singers. And then Janelle Monáe, Kate Nash, “Rhapsody in Blue” by George Gershwin is thrown in there. I go all over the place, but I think it creates a general buzzy atmosphere. I don’t want it to necessarily be as dancey as a dance party, but I also don’t want people to fall asleep, either.

What is your biggest entertaining flex to impress guests?

I really love plating things and cutting things into fun shapes and making them look pretty. I took a cooking class in Japan with Elizabeth Andoh, a very prolific cookbook writer, a couple of years ago, and after my fiancé and I walked out of it, we were just like, “Dang, our food’s real ugly!” A huge part of her class was how much presentation matters and how the first way that you are consuming the food is with your sight, with your eyes, so why not make it look cute?

Tell me about a meal so good you would hop on a flight to relive it.

While my fiancé and I were in Florence for a friend’s wedding, we knew that Italy, historically, was not the easiest place to be vegan. You can find things but maybe not that many things, and maybe not the things that look as good as the things everybody else is eating. So I was big sad the entire time until we stumbled into a tiny hole-in-the-wall vegan restaurant called Il Vegano. We found it on Google by searching “vegan restaurants near me,” and it had the best pasta with tomato sauce and tiramisù that either of us have ever had. Mind you, my fiancé is not vegan and very much could still eat real tiramisù and did on that trip. And the night ended with us essentially begging in broken Italian for the head chef to write a cookbook. We waddled back to our hotel saying it was the best meal we’ve ever had.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Latest Update: Chicken Francese

📅 21 Jul 2021 | ⏱️ 3 min read (602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chicken Francese is a staple at your favorite Italian restaurants.
  • Francese is a preparation (much like Milanese) that can be used with all types of meat and seafood from shrimp to veal.
  • It might seem strange, but it’s such an iconic flavor/texture combination.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chicken Francese is a staple at your favorite Italian restaurants. But sometimes, you don't want to empty your wallet for this classic dinner favorite. That's where I come in!

Francese is a preparation (much like Milanese) that can be used with all types of meat and seafood from shrimp to veal. For chicken, it involves dredging cutlets in flour and beaten egg, creating a pseudo batter. The cutlets are then pan-fried and made crispy, albeit temporarily. See, chicken Francese is one of those dishes that epitomizes "crispy gone soggy"—a texture sensation that is one of my absolute favorites. In this case, the chicken becomes "soggy" because you finish them by simmering in a rich, lemony sauce that will knock your socks off.

It might seem strange, but it’s such an iconic flavor/texture combination. Also, it is very easy to make and comes together in under an hour. What could be better?!

Place 1 chicken breast on a cutting board. Using a sharp chef’s knife held parallel to the cutting board, slice into the thickest side of the breast, cutting three-quarters of the way through. Fold the top piece back (as if you were opening a book) and continue to cut until the breast is divided into 2 thinner cutlets. Repeat with the remaining chicken breast for a total of 4 cutlets. Working one piece at a time, place each cutlet between 2 sheets of plastic wrap. Using a meat mallet or the bottom of a small heavy skillet, pound the chicken to about 1/4" thick. Season all over with salt and pepper.

Recent findings suggest that in a shallow dish, beat eggs, garlic powder, and a pinch of salt. Pour 1/2 cup flour into another shallow dish.

In a recent development, in a large, heavy skillet over medium heat, heat oil. Working in batches, coat cutlets in flour, shaking off excess, then dip into the egg mixture, turning to coat.

Place cutlets in the oil, being careful not to overcrowd the skillet, and cook, turning halfway through, until golden brown, 5 to 7 minutes.

Transfer cutlets to a paper towel-lined plate to drain and season with salt and pepper.

It has been revealed that wipe out the skillet, then heat over medium heat. Add five Tbsp. butter and the remaining one Tbsp. flour, stirring until just beginning to foam and the butter is melted, 3 to 5 minutes. Whisk in wine. Increase heat to medium-high and bring to a boil. Cook, stirring, until slightly reduced, 1 to 2 minutes. Add stock, lemon zest, and lemon juice and return to a boil. Reduce heat to medium and cook, whisking constantly, until the sauce is reduced by about one-third, 3 to 5 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add lemon slices and remaining 1 Tbsp. butter and cook, stirring, until the sauce is glossy, 2 to 3 minutes more.

Return chicken to the sauce and cook, turning halfway through, until heated through, 2 to 3 minutes.

Industry observers note that transfer chicken to a platter and pour the sauce over. Top with lemon slices and parsley.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

To complete your Italian feast, serve this chicken up with fresh garlic bread and a simple salad topped with red wine vinaigrette.

According to recent reports, if you have any leftovers, store them in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Luckily, this dish is used to being a tad soggy and lends itself well to being reheated in the microwave.
