It has been revealed that since I grew up in Los Angeles and had never heard of buttermilk pie, it may come as a surprise that it’s one of my go-to pies to make. I discovered it seven years ago on a Twitter thread about unique, regional pies and was fascinated enough by this classic Southern dessert to attempt it, trying the first recipe that came up on my Google search. This is that recipe, and it has been consistently easy and perfect since that very first pie I made. The filling is smooth and velvety with subtle notes of nutmeg and a kiss of lemon. It reminds me of dan tat, or Chinese egg tarts, but it’s way less fussy. Yes, you can make your own pie crust, but storebought works well here, too, because the real star is the wobbly buttermilk custard. — Kat Thompson, audience editor.

When fall comes around, I turn to this tried and true caramelized onion and butternut squash tart from Food 52 over and over again. It’s a perfect savory option to bring to Friendsgiving, Thanksgiving, or any autumnal get together. What I love most about it is that it highlights flavors and ingredients of the season while standing out from the plentiful pumpkin and pecan pies that you’re sure to find at any gathering. To make it heartier, I sometimes add crumbled sausage to the mix. — Terri Ciccone, deputy director of audience development.

The only thing my mom and I love more than re-invigorating this incredibly simple chess pie recipe is telling the (most likely made up) story behind the name. Trying on my grandmother’s Texas twang, we explain how a server at a diner was once asked the flavor of the custard pie that day. She stated, “It’s just pie,” but with her Southern accent that was mistaken as “chess pie.” And so we got this simple custard pie, which is filled with evaporated milk and set perfectly with cornmeal. My mom started experimenting with adding edible lavender oil to the recipe, which has became my favorite way to bake it, but she’s also added a tablespoon or two of my dad’s “Mexican mocha” (spiced hot chocolate) mix to make an incredible chocolate custard pie with a kick. But even plain, this pie recipe is always a substantial hit. — Emily Venezky, social media manager.

I have nothing but the utmost respect for people who lovingly make intricately crafted, high-maintenance pies with lattice crusts and the whole shebang, but my personal tried-and-true, always-go-back pie recipe is one I’ve frequently revisited since high school: no-bake chocolate peanut butter pie. I do not know the true origin of the semi-homemade, Sandra Lee-esque creation, but if you stumble upon some version of the five-ish-ingredient recipe that includes Cool Whip, like this one on the blog Crazy for Crust, that’s what I’m referring to. Rest assured that I generally have the taste and standards of a bougie person, but this extremely simple, absolutely-not-healthy recipe is just perfection. It’s sweet, salty, creamy, and simultaneously light, fluffy, rich, and decadent. Whenever I make it for a dinner party, holiday gathering, or potluck, it garners rave reviews (the word “orgasmic” has been used to describe it more than once). And as a child of the ‘90s, I love using an Oreo crust and Skippy peanut butter — forever crowd-pleasers. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

“We have Milk Bar at home, honey” is what comes to mind whenever I make this pie, which reminds me of the Fresh York City bakery’s famous, albeit once salaciously named dessert (now called the Milk Bar Pie). This butterscotch pie from Smitten Kitchen packs the same gooey, buttery taste and a satisfyingly sticky consistency — I feel like it’s a pie for people who wish they could just eat caramelized graham cracker crusts and custards for dessert. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Anna Theoktisto, Southern Living.

Recent findings suggest that this zingy citrus pie might evoke summertime, but that’s exactly why I make sure it’s on the table during the holidays. Somewhere between a lemon pie and an icebox pudding, Atlantic Beach Pie delivers the bracing acidity I crave after a marathon of rich food. It originated at a North Carolina seafood restaurant, acting as a clever loophole to the old wives’ tale that eating dessert after a seafood meal could be deadly. Believe the lore or not, this pie is bound to earn seconds, whether for its salty, buttery saltine crust, zippy custard filling, or cloud of velvety whipped cream. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Claudia Fleming, adapted by Amanda Hesser for the Newly introduced York Times.

In a recent development, I am not a pie person, per se — I hate the pressure of making a flaky crust — but I don’t mind the less-stress approach of making a tart, which asks only that I press dough into a tart pan. This famous chocolate caramel tart, a version of which my mom made frequently when I was growing up, is a dish I would definitely have on my roster if Mythical Kitchen ever invited me onto Last Meals. With dark chocolate ganache, a caramel filling that’s made more complex by the addition of salt and creme fraiche, and a sprinkling of a little more flaky salt on top, it tastes like a slightly more sophisticated Twix Bar.

I once asked my mom to make it for an ex-boyfriend, with me talking it up to him as my favorite dessert ever, and when he told me it was “just okay” — and who says that, especially when presented with a free dessert that required the dessert-giver to make a caramel? — that was the final sign I needed that he was not the one for me. Lesson learned: My husband and I are very dessert-compatible. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Josh Walker & Duolan Li, Bon Appétit.

#42694. Breaking: Scientists Discover a Disturbing Link Between Cannabis Use and Earlier Psychosis

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1172 w)

Breaking: Scientists Discover a Disturbing Link Between Cannabis Use and Earlier Psychosis

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In studies where psychosis typically emerged at age 30 or later, cannabis customers experienced it more than six years earlier, raising questions about cannabis use throughout adulthood.
  • Most discussions about cannabis and mental health focus on teenagers, but latest research suggests the conversation should extend into adulthood.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers at UNSW Sydney examined 149 studies involving more than 71,000 people, largely conducted in Europe, North America, and Australia since 2011.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In studies where psychosis typically emerged at age 30 or later, cannabis customers experienced it more than six years earlier, raising questions about cannabis use throughout adulthood.

Most discussions about cannabis and mental health focus on teenagers, but latest research suggests the conversation should extend into adulthood. A large analysis found that among people who developed psychosis, cannabis customers experienced their first episode an average of two and a half years earlier than non-users. The findings reveal a consistent association, although they do not prove that cannabis caused the difference.

Recent findings suggest that researchers at UNSW Sydney examined 149 studies involving more than 71,000 people, largely conducted in Europe, North America, and Australia since 2011. The analysis, published in Biological Psychiatry, focused mostly on people with schizophrenia.

Psychosis can involve hallucinations, delusions, disordered thinking, and changes in behavior. It is associated with schizophrenia and other mental illnesses and typically emerges in late adolescence or early adulthood. According to Psychosis Australia, up to 3% of adults experience a diagnosed disorder involving psychosis during their lifetime.

Industry observers note that the researchers found that the age difference between cannabis users and non-users grew in studies where psychosis developed later in life. When the average age of onset was between 20 and 24, cannabis users experienced their first episode 1.6 years earlier. That difference increased to 4.43 years in studies with an average onset between ages 25 and 29, reaching 6.3 years when the average onset was 30 or older.

Chief investigator Matthew Large, a psychiatrist and Conjoint Professor at UNSW’s School of Clinical Medicine, noted the findings suggest that the effects of cannabis use may accumulate over time.

It has been revealed that “We’ve tended to focus on the dangers of using cannabis in adolescence, when the brain is still developing, but the risk doesn’t disappear once you’re in your 20s,” Prof. Large said. “What we’re seeing suggests a cumulative effect, where harm builds up over time, a bit like alcohol or nicotine.”.

In a recent development, interestingly, the researchers found no statistically significant difference in the age of psychosis onset between teenagers who used cannabis and those who did not. However, because psychosis rarely develops before the mid-teens, there is a limited window in which researchers could detect an earlier onset.

In a recent development, “There may be a biological floor, in that there is only so much earlier that onset can be shifted. In younger groups, strong development, genetic or other psychosis risk factors may dominate, making any cannabis-related age shift harder to detect,” Prof. Large stated.

According to recent reports, the analysis builds on previous research led by Large. A smaller 2011 meta-analysis found that psychosis began 2.7 years earlier among cannabis owners, while a 2015 analysis found that psychosis typically developed 6.3 years after cannabis use began. Those earlier studies lacked sufficient data to compare different age groups.

Lead author Carly Stevens, from UNSW’s School of Biomedical Sciences, said the new age comparisons challenge the idea that delaying cannabis use until adulthood necessarily avoids its potential psychiatric risks.

“What we’ve found challenges the assumption that you’ll be fine if you wait to smoke weed until your mid-20s; that’s just not the case,” Ms Stevens said.

“There’s been so much emphasis on adolescents not smoking cannabis, which is important, but we need to broaden the warnings for everyone.”.

In a recent development, an notable limitation is that the research cannot establish whether cannabis directly causes psychosis or makes it develop earlier. Doing so would require experiments that deliberately expose people to potential harm, which Large said would be unethical. The findings also do not establish how likely an individual cannabis user is to develop psychosis.

“But the consistency of the evidence, particularly the strong effect in older adults who likely have been using cannabis for longer, does support the theory that cannabis plays a causal role in the timing of psychosis onset, and possibly the onset of some cases among people who would not have otherwise developed psychosis.”.

Sources indicate that for people who do develop psychosis, the timing of their first episode can affect notable stages of life. Stevens noted that even a difference of a few years could interfere with opportunities that might otherwise shape someone’s future.

“People may miss out on study, job opportunities, travel and relationships in those years, and treatment can come with physical side effects that can make life harder as well,” she noted.

Large believes reducing or stopping cannabis use could offer meaningful benefits if it helps delay psychosis, although the analysis did not directly test that possibility.

“It’s a major illness, which robs you of your shared reality with family, friends and all those around you,” he said. “If we can delay psychosis by even a few years, people will be more likely to reach crucial milestones in education and training, and develop strong support networks, which can protect against psychosocial decline.”.

Delaying the onset of psychosis could also ease pressure on healthcare systems. According to Large, psychotic disorders account for up to 3% of health-related expenditure in developed nations.

The researchers believe their findings support clearer public health warnings about the potential psychiatric consequences of cannabis use, even while questions about causation remain unresolved.

“We can’t run direct experiments, so we have to go with the best evidence available,” Prof. Large said. “In my view, the threshold for health warnings about cannabis and psychosis has definitely been met.”.

One concern is the expanding use of medical cannabis. Large said he has treated a growing number of people with psychosis who had been prescribed cannabis for conditions where evidence of benefit remains limited. He worries that its medical applications can lead people to underestimate potential risks.

“It’s got this therapeutic halo around it, which blinds people to the risk.”.

Recent findings suggest that the increasing popularity of cannabis edibles raises additional questions. Some products can contain higher concentrations of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the main compound responsible for cannabis’s psychoactive effects.

Large also sees opportunities for harm reduction through cannabis legalization. Although legalization could increase access, government oversight could allow authorities to regulate THC potency, improve consumer education, and introduce requirements aimed at helping buyers understand potential health risks.

Recent findings suggest that “You could tax it, regulate it, and require people to show they understand the risks before buying,” Prof. Large noted.

For now, the researchers want to better understand the biological mechanisms that might connect prolonged cannabis exposure with the timing of psychosis. They are calling for more research involving older cannabis customers, particularly as medical cannabis and high-potency products become more widely available.

Future studies will also need clearer, standardized measures of cannabis exposure to determine how different patterns and durations of use relate to psychosis onset.

Reference: “Cannabis Use and Age-Related Acceleration of Psychosis Onset: A Meta-Analysis” by Carly Stevens, Hannah Pincham and Matthew Large, 18 August 2026, Biological Psychiatry. DOI: 10.1016/j.biopsych.2026.06.025.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as the oldest observable light in the cosmos, the Cosmic Microwave Background is a fundamental signal that has a lot to teach us about the Universe.
  • But the CMB has also changed over time with the expansion of the Universe.
  • Recent findings suggest that two space telescopes have played important roles in mapping the CMB: the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probee (WMAP), and the Planck satellite.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as the oldest observable light in the cosmos, the Cosmic Microwave Background is a fundamental signal that has a lot to teach us about the Universe. It dates back to the recombination epoch, when photons could first travel freely through the cosmos. The CMB is like a snapshot of the state of energy and matter about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

But the CMB has also changed over time with the expansion of the Universe. As the Universe has expanded, the CMB has been stretched into microwave wavelengths that we can't see. That's why, despite containing the overwhelming majority of the Universe's photons, we can't see it without the help of telescopes.

Recent findings suggest that two space telescopes have played important roles in mapping the CMB: the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probee (WMAP), and the Planck satellite. They were both up above the obscuring effect of Earth's atmosphere, which is the main obstacle to observing the CMB. The CMB is nearly uniform, but not quite. It has tiny irregularities that cosmologist have mapped in increasing detail. These small temperature inhomogeneities can reveal a lot about the Universe and the Massive Bang.

In a recent development, this is the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe's heat map of temperature fluctuations in the Cosmic Microwave Background. (Credit : NASA / WMAP Science Team).

In a recent development, but there's also another way of studying the CMB. The South Pole Telescope is a 10-meter radio telescope in Antarctica that takes advantage of a small atmospheric window to observe part of the CMB. It's also in a designated "radio-quiet zone." It's credited with discovering a new feature of the CMB called the B-mode polarization. Gravitational lensing by intervening matter like galaxy clusters created this B-mode polarization. That proved that the CMB can hold evidence of gravitatonal effects.

It has been revealed that that was a substantial deal because the polarization had been predicted decades earlier. The CMB's polarization is almost perfectly uniform. But almost isn't completely, and there are tiny variations in the B-mode polarity. In this case, these tiny changes were created by intervening matter.

Recent findings suggest that the CMB's polarization was first detected in 2002, and that was a massive accomplishment. John Carlstrom from the University of Chicago led the collaboration that detected it, and he is now the director of the South Pole Telescope. âWe were sitting around with a small team, looking at our computer. There were peaks and wiggles, just as predicted,â Carlstrom remarked. âWe were just staring at it and it was just phenomenal.â.

It has been revealed that the South Pole Telescope hard at work during the long polar night. Image Credit: Report of the U.S. Antarctic Program Blue Ribbon Panel - More and Better Science in Antarctica Through Increased Logistical Effectiveness, Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/25790806.

It has been revealed that âItâs one of the ways that we can understand gravity at these very extreme scales,â said Kimmy Wu, an assistant professor at the California Institute of Technology, one of the institutions involved in the south pole observations. âThe fact that there could be primordial gravitational waves means that at the early fraction of a second when the universe was quantum fluctuations, gravity worked.â.

Quantum gravity can only be detected in this very early fraction of a second. It's beyond the capabilities of supercolliders to examine, and these tiny waves are the only way to observe quantum gravity. If quantum gravity can be detected in the very first moments of the Universe, then it can help physicists bridge the gap between General Relativity, which describes things on a massive scale, and quantum physics, which describes things on a tiny scale. So finding these tiny primordial gravitational waves brings us closer to a unified theory of how everything works. That would be nice; just ask any physicist.

It has been revealed that this graphic helps explain the complicated problem facing physicists. If they can detect B-mode polarization in the CMB, it's evidence that quantum fluctuations generated primordial gravitational waves. Image Credit: By Original: DrbogdanâVector: Yinweichen - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/31825049.

But as stated earlier, these first B-mode detections were due to gravitational lensing, not quantum gravity. The next natural question was, can the B-mode contain evidence of primordial, quantum gravity? A fresh instrument was needed to find out.

Next to the South Pole Telescope is the Background Imaging of Cosmic Extragalactic Polarization (BICEP) array. BICEP was built to measure the B-mode polarization of the CMB that come directly from quantum gravity. The current iteration of BICEP is the fifth, and overall, it's been working since 2006.

Sources indicate that if BICEP can detect these tiny gravitational ripples from the Universe's very beginnings, then our understanding of the tiniest workings of the Universe will take shape. It would provide the most robust evidence for inflation and Significant Bang cosmology.

In a recent development, members of the BICEP team in front of BICEP. The array is articulated and sits inside a specially designed protective blue windproof and thermally insulated cover. Image Credit: BICEP Array.

âIf we could detect these B-modes robustly, then itâs bulletproof,â said Lindsey Bleem, a physicist at DOEâs Argonne National Laboratory who worked at the South Pole in 2008 and 2014.

If they can rule out these B-modes, then physicists need to revise models of inflation or work on other ones. Either way, it's progress.

It has been revealed that but there's another mode of CMB polarization called E-mode. They are both weaker and harder to detect than temperature fluctuations in the CMB. In fact, the E-mode is only one-tenth as strong as the temperature fluctuations, and the B-mode is even weaker.

Recent findings suggest that âWe are here in the business of making a super, super precise measurement. This is basically a few nanokelvin on top of the 2.725 [degrees] of the CMB,â said Zeeshan Ahmed, associate professor at Stanford University and researcher at DOEâs SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory.

This image shows an illustration of the Planck satellite over the satellite's map of the CMB. It's work was an improvement of the WMAP's map. Image Credit: ESA and the Planck Collaboration - D. Ducros.

In a recent development, when measuring something so faint, interference becomes a major problem. Other radiation sources can pollute signals, the Milky Way's dust can add its own polarization, and some E-modes can transform into B-modes. It all adds up to one of the most complicated challenges in science.

Sources indicate that but the SPT and BICEP each have different strengths, and by working together, scientists think they can find a way forward. âItâs like a marriage,â said Bleem. âBICEP has the intense sensitivity at large scales and SPT can make these wonderful gravitational lensing maps, without which BICEP would be completely limited by the systematics. Together, they can achieve the targeted goals.â.

Other telescopes like Herschel and Planck contribute too, by sorting out and mapping sources of interference in the signal that can lense the E-mode signal.

In a recent development, âIf there is a signal, you should be able to see that in both places,â noted Wu. âThese are excellent ways to really check whether a claim of detection is substantiated.â.

According to recent reports, that was an important step. It provided a way to determine what E-modes had been warped by gravity to appear like B-modes. That was a potential way through the mess.

âBeing able to measure that signal for the first time â¦ was very exciting,â recalled Carlstrom.

In 2014, the BICEP2 team presented a paper to their peers showing that they had detected B-mode polarization indicating a gravitational wave signal from inflation. Their excitement was short-lived though. Subsequent examination and new data from other researchers revealed that the signal could be attributed to the Milky Way's problematic dust.

According to recent reports, this image illustrates how the Milky Way's dust can polarize the CMB. Image Credit: ESA.

âWe dialed up our skepticism on these things in the last ten years,â said Ahmed, who works on the BICEP Array. âIf fresh data is coming in and it can be co-analyzed with ours, we would love that.â.

According to recent reports, work continues on this complicated problem, and the potential payoff is so monumental that setbacks aren't deterring the researchers. They continue to work on eliminating sources of uncertainty in the data.

It has been revealed that they're getting a better handle on how gravitational lensing affects data and how to understand what mode of polarization they're sensing. They're improving instrument precision and eliminating more noise. Upcoming improvements to both the South Pole Telescope and BICEP will drive further progress.

It has been revealed that for now, there's no unambiguous detection of primordial gravitational waves. But work continues in the extreme conditions at the bottom of the world, with ever-improving telescopes and the apparent unbreakable will of the dedicated researchers.

âIt is really rewarding to see the SPT. When I started working on it, it was just a proposal â we hadnât built the telescope yet,â said Benson. âThe fact that we can still do cutting-edge science with it and sustaining it over 20 years has been really satisfying.â.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As Democrats continue their victory lap after their massive wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer greets House Minority Whip Katherine Clark at the Center for American Progress Action Fund’s “Results to Roadmap” event on Thursday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

As Democrats continue their victory lap after their massive wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

For Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, it bears repeating that “the Democrats aren’t all exactly the same.”.

“The most important lesson of this whole election, and one we all need to internalize if we’re going to truly build a durable majority, is populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said at a Center for American Progress Action Fund event on Thursday.

Voters are expecting results as Democrats claim a mandate to address costs and corruption. “Our majority will be measured against one test and one test only: Have we made your life better?” Schumer remarked.

He acknowledged, however, that their intends could run into a President Donald Trump-sized wall: the presidential veto.

It has been revealed that “Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’  intransigence, of course not. But I will promise the American people: The Democratic Party will fight to make your life more affordable, your government more competent, your capital less corrupt, bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes for you to feel the difference,” Schumer said, hinting the road could be a long one.

But several progressive lawmakers and groups say the next Congress cannot be business as usual.

Indivisible, a progressive political organization that has described the Trump administration as a “fascistic clown show,” sent a memo to Senate Democratic offices Thursday morning urging them not to “squander” their momentum and to “fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action.”.

It has been revealed that “Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be,” the memo reads.

The group has been encouraging voters to speak up and demand their senators hold “a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Schumer has projected confidence he will keep his spot atop the caucus, especially after he helped pave the way for Tuesday’s blue wave. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he mentioned Wednesday. But the pressure campaign points to some tough math and harsh realities for the top Democrat — including some that mirror the woes of the outgoing Republican Majority Leader John Thune.

Among the demands outlined by Indivisible is one with a troubled recent history: “Breaking the filibuster on the first day of the new session.”.

Democrats need to leverage “every procedural tool” if they “want the public to believe their campaign promises weren’t just more talk from politicians who are just like the old politicians they hated,” the memo reads.

The group isn’t alone in floating a latest approach to the chamber’s 60-vote threshold for invoking cloture and ending debate. Some current and incoming lawmakers have signaled they would be open to going “nuclear” and abolishing the legislative filibuster, following in the footsteps of past majorities in both parties who have similarly changed how other Senate business is handled, like judicial nominees.

Sources indicate that sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued in an op-ed in Time this week that Democrats could in some cases use existing tools, like a party-line process known as budget reconciliation, to pass their priorities. For non-budget items, like “bills to ban stock trading by federal officials or crack down on Trump’s corruption in plain sight,” Democrats should start by putting them up for a vote on the floor and letting “Republicans decide if they want to stay tied to such corruption.”.

“And, if they do, then let’s clear away Senate filibuster rules and pass the laws anyway,” she wrote.

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas told NBC News on Monday ahead of his victory, “I believe the majority has the right to govern in this country, and the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution and is a Jim Crow relic, is leading to gridlock in our nation’s capital.”.

Schumer ignored a question about nuking the filibuster at Wednesday’s event, saying instead, “The first thing we’ll do is reduce costs and work the legislative process.”.

It would take 51 votes in the Senate for Democrats to go “nuclear” and establish a newly introduced precedent, a math problem that Thune knows all too well. The Republican from South Dakota faced loud criticism from conservatives online and hard-liners in his own party who stated he wasn’t doing enough to try to pass a sprawling voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act. But Thune repeatedly insisted he didn’t have the votes to change the chamber’s filibuster rules.

Industry observers note that many senators fear that blowing up the 60-vote threshold would fundamentally change the role of the Senate and its ability to tap the brakes on legislation that doesn’t have durable bipartisan support. Democrats went through a similar debate over the filibuster in 2022, during Schumer's first stint as majority leader. Even as others in their party pushed to pass sweeping voting rights legislation by any means necessary, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin, then moderate Democratic senators, held firm against filibuster changes.

In a recent development, and Schumer will have at least one Democrat on his hands who has already spoken up in defense of the filibuster, reversing his previous position. “I now recognize how important the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it,” Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania wrote in a Washington Post op-ed earlier this summer, praising Sinema and Manchin as “courageous” holdouts who were wrongly “vilified” for holding the line.

Recent findings suggest that none of that points to an easy ride for the incoming Democratic majority leader. And if fights over the filibuster weren’t enough, the caucus is also bracing for a different kind of intraparty angst, this time over impeachment.

According to recent reports, the next likely House Judiciary Committee chairman, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told reporters on Thursday: “I have not had a single member of Congress or even a candidate say we’ve got to start out by impeaching Donald Trump.”.

“For us, impeachment is not a fetish. It’s certainly not a taboo. We’ve impeached the guy twice,” he said, referring to Democrats’ efforts during the first Trump administration. “The problem has been over on the Senate side, and for us, it is a tool in the constitutional toolkit.”.

Sources indicate that even if the House were to impeach Trump, a conviction would require a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Senate. And some Democrats are eager not to waste their hard-earned political capital on an impeachment quest that could alienate moderate voters and do nothing to bring down costs for everyday Americans.

In a recent development, illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who boosted candidates in battleground races and recently released a roadmap for the new Congress, said at the CAP event on Thursday that lawmakers should “hold oversight hearings and expose the corruption of this administration. I’m not suggesting that that necessarily leads to impeachment. Maybe it does.”.

Sounding more certain for Democrats in both chambers is their desire to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

It has been revealed that but that could be dealt with in the lame duck if Rep. Thomas Massie’s, R-Ky., resolution prevails next week. His proposal includes eight articles of impeachment, including allegations that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Recent findings suggest that hegseth said in a video on Thursday of impeaching: “Didn’t work against President Trump. Won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”.

Indivisible’s memo names impeaching Hegseth as a priority, as well as blocking a “business-as-usual” National Defense Authorization Act in the lame duck and refusing to fund the Department of Defense if “it doesn’t cut off money for the war.”.

It has been revealed that but it’s not clear that Democrats in Congress are ready to play that kind of hard ball. As they weigh their approach to the next era, they’re still half-stunned themselves by their larger than expected wins — and trying to put themselves in the best position ahead of the next elections in 2028.

Sources indicate that GOP Rep. Christopher H. Smith of Fresh Jersey told reporters on Thursday at the Capitol he hopes Democrats don’t hold up the NDAA “for the good of the country.”.

Sources indicate that “The NDAA is such an vital bill for our national security, and it’s usually very bipartisan. I hope it is,” he noted.

Black Holes and Their Mysterious Bright Structures Explained

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1524 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that astrophysical jets launched from black holes aren't shy.
  • In a recent development, supermassive black holes (SMBH) emit the largest astrophysical jets, and they come from active galactic nuclei (AGN) which are SMBH that are actively accreting material.
  • These jets are impossible to ignore.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that astrophysical jets launched from black holes aren't shy. They announce their presence with enormous blasts of energy that extend extreme distances into space. They're the most long-lasting and luminous sources of electromagnetic energy in the Universe.

In a recent development, supermassive black holes (SMBH) emit the largest astrophysical jets, and they come from active galactic nuclei (AGN) which are SMBH that are actively accreting material. As material gathers in an accretion disk around a SMBH, it rotates and heats up. Some of the material is ejected out of the black hole in the powerful jets.

These jets are impossible to ignore. No astrophysicist could feign their interest. Exactly how these powerful expressions of cosmic energy are created isn't clear, though some things are known.

It has been revealed that astrophysicists know that they're powered by a SMBH's rotational energy and their extremely powerful magnetic fields. They know that they move at relativistic speeds. And they know that they can inject gigantic amounts of energy into the intergalactic medium, heating up gas and introducing turbulence, two things that act against star formation.

One thing that puzzles researchers is how the different regions in a black hole jet have different brightnesses. The expectation is that the center of the jets would be brightest, because this is where energy is most concentrated. But when researchers examine the jets coming from the SMBH in Centaurus A, the closest radio galaxy to Earth, that's not what they see.

In a recent development, since it's so close and so bright, Centaurus A is one of those natural laboratories for extreme physics that makes astrophysicists' eyes light up. They've been observing the jets in Centaurus A in detail for many years. Observations with the Event Horizon Telescope spanning a decade have revealed that its jets are brighter at their edges than in their centers, in a phenomenon called limb brightening. Why is that?

Industry observers note that upcoming research in Astronomy and Astrophysics has an explanation. It's titled "Probing anisotropic particle acceleration and limb brightening in Centaurus Aâs jet." The lead author is Felix Glaser, Master's student at the Chair of Astronomy at the University of WÃ¼rzburg in Germany.

"Relativistic jets are among the most fascinating phenomena in the universe, and recent high-resolution very long baseline interferometric (VLBI) observations, including the Global mm-VLBI Array and the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), are able to resolve their structure close to their launching site," the authors write. The combined observations show the black holes with brighter limbs are not only found in Centaurus A, but in M 87 and 3C 84, too.

Industry observers note that this image shows four different looks at the central region of M 87. The top image from the Hubble is in visible light. The other three are all in polarised light. The lines mark the orientation of polarisation, which is related to the magnetic field in the regions imaged. Though the researchers focused on Centaurus A, this image highlights how magnetic fields and polarity influence astrophysical jets. Image Credit: EHT Collaboration; ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO), Goddi et al.; NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA); VLBA (NRAO), Kravchenko et al.; J. C. Algaba, I. MartÃ­-Vidal.

It has been revealed that each of these three galaxies are different from one another, making it difficult to understand the cause of their limb brightening. "Therefore, as a pilot study, we aimed to model the EHT observations of Cen A," the authors explain. It's the closest, so that makes sense.

Recent findings suggest that this is a composite image of Centaurus A, with the individual images and their wavelenghts on the right. The image is from the Hubble (visible), Chandra (X-ray), Spitzer (infrared), and the Very Large Array (radio). Image Credit: NASA, CXC, SAO, Astrophotography by Rolf Olsen, NASA-JPL, Caltech, NRAO, AUI, NSF, UOH, M. Hardcastle.

The researchers performed a magnetohydrodynamic simulation of an accreting supermassive black hole and how it released it jets to observe the plasma dynamics involved. Since these jets are relativistic, the simulation included general relativistic effects. They also adjusted their simulation to match the properties of Centaurus A. "In order to match our model to the EHT observations, we adjust several free parameters..." the authors write, including black hole mass and the viewing angle.

The simulation successfully mimicked the recent observations of Centaurus A with the EHT.

"Our results demonstrate that the edge-brightening observed in Cen A can be naturally reproduced by an anisotropic particle distribution," the researchers write.

It has been revealed that that means that the electrons emitted in the jets aren't distributed evenly over pitch angles. Pitch angles are the difference between the magnetic field and each electron's velocity. This is where synchrotron radiation enters the picture. Synchrotron radiation is when particles are forced to follow the curve of a magnetic field.

Recent findings suggest that the emission of synchrotron radiation is strongly dependent on the pitch angle. So as a result, the observed brightness of the radiation changes depending on the viewing angle of the magnetic field the particles are forced to follow.

This figure from the research shows the synthetic polarized intensity images of our Cen A model at four representative frequencies: 86 GHz (panel A), 230 GHz (panel B), 680 GHz (panel C), and 3 THz (panel D). Each one zooms in closer and shows more detail in the model. Image Credit: Glaser et al. 2026.

âWhat is truly amazing is that microscopic plasma effects can shape structures on vastly larger scales,â noted Dr. Christian Fromm, leader of the Computational Astrophysics Group. âFuture observations will reveal even more of these plasma signatures, making it increasingly crucial to include realistic plasma physics in our models already today and to further investigate the highly nonlinear effects of relativistic plasma.â.

Sources indicate that this figure indicates how microscopic plasma effects can shape the large-scale structure of black hole jets. The hot accretion flow surrounding the supermassive black hole is shown in red, the relativistic jets in blue, and the magnetic field structure by gray helical field lines. Colored particles and arrows illustrate the motion of accelerated particles along the jet. Top right: The Event Horizon Telescope image of the inner jet of Centaurus A at a wavelength of 1.3 mm. Bottom right: The synthetic EHT observation generated from the latest plasma-informed model. (Image Credit: Christian M. Fromm, Janssen et al. 2021 and Glaser et al. 2026).

âCen A is our closest window into the physics of relativistic jets,â remarked lead author Glaser. âThe fact that our plasma-informed model reproduces the observed edge brightening suggests that we are capturing an notable piece of the underlying physics. These processes may not be unique to Cen A, but could be common in relativistic jets throughout the Universe.â.

Recent findings suggest that this study makes real progress in understanding the details of astrophysical jets, and how they exhibit things like limb brightening. It links the small scale of plasma physics with the jets and their characteristics. It's all because of a focused, multi-disciplinary effort.

âBy bringing together expertise in high-resolution observations, numerical simulations, and plasma physics, we are making progress toward understanding how black holes launch powerful jets and how these jets produce the radiation we observe. The latest study is an excellent example of this approach,â said Fromm.

Industry observers note that new telescopes are coming online that will take this work even further. The Square Kilometre Array will be the world's largest and highest-resolution radio telescope when it comes online in 2027. Updates to the Very Large Array will also drive progress when they're completed in 2031.

Industry observers note that this work may affect more than our understanding of black hole jets. On a detailed plasma physics level, there are similarities between the jets and fusion. If we ever have a functioning fusion reactor, it will involve extremely powerful artificial magnets to generate powerful fields that confine the plasma.

This illustration reveals some of the "D"-shaped toroidal field magnets in the ITER international nuclear fusion research and engineering project being built in France. Each magnet weighs 330 tons, and their job is to confine the plasma inside ITER's vacuum vessel. Lessons learned by studying plasma physics in black hole jets are applicable to fusion reactors. Image Credit: ITER Consortium.

It has been revealed that âA black hole and a fusion reactor may sound like completely different worldsâbut both are governed by the physics of plasma,â says Professor Karl Mannheim, holder of the Chair of Astronomy at the University of WÃ¼rzburg. âAt Centaurus A, we can study plasma under conditions that cannot be created on Earth. These insights not only help us understand the Universe, but may also contribute to the development of future fusion energy.â.

A Five-Day Experiment Reveals a Surprising Secret of Deadly Brain Cancer

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (964 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers tracking glioblastoma cells in living mouse brain tissue discovered how quickly they can change their paths, revealing a hidden challenge in stopping this aggressive brain cancer.
  • Industry observers note that glioblastoma is one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer, largely because its cells can spread deep into surrounding healthy tissue.
  • According to recent reports, understanding how these cells spread has been difficult because researchers have largely relied on images that capture only individual moments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers tracking glioblastoma cells in living mouse brain tissue discovered how quickly they can change their paths, revealing a hidden challenge in stopping this aggressive brain cancer.

Industry observers note that glioblastoma is one of the most aggressive forms of brain cancer, largely because its cells can spread deep into surrounding healthy tissue. Even after surgeons remove the main tumor, scattered cancer cells may remain in the brain and eventually contribute to the disease returning.

According to recent reports, understanding how these cells spread has been difficult because researchers have largely relied on images that capture only individual moments. Scientists at Uppsala University have now developed a method that lets them watch thousands of glioblastoma cells move through living brain tissue, revealing how they change their behavior over time. The findings, published in Nature Communications, could help researchers better understand why this cancer is so difficult to contain.

“Until now, we have mostly seen snapshots of how glioblastoma spreads. This method combines microscopy with artificial intelligence and allows us to watch the process unfold in living brain tissue. We could also compare tumors from different patients and investigate how they respond to treatment,” says Hitesh Mangukiya, researcher at the Department of Immunology, Genetics and Pathology at Uppsala University and one of the study’s lead authors.

The new method, called GlioTrace, combines automated microscopy with machine learning to follow individual cancer cells as they travel through brain tissue. To test it, the researchers collected glioblastoma cells from six patients and grew them as tumors in mouse brains. They then cut the brains into thin slices, kept the tissue alive in the laboratory, and photographed it at intervals of no more than two hours for up to five days.

A computer system identified and tracked individual tumor cells across the images, while statistical models helped researchers calculate when cells switched between different states. Unlike techniques that examine only small regions of the brain, GlioTrace can monitor cells across entire brain slices using standard microscopes.

The observations revealed that glioblastoma cells do not all spread in the same way. Some tumors showed a preference for traveling along blood vessels, while others spread more diffusely through the surrounding brain tissue. These differences were apparent between tumors derived from different patients.

Individual cells were also remarkably adaptable. A cancer cell moving along a blood vessel could later leave that route and travel independently through the tissue. Some cells changed their shape and movement patterns over just a few days, suggesting that their behavior is far less fixed than individual images might imply.

It has been revealed that “What surprised us most was how flexible the tumor cells are. The same cell can change how it moves over just a few days. To develop treatments that stop tumor cells from spreading, we need to understand this ability to switch between different behaviors,” states Madeleine Skeppås, PhD student at Uppsala University and co-lead author of the study.

The team also used GlioTrace to examine how cancer treatments influence cell movement. Two drug substances reduced the movement and spread of tumor cells in the brain slices, although their effectiveness varied between patient-derived tumors. Even within the same research setting, cells with different movement patterns did not respond equally to the drugs.

Another experiment raised questions about what happens to invasive cells during treatment. In some tumor models, combining radiation with chemotherapy increased the proportion of cells with a particular shape. These cells were among the fastest moving and occupied a central position in the network of transitions between different cell states, indicating that they were closely connected to changes in cell behavior.

In a recent development, the findings suggest that certain highly invasive cells might persist during treatment. However, the researchers have not established whether these cells are more resistant to therapy or whether they contribute to tumor recurrence. Further studies will be needed to determine what this response means for treating glioblastoma.

Sources indicate that “Using this method allows us to monitor, for the first time, how thousands of individual tumor cells move through living brain tissue and to see how they adapt their behavior in real time. It opens up newly introduced possibilities to understand and, in the long term, halt the invasion process,” says Sven Nelander, Professor of Integrative Cancer Research at Uppsala University.

An key part of GlioTrace is the computational analysis system developed by Skeppås together with colleagues at Chalmers University of Technology and the University of Gothenburg. The software processes microscopy images, recognizes the different shapes of cancer cells, and estimates how their characteristics change over time. It has also been made freely available, allowing other researchers to investigate how tumor cells interact with their surroundings and respond to potential treatments.

Although GlioTrace offers a more detailed view of cancer cell invasion, it remains a laboratory research method rather than a tool for making clinical decisions.

Recent findings suggest that “We hope that the method will help us understand how tumor cells interact with their surroundings and identify treatments that can prevent cancer from spreading through the brain. However, for now, GlioTrace is a research method, and further studies are needed before it could be used to guide treatment decisions in patients,” says Hitesh Mangukiya.

Reference: “Reconstructing the single-cell spatiotemporal dynamics of glioblastoma invasion” by Hitesh Bhagavanbhai Mangukiya, Madeleine Skeppås, André Lasses Armatowski, Irem Uppman, Linnea Hallin, Filippa Kruse, Clara Nordquist, Soumi Kundu, Maria Berglund, Adam A. Malik, Cecilia Krona, Rebecka Jörnsten and Sven Nelander, 2 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78908-9.

The research was supported by the Swedish Research Council, the Swedish Cancer Society, the Swedish Foundation for Strategic Research and the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation.

Tech Report: Computer Simulations Provide the Best Explanation for Those "Little Red Dots" Yet!

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) made its famous observations of several deep fields in the cosmos, astronomers were surprised to see numerous galaxies that defied expectations.
  • Industry observers note that however, this also conflicted with cosmological models, as it seemed unlikely that many galaxies could have formed with massive black holes less than one billion years after the Massive Bang.
  • Industry observers note that the study was led by Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) made its famous observations of several deep fields in the cosmos, astronomers were surprised to see numerous galaxies that defied expectations. These galaxies were bright and red - earning them the nickname Little Red Dots (LRDs) - and far more abundant than cosmological models predicted. Scientists theorized that these were early quasars, galaxies with active galactic nuclei (AGNs) powered by the "seeds" that would grow to become supermassive black holes (SMBHs).

Industry observers note that however, this also conflicted with cosmological models, as it seemed unlikely that many galaxies could have formed with massive black holes less than one billion years after the Massive Bang. This led scientists to consider various theories, compact collections of stars, "dusty" galaxies, supermassive stars, and "black hole stars." While the more recent Direct Collapse Black Holes (DCBHs) theory offered the most compelling argument to date, new simulations by an international team of astronomers indicate that they may be the remnants of collapsed supermassive primordial stars.

Industry observers note that the study was led by Dr. Daniel Whalen from the University of Portsmouth's Institute of Cosmology and Gravitation. His colleagues included researchers from United Arab Emirates University, the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, the Institute for Astronomy and Royal Observatory at the University of Edinburgh, and the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics (CfA). The paper detailing their findings was published in the The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The little red dots could represent galaxies in an evolutionary phase predating the luminous quasar phase. Credit: NASA/ESA/CSA/ISTA)/ETH Zurich/NAOJ.

Sources indicate that previous attempts to explain the rapid formation, abundance, and spectral characteristics of LRDs all suffered from the same problem. While each explained some characteristics, none could account for everything the JWST revealed in its deep field surveys. Then came the DCBHs theory, which argues that SMBH seeds formed directly from massive clouds of cold gas. While this theory did fit Webb's observations nicely, it still faces numerous theoretical and environmental challenges.

For starters, the core premise of the DCBH theory is that a massive cloud of cold gas could collapse under its own gravity. However, gas tends to fragment into smaller clouds as it cools, leading to a cluster of primordial (Population III) stars instead of a black hole seed. To prevent fragmentation, the gas cloud must remain hot, requiring a very specific amount of Lyman-Werner (LW) radiation from a synchronized star-forming galaxy in its vicinity to destroy the main coolant - i.e., molecular hydrogen (Hâ).

Industry observers note that this raises additional problems, including the self-shielding nature of molecular hydrogen. As a gas cloud becomes increasingly dense, its outer layers absorb the LW radiation, shielding the inner core. This means that the critical amount of radiation required to suppress cooling across the entire cloud would be much higher. Even if the SMBH seed did manage to form, the radiative pressure it would emit (plus mechanical feedback from the disk and jets) would slow the accretion rate, significantly slowing further growth.

Whalen and his team found another explanation borne out by advanced cosmological simulations. As he said in a University of Portsmouth press release:.

Industry observers note that LRDs have been one of the most surprising discoveries made by the James Webb Space Telescope. They are compact, only a few hundred light-years across, but are as bright as much larger galaxies, and their unusual V-shaped spectra have defied the usual astrophysical explanations. Their lack of detectable X-ray and radio emissions has left astronomers struggling to explain what they are.

According to recent reports, artist's impression of a galaxy forming stars within powerful outflows of material blasted out from supermassive black holes at its core. Credit: ESO/M. Kornmesser.

According to recent reports, based on their simulations, the team produced a model showing that LRDs are most likely galaxies with AGN powered by massive black holes that formed through the collapse of supermassive primordial stars. What's more, their model suggests that the black holes are largely concealed by dense, massive discs of the gas that created them. These gaseous envelopes trap high-energy X-rays while allowing some visible, ultraviolet, and infrared light to escape, which fits with the unusual light signatures detected by the JWST.

Industry observers note that the simulations also explain another long-standing mystery about LRDs: that a large cluster of stars in the disks of these small galaxies produces the blue part of the spectrum Webb observed. These disks, according to the models, contain around 100 million stars densely packed into regions measuring only 500 light-years in diameter, matching what astronomers observed in LRDs. Based on the available data, the team further concludes the black holes at the center of these primordial galaxies are only about 10 million Solar masses.

This is a few orders of magnitude less than previous estimates, which indicated a maximum of 100 million Solar masses. While this research is unlikely to be the final word on the nature of LRDs, it offers what is (to date) the most fitting explanation that matches the observations. "What makes this discovery so exciting is that we may be witnessing the birth of the first supermassive black holes," noted Whalen. "For decades, simulations have predicted that these objects should exist, and now the James Webb Space Telescope may finally be allowing us to see them.".

Further Reading: University of Portsmouth, The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.

In a recent development, the sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

While we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever new ideas have been simmering since last year’s massive meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

According to recent reports, stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

It has been revealed that I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

It has been revealed that while more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman.

Recent findings suggest that tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest.

This is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

It has been revealed that I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

Mitchell Davis, Cook and Eat Better.

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated swiftly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be said is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

#42685. A Common Gut Antibody May Be the Key to Preventing Colon Cancer Before It Starts

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (709 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

A Common Gut Antibody May Be the Key to Preventing Colon Cancer Before It Starts

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People who lack a common gut antibody face higher colorectal cancer risk, and experiments in mice are beginning to explain how that missing protection may matter.
  • Long before colon cancer develops, cells lining the intestine can begin dividing too swiftly.
  • According to recent reports, in a study published in Nature, mice lacking immunoglobulin A (IgA) developed more than twice as many colon tumors as mice with normal antibody levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People who lack a common gut antibody face higher colorectal cancer risk, and experiments in mice are beginning to explain how that missing protection may matter.

Long before colon cancer develops, cells lining the intestine can begin dividing too swiftly. Scientists at Rockefeller University have discovered that a common gut antibody helps keep this growth under control in mice, raising the possibility of preventing tumors before they form.

According to recent reports, in a study published in Nature, mice lacking immunoglobulin A (IgA) developed more than twice as many colon tumors as mice with normal antibody levels. Giving the deficient mice IgA by mouth eliminated their increased cancer risk.

The findings may help explain why people with IgA deficiency, which affects about 1 in 500 Americans, face a higher risk of colorectal cancer.

“One intriguing aspect of this work is that it reveals how a natural defense in the gut restrains the cell division that can lead to cancer,” says senior author Daniel Mucida, head of Rockefeller’s Laboratory of Mucosal Immunology. “Most cancer research focuses on trying to destroy a tumor that already exists, but what if we could intervene before tumors form?”.

It has been revealed that igA is one of the immune system’s first lines of defense. Unlike antibodies that target specific pathogens, it can bind to many kinds of gut bacteria and even some healthy human cells. Scientists have long known that these antibodies are abundant in the digestive system, although their full purpose has remained unclear.

Gregory Donaldson, a former Rockefeller postdoctoral fellow who is now an assistant professor at UCLA, investigated whether IgA’s interactions with gut bacteria could explain its connection to cancer. He compared mice lacking IgA with normal mice raised alongside them, ensuring both groups encountered the same food and germs.

The increased cancer risk appeared across several different models of colon cancer. More importantly, the researchers found changes in genes controlling cell division before any tumors developed, suggesting that IgA influences cancer risk at an early stage.

The team traced this effect to DMBT1, a receptor on the surface of intestinal cells. Gabriella Lima dos Reis, a graduate student in Gabriel Victora’s laboratory, helped identify its role.

In a recent development, in the presence of gut bacteria, DMBT1 encourages intestinal cells to multiply. IgA acts like a brake by binding to the receptor and limiting that growth. Without IgA, the signal can become overactive, allowing cells to divide excessively and form tumors. The researchers found that removing gut bacteria or DMBT1 signaling also prevented this uncontrolled growth.

Recent findings suggest that “If IgA is missing, epithelial cells that are performing their normal function—responding to bacteria by producing newly introduced cells—can keep dividing unchecked, leading to cancer,” Mucida says. “We think this homeostatic effect is IgA’s main function. This was a significant surprise.”.

The discovery could eventually lead to upcoming ways of reducing colon cancer risk, particularly for people who have had polyps removed. Polyps increase the likelihood of developing colon cancer, and Mucida believes targeting this pathway could offer a way to lower that risk.

Industry observers note that donaldson also sees potential in beneficial gut bacteria. Although much research has focused on microbes that encourage tumor growth, some bacteria may help protect intestinal cells. One possibility is developing probiotics that stimulate protective IgA responses.

Sources indicate that both approaches remain speculative, and the findings have not established a cancer-prevention treatment for humans. However, the study suggests that understanding how gut bacteria, antibodies, and intestinal cells interact could reveal upcoming opportunities to prevent cancer before it starts.

Reference: “Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA” by Gregory P. Donaldson, Gabriella Lima dos Reis, Marwa Saad, Christopher Wichmann, Izabela Mamede, Guo Chen, Caroline E. Harrer, Nicole L. DelGaudio, Dayu Zhang, Begüm Aydin, Tiago B. R. Castro, Sergei I. Grivennikov, Bernardo S. Reis, Elise G. Liu, Stephanie C. Eisenbarth, Kivanç Birsoy, Sohail F. Tavazoie, Beth M. Stadtmueller, Gabriel D. Victora and Daniel Mucida, 11 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11264-2.

Tech Report: Microscopic Space Dust Reveals A Hidden Reservoir Of "Heavy Water" Beyond Neptune

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1259 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers can find valuable information in even the tiniest objects.
  • In this context âheavy waterâ doesnât mean the type formed with deuterium, like the kind used in nuclear reactors.
  • Industry observers note that in 2011, NASAâs Genesis mission caught particles in the solar wind that highlighted the Sun housed an overwhelming amount of regular oxygen-16.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers can find valuable information in even the tiniest objects. That was certainly the case recently when twelve dust grains collected by a high-altitude aircraft helped solve a mystery about the birth of our Solar System. Or at least that is the argument in a new paper published in Science Advances by researchers at NASAâs Johnson Space Center and UCLA. According to the paper, the region beyond Neptune once had a massive isolated reservoir of âheavy waterâ that never mixed in with the inner planets.

In this context âheavy waterâ doesnât mean the type formed with deuterium, like the kind used in nuclear reactors. Instead, it refers to a heavier version of the other element in good old H2O - oxygen. Most of the universeâs oxygen atoms are an isotope called oxygen-16, with eight protons and eight neutrons. However, a small percentage weighs in a bit heavier - oxygen-17 and oxygen-18, which carry an extra neutron or two, respectively.

Industry observers note that in 2011, NASAâs Genesis mission caught particles in the solar wind that highlighted the Sun housed an overwhelming amount of regular oxygen-16. However, Earth, Mars, and the asteroid belt seemed to have much more of the heavier oxygen isotopes. Which meant thereâs a mismatch between what we see inside the Sun and what the planets were formed out of. Scientists have been attempting to explain why for years.

Fraser explains the crucial of cosmic dust to life on Earth.

The most common explanation of why is known as carbon monoxide self-shielding. Around 4.5 billion years ago, when our Solar System hadnât fully formed yet, ultraviolet light from the Sun blew apart carbon monoxide molecules at the outer edges of the protoplanetary disk of gas and dust. Because oxygen-16 was the most prominent in the disk, the carbon monoxide particles that were made out of it would absorb much of the UV light that was directed at the disk, breaking the ones that were closest the light source (i.e. the Sun) apart. They eventually reformed with hydrogen to make âregularâ water.

However, that left other wavelengths of UV free to travel into the farther reaches of the protoplanetary disk. And some of those wavelengths were particularly good at breaking apart carbon monoxide molecules that had formed with oxygen-17 and oxygen-18. So, in the outer disk, those heavier isotopes made up a higher percentage of the free-floating ions that eventually bonded to hydrogen, in their case creating âheavyâ water.

Recent findings suggest that that makes sense from a theoretical standpoint at least, but proving this âheavy waterâ reservoir exists has been tricky. Almost all the meteorites we have found were formed in the main asteroid belt - not far enough out to capture particles of the reservoir. Some cometary sample missions, such as Rosetta and Stardust, have tried to capture water samples from these ambassadors of the outer solar system, but their method of capture resulted in the water-bearing materials melting, leaving no trace of their isotopic configuration.

Fraser explains the Kuiper Belt.

Industry observers note that enter the new paper. Lead author Lindsay Keller and his team turned to interplanetary dust particles (IDPs). These microscopic grains are formed when comets and other icy bodies out in the Kuiper belt, the area past Neptune, collide and break apart. Some of the grains that result from those collisions are pulled inward by the Sunâs gravity, eventually intersecting the orbits of the inner planets - including Earth.

In a recent development, during their journey, they are subjected to extreme amounts of high energy particles from solar flares, which leaves microscopic scars on them called solar energetic particle tracks. Previous studies had proven that one way to prove a piece of dust had traveled from the Kuiper Belt is that have around a hundred times more energetic particle tracks, due to their much longer time in interplanetary space, than particles from asteroids do. In other words, if you can count the radiation tracks, you can prove whether a grain of dust came from beyond Neptune or not.

That is exactly what they proved with twelve dust grains collected during NASAâs Cosmic Dust program - an ongoing airborne sampling program running out of Johnson Space Center since 1981. Shockingly, the collected particles still had lots of clays, like saponite, which are made with water, as well as iron-nickel sulfides and around four times as much carbon as would be expected for a primitive meteorite. The minerals proved that liquid water once flowed inside its parent Kuiper Belt object, either heated by radioactive decay or the kinetic energy of another impact.

Sources indicate that using a specialized microscope, the researchers measured the exact oxygen isotope ratios in the clays in the samples. They then worked back through chemical modeling to determine the original recipe for the water on the parent rock that formed the grains. They found that the primordial Kuiper Belt objects these grains came from were extraordinarily enriched with oxygen-17 and oxygen-18 - definitively proving that the reservoir of heavy water does exist out beyond Neptune.

Fraser talks about how there was liquid water on the asteroid Ryugu.

As a consequence, they also, tangentially, provided a significant bump to the carbon monoxide self-shielding theory. And also noted the similarities to a specific unusual meteorite known as Acfer 094, which they hint might actually be a meteor from the Kuiper Belt itself. But there was one final mystery the paper needed to resolve - if there was all this heavy water out in the outer solar system, why didnât it migrate in when the planets were forming?

In a recent development, the authors offer a simple explanation - Saturn. As Saturn grew in the early solar system, its gravity created a high-pressure ridge in the protoplanetary disk, acting as an invisible barrier to keep lightweight material from being pulled too far in towards the Sun. So, thanks to around a dozen specks of dust, we now have a more clearly defined picture of what our solar system looked like in the very early days of its formation - and it seems we can thank our giant ringed neighbor for some of how Earth ended up with its current isotopic balance.

L. Keller et al - A primordial heavy water reservoir in the outer solar system.
