Euclid space telescope unveils first major data release, including map of 900 million galaxies

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (799 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.
  • Recent findings suggest that on Thursday (Nov.
  • Recent findings suggest that "These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

Recent findings suggest that on Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

Recent findings suggest that "These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery.".

Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, "Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here.".

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

The Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

Industry observers note that among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid indicates a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope plans to survey.

This image shows the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

In a recent development, with about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.

He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

What Is a Thought Made Of? Scientists Reveal Why Human Consciousness May Be Beyond the Reach of AI

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A familiar song can pull you back decades in an instant, and the chemistry behind that rush of memory may hold clues to what separates human minds from AI.
  • How does the brain turn a collection of memories into thoughts, emotions, and the experience of being conscious?
  • Recent findings suggest that A new scientific review suggests that part of the answer may lie in the complex chemistry surrounding brain cells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A familiar song can pull you back decades in an instant, and the chemistry behind that rush of memory may hold clues to what separates human minds from AI.

How does the brain turn a collection of memories into thoughts, emotions, and the experience of being conscious? Scientists have spent decades studying how neurons communicate through electrical and chemical signals, yet the physical processes that allow us to recall experiences, attach feelings to them, and give them meaning remain incompletely understood.

Recent findings suggest that A new scientific review suggests that part of the answer may lie in the complex chemistry surrounding brain cells. Rather than viewing memory primarily as a product of neuronal activity, the researchers propose that interactions among neurons, supporting brain cells, and molecules in their surrounding environment could play a fundamental role in shaping thought and conscious experience.

According to recent reports, dr. Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Prof. Chaim Gilon of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem’s Department of Chemistry present their theory in Consciousness, Memory, and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective. Building on earlier research into how experiences might be physically stored in the brain, they examine whether the chemistry of memory could help explain the origins of thought and consciousness.

Their proposal also raises a question about artificial intelligence: If human memory and emotion depend on the chemistry of living cells, can computers ever develop consciousness simply by becoming more powerful?

Scientists have long studied how neurons communicate to form and retrieve memories. But Marx and Gilon suggest that vital parts of this process may also occur in the molecular environment surrounding brain cells.

Their model, called the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory, involves three interacting components: brain cells, particularly neurons and astrocytes; the molecular material surrounding those cells; and chemicals such as metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters.

According to the theory, these components could allow the brain to chemically encode and retrieve information. Rather than serving only as a support structure, the environment surrounding brain cells may actively participate in memory storage.

Recent findings suggest that astrocytes, star-shaped cells that interact closely with neurons, play a central role in the proposed mechanism. The researchers suggest that coordinated activity among these cells, neurons, and surrounding molecules could contribute to how memories are formed and processed.

A familiar song can bring back memories from decades ago, complete with feelings that seemed long forgotten. Such experiences show that remembering involves more than retrieving information.

It has been revealed that marx and Gilon propose that the emotional content of memories may be linked to their chemical encoding. In their model, signaling molecules, including neurotransmitters and gliotransmitters, help connect stored information with the feelings associated with an experience.

It has been revealed that the researchers also suggest that retrieving and interpreting these chemically stored memories may contribute to the emergence of thought. In this view, memory is not simply a record of past events but an active process through which the brain assigns meaning to experience.

Recent findings suggest that computers and brains both store and process information, but the underlying mechanisms differ. While computers rely on electronic hardware, biological memory involves living cells and complex chemical interactions.

Marx and Gilon argue that this distinction could matter for consciousness. AI systems can perform increasingly sophisticated intellectual tasks, but their ability to process information does not establish that they experience thoughts or emotions.

Industry observers note that for example, an AI system can identify a familiar song and describe the memories or feelings it might evoke in a person. Whether such a system could actually experience nostalgia is a different question.

The researchers suggest that if consciousness depends partly on the biochemical processes involved in human memory, greater computational power alone may not be sufficient to reproduce it.

The proposed model offers a possible connection between memory, emotion, and thought, but it does not establish how physical processes in the brain produce conscious experience.

The authors acknowledge that consciousness remains poorly understood and do not claim to have demonstrated that AI cannot become conscious.

It has been revealed that instead, their work suggests that investigating the chemical mechanisms of memory could help explain how stored experiences acquire emotional meaning and contribute to thought. Whether those processes are essential for consciousness remains an open question.

Reference: “Consciousness, Memory and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective” by Gerard Marx and Chaim Gilon, 4 August 2026, International Journal of Psychiatry Research. DOI: 10.33425/2641-4317.1251.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Here’s a newly introduced reason to eat your beans and greens.
  • Industry observers note that A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Here’s a newly introduced reason to eat your beans and greens.

Industry observers note that A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng claims, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he claims.

In a recent development, the researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

In a recent development, it’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

Longtime West Virginia Sen. Rockefeller dies

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011.
  • Recent findings suggest that former Sen.
  • Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011. (Scott J. Ferrell/CQ Roll Call).

Recent findings suggest that former Sen. Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.

Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.

According to recent reports, A staunchly progressive lawmaker, he represented a deeply conservative state that turned further to the right in his later years. Rockefeller, scion of a famous New York family renowned for its wealth, never wavered in his convictions and retired rather than face a potential backlash from voters upset by the then-Obama administration’s attempts to rein in the coal industry.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who challenged Rockefeller for his seat before he decided not to seek reelection, released a statement Friday praising her predecessor’s legacy.

“Jay dedicated his life to serving West Virginia and our nation, leaving a lasting legacy. He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” Capito said. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.”.

It has been revealed that west Virginia’s Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey — himself a transplanted Northerner, with roots in Brooklyn and Upcoming Jersey — lauded Rockefeller’s record on health care and aid for coal miners and veterans in their adopted state.

“His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians,” Morrisey said.

Industry observers note that rockefeller was born in New York City on June 18, 1937, the great-grandson of Standard Oil Co. founder John D. Rockefeller, who was once considered the world’s richest man. Rockefeller attended Harvard University, graduating with an A.B. in 1961. His passion was for the Far East and he spent three years studying at the International Christian University in Tokyo.

He returned to the states and was appointed by President John F. Kennedy to the National Advisory Council of the Peace Corps in 1961, spearheaded the Peace Corps initial program in the Philippines. He worked for a brief time in what was then known as U.S. Department of Far Eastern Affairs before deciding to embark on a public service role of a more personal nature. He enrolling as a VISTA volunteer, in the program which would later be known as AmeriCorps, and moved to the small mining community of Emmons, W.Va., in 1964 at age 27.

According to recent reports, in West Virginia, Rockefeller found his life’s work. He described the experience as being “reborn,” and spoke often the poverty and hardship he encountered living in the small town. “I could not leave,” he noted of West Virginia. “I [had] become so devoted to those people and the unfairness.".

He had planned to remain only one year, but decided to stay and became active in local politics. He broke from his family's long tradition of Republican loyalty and ran successfully for the House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. Two years later, he was elected secretary of state.

It has been revealed that rockefeller lost a bid for governor in 1972, but he became the president of West Virginia Wesleyan College and continued to place roots in the state. He married Sharon Percy Rockefeller in 1967 and they started their family. When he ran for governor again in 1976, he won, and served two terms before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 1984, ultimately serving five terms before retiring in 2014.

It has been revealed that rockefeller was determined to increase economic opportunities for West Virginia, for whom he felt was forgotten and abandoned by the rest of the country. He called the people of his state “the hardest-working people I know,” and believed that bringing more business opportunities would help lift the state out of severe rural poverty and the dependence on the coal industry.

It has been revealed that rockefeller traveled to Japan and worked tirelessly to bring a Toyota manufacturing plant to Buffalo, W.Va, one of over twenty Japanese companies he’d brought to West Virginia. He fought for fair trade policies and targeted tax relief to protect West Virginia industries such as steel and chemicals.

Coal mining had long been the economic backbone of West Virginia, but Rockefeller felt more must be done to protect miners, many of whom worked in unsafe conditions or fell ill with pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease, after years of inhaling coal dust.

But defying the coal industry came with a political cost. When Rockefeller originally ran for governor in 1972, he had opposed mountaintop mining, also called strip mining, or the practice of removing large amounts of earth and rock in order to access underground seams of coal. When he ran again in 1976, he reversed his position and won.

But even as he ascended to the Senate, Rockefeller remained both friend and foe to the coal industry.

According to recent reports, despite growing up on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, figuratively and literally hundreds of miles away from coal mines, Rockefeller understood its deep roots in West Virginia’s economy and culture. He believed it was the miners — rather than industry — for whom he was defending.

He hung a century-old photo of a coal miner in his Senate office in the Hart building, and would point to the photo and remark to visitors that “this is why I’m here and who I work for.”.

Rockefeller fought to secure pensions for miners, especially as coal companies would file for bankruptcy and immediately restructure to do away with pension looks.

Sources indicate that in 1990, Rockefeller was one of only 11 senators to vote against the bipartisan Clean Air Act, which he felt disadvantaged workers in West Virginia. But those close to him mentioned the decision weighed heavily on him, and Rockefeller privately worried that the lack of such regulations would pollute the air and destroy waterways, the brunt of which would be born by the same disadvantaged people whom he vowed to protect.

In a recent development, he believed strongly in the deliberative aspects of the legislative process, consuming great amounts of reading material to familiarize himself with the issues. During a time of increasing partisan rancor, Rockefeller still reached across the aisle to find a willing partner, even when there was not one to be found.

In 2010, as the Environmental Protection Agency’s greenhouse gas regulations were coming to fruition, Rockefeller came up with a compromise to delay implementation for two years.

Recent findings suggest that he viewed himself as a broker between industry interests and the hard working people from coal-states like West Virginia. He had hoped that his years of standing up for coal miners and West Virginia interests would foster enough goodwill among industries primed to oppose any compromise that was less than an all-out rejection of the existing EPA statutes.

But industry walked away from Rockefeller, preferring a hard-line opposition to EPA regulations, and lobbied other senators to vote against Rockefeller’s measure. Furious, Rockefeller took to the floor of the Senate to denounce the coal industry and its leaders, an unprecedented action for a popular coal-state senator.

Sources indicate that “The reality is that many who run the coal industry today would rather attack false enemies and deny real problems then find solutions,” he mentioned on the Senate floor in June 2012. “Scare tactics are a cynical waste of time, money and, worst of all, coal miners’ hopes. But sadly, these coal operators have closed themselves off from any other opposing voices and few dared to speak out for change — even though it’s been staring them in the face for years.”.

His fury against the coal industry was heard loudly, many speculating that he would retire rather than face reelection.

It has been revealed that he had won reelection to the Senate handily during his five campaigns. In 2008, his final election, he was reelected with nearly 64 percent of the vote. But six months following his fated coal speech, in January 2013, Rockefeller announced he would retire at the end of his fifth term.

According to recent reports, rockefeller’s legacy may best be known for his fight to expand health care for vulnerable populations, including children, the economically disadvantaged and the elderly. Rockefeller served as one of the chief congressional champions for President Bill Clinton’s proposed health care overhaul, and later he played a critical role and was a loud progressive voice in writing and passing the Affordable Care Act in the Senate.

Industry observers note that rockefeller believed strongly in a public health insurance option, offering it as an amendment in the Senate Finance Committee during the ACA markup. A public-run insurance plan, he said, would put patients before profits, and help those people, especially West Virginians, with high health care costs and poor coverage who were left “out in the cold.”.

Sources indicate that "These are people," Rockefeller mentioned, visibly emotional during his closing arguments to the Senate Finance Committee. "Eleven-year-old kids. These are families, and we have to respect them. And you respect them by giving them a choice.".

The amendment was rejected. Rockefeller pivoted to strengthening Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program provisions, believing that poor and disadvantaged families could seek refuge within those programs. CHIP had been one of Rockefeller’s signature legislative victories, helping to write that program initially in 1997 and later working on a major expansion that became law in 2009.

Despite his initial concerns and later disappointments — at one time saying publicly he could not support the measure as it stood — he later added his support to the ACA, citing it as a win for all Americans and actively lobbied his colleagues to support it.

According to recent reports, rockefeller was also known for his role on the Senate Intelligence Committee. A former chairman, he was critical of the nation's mismanagement of the Iraq war and clashed frequently with Republicans over the treatment of detainees. After he retired from Congress, Rockefeller served as a distinguished fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Respect for Rockefeller ran deep on Capitol Hill. He was beloved by staff and known as a thoughtful, deliberative lawmaker. He had a fondness for classical music and served as a board member of the Bach Consort, an organization in Washington devoted to the study and performance of the music of Bach and his contemporaries. He admired art and Asian culture, and served as a board member of the Asia Society.

Industry observers note that rockefeller is survived by his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller; four children: John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.

Disclosure: the author served as a staffer in Rockefeller’s Senate office from 2009-11.

Latest Update: Stanford Scientists Discover 3 Hidden Brain Types in Children With ADHD and Anxiety

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (933 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have identified three distinct patterns of brain activity in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both, revealing biological differences that traditional diagnoses often overlook.
  • According to recent reports, brain scans have uncovered three distinct patterns of disrupted brain activity in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both conditions.
  • In a recent development, the findings come from a Stanford Medicine-led study published October 16 in Nature Mental Health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have identified three distinct patterns of brain activity in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both, revealing biological differences that traditional diagnoses often overlook.

According to recent reports, brain scans have uncovered three distinct patterns of disrupted brain activity in children with ADHD, anxiety, or both conditions. These patterns do not align neatly with conventional diagnoses, suggesting that children with similar symptoms may have different underlying neurological differences. Some patterns were even detectable years before children received a diagnosis.

In a recent development, the findings come from a Stanford Medicine-led study published October 16 in Nature Mental Health. By combining artificial intelligence with thousands of functional MRI (fMRI) scans, researchers identified three brain biotypes associated with different combinations of behavioral, emotional, and attention difficulties.

According to recent reports, ADHD and anxiety are among the most common childhood mental health disorders, and their symptoms frequently overlap. Clinicians typically diagnose these conditions using behavioral assessments and symptom checklists, but those categories may not fully capture the neurological differences between children.

“The high overlap between ADHD and anxiety actually hinders our understanding of the neurobiology underlying traditional, symptom-based diagnoses,” said Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford Medicine and co-senior author of the study.

“We wanted to know whether the biological differences among children with ADHD and anxiety follow the diagnostic labels used in the clinic,” Zhang noted.

The researchers found that children diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety, or both could belong to any of the three biotypes. Although particular brain patterns were more common with certain diagnoses, no biotype corresponded exclusively to a single disorder.

The researchers identified three neurological profiles, each associated with a distinctive combination of symptoms:.

Each child belonged to just one biotype (each child was in only one biotype), but the three patterns appeared across all conventional diagnostic categories.

The model also identified two underlying dimensions of brain dysfunction: cognitive-behavioral dysfunction and emotion-attention dysfunction. Each involved different networks of brain regions, with the three biotypes reflecting distinct combinations of these disruptions. The findings suggest that differences in how brain circuits communicate may help explain variations in children’s symptoms.

In a recent development, the researchers drew on the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, a long-term investigation of more than 11,000 U.S. children who entered the project at ages 9 or 10.

It has been revealed that their analysis included 3,508 children initially diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety, or both; 693 children who received one or both diagnoses later; and 1,947 children who never received either diagnosis. The researchers also examined brain scans from 224 children with ADHD or anxiety in the separate Healthy Brain Network study to validate their findings.

According to recent reports, an AI model examined functional connectivity, which describes how activity in different brain regions is coordinated. By combining these measurements with diagnostic records and cognitive and behavioral assessments, the researchers identified brain connectivity patterns associated with ADHD and anxiety that differed from those seen in children without either diagnosis.

Sources indicate that the researchers also detected the biotypes in initial brain scans from children who had not yet been diagnosed with ADHD or anxiety but developed one or both conditions later. This suggests that certain patterns of brain connectivity may emerge before symptoms lead to a clinical diagnosis.

“We think this means we may be able to use the biotypes as an early indicator of these conditions,” Zhang said. He identified the early appearance of these patterns as one of the study’s most surprising results.

“It could help us provide more timely intervention for these conditions and slow down or, we hope, even reverse their progression.”.

In a recent development, the findings do not establish that brain scans can reliably predict which individual children will develop ADHD or anxiety. Further research is needed to determine whether the biotypes can serve as clinically useful biomarkers for early identification.

Beyond early detection, the researchers hope the findings could eventually help clinicians select treatments based on a child’s underlying brain activity rather than relying entirely on symptoms.

Current treatment decisions often involve considerable trial and error, particularly when medications do not produce the expected improvement.

“When doctors prescribe a new medication, it can take quite a long time, a couple of weeks or months, to see a response,” Zhang mentioned. “If the first medication doesn’t work, they switch to a different one,” a process that can be costly, slow, and frustrating for families.

Zhang does not expect brain biotypes to replace existing diagnostic methods. Instead, he envisions using them alongside conventional assessments to provide a more detailed picture of each child’s condition.

It has been revealed that future clinical trials could investigate whether particular treatments improve the brain connectivity abnormalities associated with each biotype. Researchers could then examine whether these neurological patterns help predict treatment responses.

“We want to find biomarkers that can really inform the right treatment at the right time,” Zhang noted.

Reference: “Deep learning of brain–behavior dimensions identifies transdiagnostic biotypes in youth with ADHD and anxiety disorders” by Yong Jiao, Xiaoyu Tong, Gregory A. Fonzo, Ian H. #42636. Breaking: Scientists Find That Mice, Not Deer, Hold a Major Clue to Lyme Disease Risk

Breaking: Scientists Find That Mice, Not Deer, Hold a Major Clue to Lyme Disease Risk

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1478 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 35-year study reveals that mice, acorns, and unexpected environmental forces hold surprising clues to predicting Lyme disease risk.
  • Diseases transmitted by ticks are becoming increasingly common across the United States.
  • For more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, Latest York, have investigated the complicated relationships among oak trees, acorns, rodents, predators, ticks, and climate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 35-year study reveals that mice, acorns, and unexpected environmental forces hold surprising clues to predicting Lyme disease risk. A remarkable 35-year study is challenging long-held assumptions about Lyme disease, revealing that mice, acorns, and even extreme weather influence tick populations in unexpected ways. One of the biggest surprises is that deer, often associated with the spread of Lyme disease, may be less notable in predicting the numbers of dangerous ticks than researchers once believed.

Diseases transmitted by ticks are becoming increasingly common across the United States. Lyme disease is the most frequently reported, with nearly 500,000 people diagnosed annually. The infection is caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, which typically reaches humans through bites from infected blacklegged ticks. Antibiotics can successfully treat Lyme disease, but without treatment, the infection may spread to the joints, heart, and nervous system. Some patients also experience symptoms that persist over time.

For more than 35 years, scientists at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in Millbrook, Latest York, have investigated the complicated relationships among oak trees, acorns, rodents, predators, ticks, and climate. Their goal has been to understand how these interconnected factors influence the risk of Lyme disease in humans.

In a recent development, A latest study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences highlights nine particularly unexpected discoveries from this decades-long research effort. Several findings challenge conventional thinking about how tick populations grow and what determines the likelihood of disease transmission.

“On balance, these surprises have enriched our knowledge of this system, helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk,” noted lead author Richard Ostfeld, a disease ecologist at the Cary Institute who leads the research program alongside Shannon LaDeau.

Sources indicate that according to Ostfeld, the unusually extensive dataset has been essential for separating meaningful ecological patterns from random fluctuations and misleading correlations. Relationships that seem convincing over a few years can look very different when examined across several decades.

“Studies of this depth and length are incredibly rare,” stated LaDeau. “This research has followed an ecological community — including oak trees, mammals, and microorganisms — examining how interactions like predation, parasitism, and competition shape the system over time. The evolution of understanding summarized in this paper is something you simply cannot get without such a long-term and system-focused study.”.

When scientists first identified Lyme disease in the United States during the 1980s, white-tailed deer were considered a likely factor in the disease’s spread. Hunters frequently encountered deer carrying large numbers of adult ticks, suggesting that deer populations might strongly influence how many ticks would emerge in subsequent seasons.

Deer do not directly transmit the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks. However, they provide blood meals for adult female ticks, allowing those ticks to reproduce. Researchers therefore suspected that larger deer populations would support more egg-laying females and ultimately produce more young ticks.

Decades of field observations have complicated that theory. At the Cary Institute’s 2,000-acre forested research site in Dutchess County, New York, researchers found no statistically significant relationship between deer abundance and the number of nymphal ticks. Nymphs are immature ticks and represent the life stage most likely to transmit Lyme disease to humans.

“We had detected a weak positive relationship between deer and subsequent nymph abundance over short subsets of the data,” said Ostfeld, “but the whole data set in its entirety indicates no such thing.”.

Although deer numbers did not reliably predict nymph populations, mouse numbers told a different story.

The researchers discovered that years with abundant mice were followed by an approximately 40% increase in nymphal ticks the next year. This relationship makes white-footed mice particularly crucial to understanding changes in tick populations.

These small rodents provide an excellent food source for blacklegged tick larvae. They are also highly effective at transmitting Borrelia burgdorferi to the young ticks feeding on them.

Once infected as larvae, ticks can carry the bacteria into their next developmental stage. When they feed again as nymphs, they can transmit the infection to humans.

One of the study’s most striking discoveries involves something seemingly unrelated to human disease: acorns.

Oak trees occasionally produce unusually large quantities of acorns in a synchronized event known as acorn masting. The sudden abundance of food benefits mice, allowing their populations to increase during the following year.

Industry observers note that that population boom then provides more feeding opportunities for young ticks. As a result, the researchers found that a particularly large acorn harvest can reliably predict increased numbers of nymphal ticks two years later.

This creates a remarkable ecological chain reaction in which events beginning in the forest canopy can influence tick populations years afterward.

The relationship between mice and Lyme disease produced another unexpected finding.

According to recent reports, because mice are so effective at transmitting B. burgdorferi, the scientists initially assumed that years with more mice would also have a higher percentage of infected nymphal ticks. Early observations appeared to support that prediction.

However, the connection gradually disappeared as the research team accumulated more years of data.

“It kept me up at night,” said Ostfeld, “because it meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong.”.

Further investigation pointed toward a more complicated explanation involving other animals that provide blood meals for ticks.

When mouse populations increase, populations of other potential hosts, including squirrels, skunks, and opossums, may also rise. Most of these animals are much less effective at transmitting the Lyme disease bacterium to ticks.

Consequently, a greater share of ticks feeding on these alternative hosts can reduce the overall percentage of infected nymphs, even when mice are plentiful.

“So the infection prevalence in the nymphs really depends on how all the larval tick meals are distributed across all the hosts,” explained Ostfeld. “It would have been convenient if one host predicted that for us, but that has not been the case.”.

The findings demonstrate why predicting the total number of ticks is different from predicting how many of those ticks carry Lyme disease.

Another surprise emerged when the researchers compared laboratory experiments with conditions in the wild.

Previous laboratory studies had suggested that extreme heat and severe cold could kill blacklegged ticks. Yet observations in natural habitats revealed that the insects were far more resilient than expected.

The researchers suspect that ticks escape dangerous temperatures by moving deeper into the soil or hiding beneath fallen leaves, where conditions are less extreme.

In a recent development, however, temperature still appears to influence tick populations in notable ways. The team found that years with generally warmer conditions tended to be followed by fewer nymphal ticks than usual.

Industry observers note that this creates an intriguing contradiction. Warmer years typically benefit mice, which should help support larger tick populations, yet the researchers have not observed a corresponding overall increase in nymphs.

Understanding how these opposing effects interact remains an important focus of the ongoing research.

Together, the discoveries suggest that Lyme disease risk is shaped by a complicated network of ecological relationships, but one that contains patterns scientists can use to make predictions.

It has been revealed that the strong connection between mouse abundance and future tick numbers could help public health officials anticipate periods of elevated risk. Likewise, recognizing that deer abundance is not a reliable predictor of nymph populations at the study site, and that severe winter weather may not substantially reduce tick numbers, could improve disease prevention strategies.

Key questions remain, particularly about how climate change will influence the relationships among ticks, rodents, oak trees, and other wildlife.

Recent findings suggest that “You would expect that a warming climate, which makes life better for the mice, would eventually make life better for the ticks, but we have not seen that so far,” mentioned Ostfeld. “We need to know what to expect from the different manifestations of climate change, which are sometimes warmer and drier, and sometimes warmer and wetter. The time of year when it’s very warm also matters to ticks, oaks, and acorn production.”.

Since the monitoring program began in 1991, its research site in Dutchess County has undergone numerous environmental changes, including shifting climate conditions, changes to the surrounding landscape, and the arrival of invasive species.

The scientists intend to continue tracking how ticks and the animals they depend on respond to these changes. By extending an already exceptional research record, they hope to uncover more of the hidden ecological patterns that could help predict Lyme disease risk and protect human health in the years ahead.

Industry observers note that reference: “The ecology of Lyme disease: Long-term data, surprises, and a synthesis” by Richard S. Ostfeld, Shannon L. LaDeau, Kelly Oggenfuss, Charles D. Canham, Michael Fargione, Raymond J. Winchcombe and Felicia Keesing, 17 August 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2610907123.

  • Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.
  • Sources indicate that the well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

Sources indicate that the well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, claims Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

Industry observers note that chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

In a recent development, patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the upcoming study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is crucial because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, states Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Sources indicate that researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Improvements in education, lifestyle, and health during early life are slowing rates of cognitive decline in older people.Credit: Laura Olivas/Getty.
  • People born later in the twentieth century have a better memory when they enter old age and experience slower cognitive decline than do those born earlier, according to a study1 published in Nature Medicine on 17 November.
  • Recent findings suggest that the researchers analysed data from memory tests that required participants to recall lists of words.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Improvements in education, lifestyle, and health during early life are slowing rates of cognitive decline in older people.Credit: Laura Olivas/Getty.

People born later in the twentieth century have a better memory when they enter old age and experience slower cognitive decline than do those born earlier, according to a study1 published in Nature Medicine on 17 November. The analysis offers clues about why dementia rates have fallen by 13% per decade over the past 27 years in Europe and the United States2.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers analysed data from memory tests that required participants to recall lists of words. The study included 219,000 people aged 50 and older who were born between 1910 and 1964, and tracked changes in their scores over three decades. These list-based tests are commonly used to screen for dementia and Alzheimer’s disease.

It has been revealed that consistent with previous studies3, people born more recently entered old age with better memory performance compared with those born in earlier generations. A ten-year jump in birth date was associated with a 10% higher memory score at the age of 60. Memory decline also appears to have become less steep across successive generations, indicates study co-author Anders Fjell, a neuropsychologist at the University of Oslo in Norway.

Sources indicate that the findings are “confirmatory” of other studies on the topic, which indicated that the rate of memory decline is slowing down but weren’t statistically significant, states Carol Brayne, an epidemiologist who studies dementia at the University of Cambridge, UK. “It is another piece of the jigsaw.”.

It has been revealed that because many populations around the world are ageing — that is, older individuals are becoming a larger proportion of the total population — the number of people living with dementia is increasing worldwide. But an individual person’s risk of dementia at any given age has dropped by two-thirds over the past 40 years in the United States4. “For those who reach 80, a smaller percentage [of people] will get dementia than before,” explains Fjell.

Memory stays strong in old age when this brain enzyme is active.

Memory stays strong in old age when this brain enzyme is active.

It has been revealed that to understand what might be driving this trend, Fjell and his colleagues used longitudinal data on individuals’ cognitive performance to estimate their memory trajectories over time. The authors examined whether people born later in the twentieth century demonstrated differences in their memory performance and their rate of memory decline compared with those born earlier.

The analysis found that with each successive birth decade, people were 64% more likely to maintain stable memory function — that is, experience little or no memory deterioration.

The authors also investigated brain imaging data from nearly 2,000 people over a median of four years. They found that a stable memory during ageing also corresponded to a decrease in shrinkage of the hippocampus — a brain region involved in memory formation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A supplement containing a substance naturally made by gut bacteria increased blood flow to a memory-related brain region in adults with obesity, raising latest questions about its potential benefits.
  • In a recent development, when the brain works harder, it needs more blood to supply oxygen and nutrients.
  • Sources indicate that researchers at the University of Oklahoma investigated urolithin A, a substance produced when certain gut bacteria break down compounds found in foods such as strawberries, pomegranates, and walnuts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A supplement containing a substance naturally made by gut bacteria increased blood flow to a memory-related brain region in adults with obesity, raising latest questions about its potential benefits.

In a recent development, when the brain works harder, it needs more blood to supply oxygen and nutrients. For people with obesity, changes in blood vessel function can affect circulation, raising questions about how well the brain responds to these demands. A newly introduced clinical trial suggests a dietary supplement could help increase blood flow during mental activity, although researchers have yet to show that it improves memory.

Sources indicate that researchers at the University of Oklahoma investigated urolithin A, a substance produced when certain gut bacteria break down compounds found in foods such as strawberries, pomegranates, and walnuts. The amount people naturally produce varies, and existing research suggests that production declines with age and increasing body mass index. Urolithin A is also available as a dietary supplement.

In the randomized clinical trial, published in JAMA Network Open, 50 adults with obesity, ages 40 to 64, received either 1,000 milligrams of urolithin A daily or a placebo for four weeks.

Participants taking the supplement revealed a greater increase in blood flow to the brain while completing a challenging memory task. The difference was especially noticeable in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, an area involved in holding and using information over short periods. However, researchers found no significant improvements in blood vessel function in the arm or performance on memory tests.

Recent findings suggest that “The brain needs an adequate supply of blood to meet the demands of mental activity,” remarked first author Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi Langley, Ph.D., an assistant professor in the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the OU College of Allied Health on the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. “We found that urolithin A increased blood flow to the brain during a memory task, suggesting the supplement may help the brain meet its increased need for oxygen and nutrients when it is working harder. We blueprint to conduct more research to understand what this finding means for brain health.”.

Sources indicate that according to the researchers, this is the first human study to report an effect of urolithin A on blood vessel function in the brain. The supplement was well-tolerated, although the trial involved relatively few participants at a single research site. Longer studies with larger groups will be needed to determine whether the changes in blood flow lead to lasting health benefits.

“These findings offer an interesting starting point for understanding how urolithin A affects the brain,” stated study co-author Andriy Yabluchanskiy, M.D., Ph.D., an associate professor in the Department of Neurosurgery at the OU College of Medicine. “Although we saw increased blood flow to the brain during mental activity, participants did not demonstrate measurable improvements in memory or attention. Future studies will need to determine whether taking the supplement for a longer period leads to meaningful improvements in cognitive function or other health benefits.”.

The researchers ultimately hope to find ways to help people maintain their cognitive health as they age.

“The idea is to mitigate cognitive decline,” Langley mentioned. “We want to expand the time that people are living healthier lives.”.

Reference: “Urolithin A and Endothelial and Cerebrovascular Function in Middle-Aged Adults With Obesity: A Randomized Clinical Trial” by Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi-Langley, Rafal Gulej, Zalan Kaposzta, Zsofia Szarvas, Ali Shahriari, Henry Kinnard, Bryan Ticer, Camila B. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • A molecule released during exercise could help muscles fight the weakness and fatigue that make staying active so difficult for many people with type 2 diabetes.
  • Industry observers note that exercise does more than burn calories and build strength.
  • Researchers at the University of Leeds have identified a molecule that could help break that cycle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A molecule released during exercise could help muscles fight the weakness and fatigue that make staying active so difficult for many people with type 2 diabetes.

Industry observers note that exercise does more than burn calories and build strength. It triggers a complex series of chemical signals that help muscles become stronger, more efficient, and more resistant to fatigue. But for people with type 2 diabetes, muscle weakness and declining endurance can make it difficult to stay active, creating a cycle that may worsen their condition.

Researchers at the University of Leeds have identified a molecule that could help break that cycle. Known as L-β-aminoisobutyric acid (L-BAIBA), this naturally occurring compound acts as a key signal that helps muscles respond to exercise.

The researchers found that it plays an crucial role in reshaping muscle fibers, improving metabolism, and enhancing strength and endurance. It also helps protect muscles against damage and weakness associated with type 2 diabetes, raising the possibility of future treatments that preserve muscle function and make physical activity more manageable.

Published in Nature Communications, the research was led by Professor Lee Roberts and funded by Diabetes UK and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBRSC).

Exercise prompts muscles to adapt so they can better handle future demands. Scientists are still investigating how the body coordinates these adaptations, and Roberts’ team wanted to understand whether those processes could inform treatments for chronic disease.

L-BAIBA was already known for its effects on metabolism. In research published in 2014, Roberts helped show that BAIBA could boost the fat-burning effects of exercise. L-BAIBA is now sold as a nutritional supplement, although the newly introduced findings concern its biological role and potential as a future treatment.

Industry observers note that the latest study extends that earlier work by identifying L-BAIBA as a regulator of muscle remodeling. Roberts, Professor of Molecular Physiology and Metabolism at the University of Leeds, said, “Our research identifies L-BAIBA as an exercise-induced signal that helps muscles adapt, improve their metabolic capacity and ability to contract, and ultimately enhances physical performance.

“This gives us exciting new insight into how exercise benefits the body and highlights a promising target for future therapies aimed at preserving muscle function in chronic conditions such as diabetes.”.

It has been revealed that L-BAIBA’s protective effects could be particularly valuable for people with type 2 diabetes, who can experience muscle loss, declining strength, and impaired metabolism. Weakness and fatigue can make exercise harder, creating a barrier to an activity that helps manage the condition. Future treatments targeting L-BAIBA could help people stay active by improving their muscles’ resistance to fatigue.

Industry observers note that the need for better ways to manage type 2 diabetes is growing as the condition becomes more common among younger adults. Cases among people under 40 are now increasing faster than those among people over 40. The condition can lead to serious complications, including heart attacks and strokes, and develops through a complex mix of factors, with risk influenced by age, ethnicity, genetics, and living with overweight or obesity.

In a recent development, anna Morris, Assistant Director of Research Strategy and Partnership at Diabetes UK, said: “Exercise plays an crucial role in managing type 2 diabetes, but for many people muscle weakness and fatigue can make staying active a real challenge. This research helps us better understand how muscles adapt to exercise and identifies a potential new target for improving muscle health. While these findings are still at an early stage, they could help shape future approaches that support people with type 2 diabetes to remain active and live healthier, longer lives.”.

Reference: “The metabokine β-aminoisobutyric acid mediates exercise performance and skeletal muscle adaptation through a PGC1α-BAIBA-PPARδ axis” by Helene N. Daou, Nicole T. Watt, Shaimaa A. Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff, talks with reporters at the White House on April 28. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

According to recent reports, susie Wiles will depart that post and move to the Trump political organization, which appears to be in full operation, even after the president's last midterm election. Miller has been deputy chief of staff, overseeing the Trump administration's domestic policy.

Miller’s first day will be Monday, Trump said in a social media post.

The chief-of-staff change came three days after Republicans were demolished in Trump’s final midterm election, with House Democrats on pace for the largest majority in over a decade and at least a 54-seat Senate majority come January.

Trump addressed the personnel move as he departed the White House Friday for an event and weekend in Florida — though he ignored a question about his recent declaration that Wiles would be sticking around.

According to recent reports, “I wanted to make a change,” he mentioned in a roughly three-minute exchange with reporters before he walked to Marine One. “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”.

According to recent reports, trump summoned Thursday's press pool into the Oval Office for an executive order signing. On his desk was a red baseball cap with "VETO" across the front in large white lettering.

Industry observers note that miller has worked on Capitol Hill as an aide to several GOP lawmakers, including former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who became attorney general in Trump's first administration.

But making the hard-line Miller his White House chief of staff even before congressional Democrats get organized likely will draw the ire of the incoming majority.

Virginia Rep. Donald S. Beyer Jr. was among the first Democratic lawmakers to slam Trump’s decision.

Industry observers note that “Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller doubles down on the politics of hatred, lawlessness, and failure that the American people soundly rejected three days ago,” Beyer noted in a statement. "Miller embodies the worst elements of the Trump presidency. Many congressional Democrats — leaders, returning incumbents and members-elect — want to investigate Trump, his inner circle and family members while also pursuing a legislative agenda aimed at paring the cost of living.

A Study of 50,000 Children Reveals the Real Impact of Daily Iron Pills

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A major scientific review involving more than 50,000 children and adolescents reveals that daily iron supplementation can significantly reduce the risk of iron deficiency anemia.
  • A daily iron supplement can substantially reduce the risk of iron deficiency anemia in children and teenagers, but it does not appear to improve growth or protect against common illnesses.
  • Led by researchers at Cornell University’s Joan Klein Jacobs Center for Precision Nutrition and Health, the review examined daily iron supplements taken alone or combined with folic acid and other vitamins and minerals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A major scientific review involving more than 50,000 children and adolescents reveals that daily iron supplementation can significantly reduce the risk of iron deficiency anemia.

A daily iron supplement can substantially reduce the risk of iron deficiency anemia in children and teenagers, but it does not appear to improve growth or protect against common illnesses. These findings come from a major Cochrane review of 114 studies involving more than 50,000 participants.

Led by researchers at Cornell University’s Joan Klein Jacobs Center for Precision Nutrition and Health, the review examined daily iron supplements taken alone or combined with folic acid and other vitamins and minerals. Many of the studies were conducted in Asia and involved children younger than five.

According to recent reports, the strongest evidence revealed that iron alone probably reduces the risk of iron deficiency anemia compared with receiving no treatment or a placebo. Combining iron with folic acid probably offers similar protection, although that conclusion was based on just one study. Supplements containing iron alongside other vitamins and minerals may also help. Evidence suggests that iron supplementation can reduce anemia and iron deficiency more broadly, but confidence in several findings remains limited.

It has been revealed that iron is essential for producing hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that transports oxygen from the lungs throughout the body. When iron levels become too low, the body cannot produce enough healthy hemoglobin, potentially leading to iron deficiency anemia.

“Iron deficiency remains one of the most common nutritional problems affecting children worldwide,” states first author Dr Kripa Rajagopalan. “Our review demonstrates that daily iron supplements do what they are meant to do, which is reduce iron deficiency anemia, without any measurable impact on the common illnesses parents and health workers worry about.”.

Industry observers note that although iron supplements helped prevent iron deficiency anemia, the researchers found no improvement in children’s height or weight relative to others of the same age and sex. Iron alone also had no measurable effect on the occurrence of cough, fever, or respiratory illness.

Sources indicate that adding folic acid to iron made little to no difference in rates of diarrhea or respiratory illness. Results for other supplement combinations were less conclusive, with evidence ranging from moderate to very low certainty.

Sources indicate that daily iron supplementation may cause stool discoloration, but iron alone appears to have little or no effect on vomiting or diarrhea. Its relationship with constipation remains uncertain. When iron was included in supplements containing other vitamins and minerals, vomiting was probably more common than with otherwise identical supplements that lacked iron.

“While the evidence base supports the use of daily iron supplements where needed, some adverse effects do occur. Stool discoloration and, in some formulations, vomiting were more common with iron, and the certainty of evidence for several outcomes, including anemia and iron deficiency themselves, was low or very low,” explains senior author Dr Saurabh Mehta.

It has been revealed that uncertainty about longer-term outcomes has persisted for years. The World Health Organization’s guidelines, last updated in 2016, identified gaps in evidence concerning the long-term effects of iron supplementation in children. The newly introduced review brings together a much larger body of research, although the strength of the evidence still varies across outcomes.

Industry observers note that anemia affects an estimated 874 million children and women worldwide. Young children face a particularly heavy burden, with approximately 40% of children younger than five affected in 2019. Iron deficiency accounts for roughly half of these cases.

According to recent reports, preventing anemia is a central objective of the global health strategy for women, children, and adolescents through 2030. Iron supplementation is already widely used to prevent and treat anemia, particularly among adolescents and women in populations where iron deficiency is common.

“These findings give decision-makers a stronger evidence base for guidance on iron supplementation in children and adolescents,” claims co-author Dr Julia L. Finkelstein. “The data supports continued use of iron supplementation where iron deficiency is a concern.”.

The researchers caution that their findings do not justify giving every child or adolescent a daily iron tablet. Decisions about supplementation should account for individual nutritional needs, local rates of iron deficiency and anemia, and the specific supplement formulation being used.

In a recent development, reference: “Daily iron supplementation for prevention or treatment of iron‐deficiency anaemia in infants, children, and adolescents” by Kripa Rajagopalan, Laura Hackl, Juan Pablo Peña-Rosas, Maria Nieves Garcia-Casal, Mochammad Rizal, Neel H Mehta, Michael Roudik, Saiful Islam, Meghan M Trumbull-Kennedy, Nabila Reem Khondakar, Juan VA Franco, Julia L Finkelstein and Saurabh Mehta, 17 November 2026, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD013227.pub2.

  • Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.
  • The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, states Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”.

It has been revealed that for the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

In a recent development, by year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

In a recent development, it’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”.
