#42624. Tech Report: Scientists X-Ray a Narwhal Tusk and Discover Something Extraordinary

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1227 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Scientists X-Ray a Narwhal Tusk and Discover Something Extraordinary

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1227 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists are uncovering the secrets of narwhal tusks, revealing an unusual internal structure and upcoming possibilities for studying decades of environmental change in the Arctic.
  • It has been revealed that in the 17th century, King Frederik III of Denmark had a throne made entirely from unicorn horns.
  • Unlike the curved tusks of elephants and walruses or the incisors of beavers, the male narwhal’s tusk grows forward in an elegant spiral.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists are uncovering the secrets of narwhal tusks, revealing an unusual internal structure and upcoming possibilities for studying decades of environmental change in the Arctic.

It has been revealed that in the 17th century, King Frederik III of Denmark had a throne made entirely from unicorn horns. The extraordinary royal treasure came from an expedition he sent to Greenland, where the king knew the precious horns could be traced to a very real animal. It lived in Arctic waters, had fins instead of hooves, and was known as the narwhal. The expedition was a success, bringing the Danish ruler a throne that became a symbol of prestige and power across Europe. Yet the legendary horn was not a horn at all. It was a tooth.

And what a peculiar tooth it is. Unlike the curved tusks of elephants and walruses or the incisors of beavers, the male narwhal’s tusk grows forward in an elegant spiral. Usually, it is the left upper canine that extends through the upper lip, twisting counterclockwise as it reaches lengths of up to two meters (6.6 feet), sometimes half the animal’s body length.

That unusual shape has fascinated scientists for years. Now, an international research team has uncovered something remarkable inside the tusk. Its microscopic building blocks form two intertwined spirals that twist in opposite directions, creating a structure that helps the enormous tooth withstand mechanical stress. The findings, published in Nature Communications, offer a upcoming explanation for the anatomy behind one of nature’s most recognizable features.

According to recent reports, for all their fame, narwhal tusks still hold plenty of mysteries. Scientists do not know exactly how the animals use them, although evidence suggests they play an important role in mate selection and social interaction. Narwhals have occasionally been observed engaging in playful tusk duels, further supporting a possible connection to reproduction and social behavior. The tusks also continue growing throughout the animal’s life and can themselves reach 70 years of age.

Industry observers note that understanding how such a long, spiraling tooth remains strong requires looking far beneath its surface. “Like bones or other teeth in the animal kingdom, the narwhal tusk is a complex composite material whose structure extends from tiny nanoscale building blocks to the visible form of the entire tooth,” says Marianne Liebi, a researcher at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) and co-author of the study.

Sources indicate that most of the tusk consists of dentine, the same material that forms the core of human teeth. A thinner outer layer called cementum covers it, although in most other mammals, this tissue is normally found only around the tooth’s root. Both materials contain collagen fibers reinforced with tiny mineral crystals, combining flexibility with hardness.

Industry observers note that the arrangement works somewhat like reinforced concrete. In buildings, concrete withstands compression while a steel framework provides strength against pulling forces. In the narwhal’s tooth, collagen fibers serve as internal reinforcement, while mineral crystals provide hardness. “The narwhal tusk, too, must be both hard and flexible,” Liebi explains. “Only then can it withstand the strong hydrodynamic forces that swimming generates.”.

The challenge for the researchers was finding out how these microscopic materials relate to the enormous spiral visible from the outside.

“The collagen fibers and mineral crystals are on the nanometer scale, while the spiral of the tooth only becomes visible at centimeter and meter lengths,” Liebi explains.

Industry observers note that to connect these vastly different scales, the team turned to a specialized X-ray technique called tensor tomography. Unlike an ordinary dental X-ray, which produces an image based on how strongly tissues absorb radiation, this method uses patterns created when powerful X-rays scatter from regularly arranged structures inside a material.

“From these patterns, we can calculate how the nanometer-sized mineralized collagen fibers inside the material are oriented,” explains first author Adrian Rodriguez-Palomo, who joined the project as a PhD student at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden and later continued the research as a postdoctoral researcher at Aarhus University in Denmark.

The researchers conducted their investigations at three major European synchrotron facilities: the Swiss Light Source SLS at PSI in Villigen, Switzerland, the MAX IV Laboratory in Lund, Sweden, and the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in Grenoble, France. These facilities produce the powerful X-rays needed to examine extremely small structures.

Industry observers note that during tensor tomography, the tooth is rotated within the X-ray beam and scanned point by point. Millions of measurements are then combined to reconstruct a three-dimensional picture of its internal architecture, connecting the orientation of nanoscale fibers with the structure of the entire tooth.

After collecting this enormous amount of data, however, the scientists encountered an unexpected problem. The spiral they were searching for appeared to be missing.

“That puzzled us quite a bit,” Liebi recalls. Earlier mechanical tests had suggested that the tusk’s distinctive shape should already be reflected in the arrangement of its collagen fibers and mineral crystals. “But instead of a helix, all we saw was a regular pattern.”.

According to recent reports, the answer emerged when the researchers changed how they examined the data. Rather than concentrating on individual points within the three-dimensional images, they began comparing how those points were oriented relative to one another.

“When we compared how these points were oriented relative to each other, a directional trend began to appear,” recalls Rodriguez-Palomo. “All we had to do then was connect the dots – as in a children’s paint-by-numbers kit – and suddenly the structure became visible: two intertwined spirals.”.

According to recent reports, the outer cementum layer followed a left-handed helix, while the mineralized collagen structures within the dentine twisted in the opposite direction. Together, these interlocking spirals create an unusually stable architecture, much like the twisted strands of a rope. Their opposing orientations help the tooth resist twisting forces and other mechanical stresses while contributing to its distinctive external spiral.

The researchers are also interested in another remarkable property of narwhal tusks: their ability to preserve a record of the Arctic environment.

Led by Henrik Birkedal of Aarhus University in Denmark, the international team is investigating how tusk growth relates to environmental and climate conditions. Much like the annual rings of a tree, the growth structures within a narwhal’s tooth can provide clues about past conditions, including changes in climate and food availability.

Because the tusk grows continuously, it can preserve environmental information across much of an animal’s life, which can approach a century. A tooth once mistaken for evidence of a mythical creature may therefore also hold a decades-long record of life in the Arctic.

It has been revealed that reference: “The narwhal tusk assembles its macroscopic helix from building blocks with opposing twists” by Adrian Rodriguez-Palomo, Peter Alling Strange Vibe, Dimitra Athanasiadou, Jonas Palle, Leonard C. Nielsen, Jonathan T. Avaro, Thorbjørn Erik Køppen Christensen, Nina Kølln Wittig, Mads Ry Vogel Jørgensen, Innokenty Kantor, Manfred Burghammer, Jiliang Liu, Stefano Checchia, Christian Appel, Karl Anker Jørgensen, Eva Garde, Mads Peter Heide-Jørgensen, Marianne Liebi and Henrik Birkedal, 18 August 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75689-z.

The study is part of the NordForsk-funded research project “Narwhal tusks – a tale with a twist.” It was supported by the European Union’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation program under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie program.

#42622. Industry News: Scientists Just Challenged a Decades-Old Belief About How Cells Work

Industry News: Scientists Just Challenged a Decades-Old Belief About How Cells Work

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (598 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The tools scientists use to study cells may be changing the very proteins they observe, raising questions about decades of research into how cells maintain their structure.
  • For decades, textbooks and hundreds of scientific papers have described coronin proteins as vital organizers of the internal framework that gives cells their shape and helps them move.
  • In a recent development, coronins are found in organisms ranging from single-celled amoebae to humans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tools scientists use to study cells may be changing the very proteins they observe, raising questions about decades of research into how cells maintain their structure.

For decades, textbooks and hundreds of scientific papers have described coronin proteins as vital organizers of the internal framework that gives cells their shape and helps them move. Now, researchers at the University of Basel in Switzerland are revisiting that longstanding explanation, showing how scientific progress can sometimes begin by questioning what we thought we already knew.

In a recent development, coronins are found in organisms ranging from single-celled amoebae to humans. They are involved in essential processes such as immunity, development, and cell survival. Scientists have traditionally viewed them as proteins that interact with actin, a major component of the cytoskeleton. This network of tiny filaments supports a cell’s structure, allows it to move, and helps organize its contents.

A newly introduced study published in PLOS Biology, led by Professor Jean Pieters at the University of Basel’s Biozentrum, challenges that understanding. Using a broad range of experiments to examine coronins in their natural state, the researchers found that these proteins are largely unnecessary for the overall organization of the actin cytoskeleton.

“Over the years, my laboratory failed to find evidence for a direct role of coronin proteins in actin binding and modulation across a wide range of model systems,” notes Pieters. “Even cells lacking coronins continue to organize and remodel their actin networks normally. Of course, absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.”.

In a recent development, the team also identified a possible reason why earlier studies reached different conclusions. To observe proteins inside living cells, scientists often attach molecular tags that make them easier to track. Although these tools are widely used, they can sometimes interfere with the proteins being studied.

“These tags are extremely useful and assumed to be innocuous for protein function,” indicates Roko Gvozdenica, the study’s first author. “However, we found that the tagging of coronin proteins has the potential to cause loss of their function and significantly alter their localization.”.

Industry observers note that this raises the possibility that some earlier evidence linking coronins to actin resulted from experimental artifacts rather than their natural behavior. The researchers also found that many antibodies used to detect coronins lack specificity, adding to broader concerns about the reliability of these tools in biomedical research.

The findings bring attention to another important role of coronins: helping cells communicate through chemical signals.

“Over the years, we have reported that coronins are involved in cell signaling,” emphasizes Pieters. “In the immune system, for example, coronin involvement in these signaling processes was found to be essential for the maintenance of normal T cell numbers, which is vital for protecting the body against infections or cancer.”.

In a recent development, the researchers caution that their findings do not completely rule out a connection between coronins and the cytoskeleton. These proteins may still influence its organization, either directly or indirectly through cell signaling.

By reexamining an idea that has shaped research for decades, the study opens upcoming possibilities for understanding how coronins help cells communicate, survive, and maintain healthy cell numbers.

Reference: “Reassessment of the roles of coronin proteins as actin effectors and in signaling” by Roko Gvozdenica Šipić, Haiyan Zhang, Andrii Kharin, Jerneja Koren, Viviana D’Otolo, Yuko Nariai, Takeshi Urano, Pawel Pelczar, Klemens Fröhlich, Alexander Schmidt, Urszula Brykczynska Kunzmann, Tohnyui Ndinyanka Fabrice, Alexey Baldin and Jean Pieters, 18 August 2026, PLOS Biology. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pbio.3003904.

#42620. Scientists Solve a Longstanding Mystery About the Tiny Gateways That Protect Our DNA

Scientists Solve a Longstanding Mystery About the Tiny Gateways That Protect Our DNA

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Protecting our DNA takes a surprisingly flexible defense, and scientists have uncovered how cells keep this microscopic barrier fluid rather than letting it harden.
  • It has been revealed that every minute, tens of thousands of molecules pass through tiny gateways in the membrane surrounding a cell’s nucleus, where its genetic material is stored.
  • “As the nuclear pore protects the genome and controls all exchange between the cell nucleus and the cytoplasm, it is one of the most important molecular machines in the human cell,” noted Professor Miao Yu of Wuhan University in China, a co-first author of a latest study published in Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Protecting our DNA takes a surprisingly flexible defense, and scientists have uncovered how cells keep this microscopic barrier fluid rather than letting it harden.

It has been revealed that every minute, tens of thousands of molecules pass through tiny gateways in the membrane surrounding a cell’s nucleus, where its genetic material is stored. Known as nuclear pores, these openings allow certain molecules to enter or leave while blocking others. Scientists have long understood the structure of these gateways, yet the proteins controlling what gets through have remained a mystery. Do they form a rigid barrier, or something more like a constantly shifting liquid?

“As the nuclear pore protects the genome and controls all exchange between the cell nucleus and the cytoplasm, it is one of the most important molecular machines in the human cell,” noted Professor Miao Yu of Wuhan University in China, a co-first author of a latest study published in Nature. “And also one of the most complex,” added co-first author Maziar Heidari of the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics (MPI-BP) in Frankfurt am Main, Germany.

Much of the uncertainty comes from how differently these proteins behave outside living cells. Previous experiments with isolated proteins produced everything from stretched chains to liquid-like droplets and thick gels resembling gummy bears. Some even formed solid deposits.

Industry observers note that however, those observations could not establish what happens inside an actual nuclear pore, where thousands of molecular interactions help control traffic. “Such studies did not, however, allow any direct conclusions to be drawn about how the barrier behaves within the living cell,” stated Professor Edward Lemke, Professor of Synthetic Biophysics at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU).

Industry observers note that to investigate the barrier in its natural environment, Lemke and his colleagues attached fluorescent dyes to proteins inside the nuclear pores of living cells. These tiny glowing markers allowed the researchers to track protein movement and determine how flexible the barrier remained. The proteins moved rapidly throughout the entire two-hour observation period, indicating that the interior of the pore behaves more like a fluid than a solid.

It has been revealed that “For the first time, we have been able to measure intrinsic protein dynamics within the nanocanal of a living cell and demonstrate that the interior of this canal is fluid-like,” said Lemke, who led the study alongside Professor Gerhard Hummer of MPI-BP. “As the dyes move extremely quickly, the state inside the nuclear pores must be fluid-like,” he explained.

According to recent reports, the contrast became clearer when the researchers compared their observations with proteins isolated in a test tube. After approximately two hours, the protein material consistently hardened into a gummy-bear-like gel or an even more rigid solid. Some of these deposits resembled protein accumulations associated with neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. Inside living cells, however, the barrier remained flexible over the same period. “This was a crucial turning point: there had to be something keeping the barrier in the cells dynamic,” noted Lemke.

According to recent reports, the researchers identified two components that helped explain the difference. One was a transport receptor, a protein involved in moving molecules through nuclear pores. The other was glycosylation, a process that attaches sugar groups to proteins and helps prevent them from sticking together too tightly. When both were included in the laboratory model, the proteins regained much of the mobility observed in living cells. “When we add these two components, we observe a similar mobility in the model system to that found in the nuclear pores of living cells,” stated Lemke.

In a recent development, understanding the barrier’s flexibility also helped the team tackle another longstanding puzzle: where molecules actually travel as they pass through the pore. In an ordinary pipe or river, flow is generally fastest near the center and slower along the edges. Earlier research suggested that nuclear pores work differently, with much of the transport occurring near their outer walls. One proposed explanation was that a biological structure, possibly a plug, occupied the middle and forced molecules toward the sides.

Hummer’s team investigated this possibility using what the researchers describe as the most comprehensive simulation model of a nuclear pore developed to date. The model incorporated experimental measurements from the Mainz team, including how extensively the barrier proteins were linked to one another. It allowed the researchers to examine how molecules would move through a pore with the physical properties they had measured.

“The simulations confirm that the main transport route runs along the edge of the pore,” mentioned Hummer. Importantly, the calculations showed that this pattern could emerge from the pore’s physical and chemical properties without requiring a central obstruction. “While we do not rule out a biological cause such as a plug, it is not necessary from a physicochemical point of view.”.

Producing such a detailed model required enormous computing power. “These complex calculations were made possible by JUPITER, Europe’s first exascale supercomputer at the Jülich Research Center,” said Hummer.

Recent findings suggest that the experiments and simulations provide a clearer picture of how nuclear pores maintain a flexible barrier while regulating the movement of molecules into and out of the nucleus. They may also help researchers investigate why proteins that normally remain flexible sometimes harden into deposits, a process involved in neurodegenerative diseases.

Reference: “Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores” by Miao Yu (于淼), Maziar Heidari, Karen Palacio-Rodriguez, Hao Ruan (阮浩), Sara Mingu, Yu Chen (陈宇), Xu-Zhuo Gou (缑绪卓), Pingkai Shen (沈平恺), Songzi Liu (刘松子), Si-Yu Chen (陈思宇), Alam Ahmad Hidayat, Mathis Bode, Mateusz Sikora, Ai-Hui Tang (唐爱辉), Gerhard Hummer and Edward A. Lemke, 11 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11258-0.

Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (687 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.
  • Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting firm in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

The ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

Recent findings suggest that in the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

It has been revealed that the largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a big hint, McConnell indicates, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”.

It has been revealed that the most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Tech giant. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, indicates Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”.

Sources indicate that based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, presently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Sources indicate that beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Organization installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data demonstrated, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell notes, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”.

According to recent reports, these new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the newly introduced Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, mentioned Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

Recent findings suggest that “I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries stated on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”.

Industry observers note that departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

It’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for latest members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

Sources indicate that “I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island mentioned in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build significant things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs.”.

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

According to recent reports, "We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., remarked in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

There’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the latest Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

Industry observers note that “One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., remarked in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”.

It has been revealed that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

According to recent reports, absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy stated in a Friday statement.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that most of the sodium Americans eat comes from packaged and prepared foods.
  • Starting in December, a latest FDA rule will let food makers replace some or all of the added salt in products such as bread, cheese, and canned vegetables.
  • That could make a difference because Americans get more than 70% of their sodium from packaged and prepared foods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that most of the sodium Americans eat comes from packaged and prepared foods. A newly introduced FDA rule could help cut sodium at the source.

Starting in December, a latest FDA rule will let food makers replace some or all of the added salt in products such as bread, cheese, and canned vegetables.

That could make a difference because Americans get more than 70% of their sodium from packaged and prepared foods.

One option is a salt blend that replaces some sodium chloride with potassium chloride. Few Americans use salt substitutes at home.

In a recent development, daniel W. Jones, a professor emeritus at the University of Mississippi School of Medicine, chaired the committee that wrote the 2025 U.S. blood pressure guideline, which recommends potassium-enriched salt substitutes.

In the journal JAMA, Jones stated the FDA rule could help reduce sodium intake.

Sources indicate that table salt is sodium chloride. In a potassium-enriched salt substitute, some of that sodium chloride is replaced with potassium chloride.

Potassium chloride is a salt made with potassium in place of sodium.

Recent findings suggest that according to Jones, a blend of 25% to 30% potassium chloride is recommended. A higher proportion is not accepted by American tastes, which is part of the reason.

Stores sell a wider range, from blends of equal parts to pure potassium chloride. The equal-part products are usually labeled “light” salt.

Wanpen Vongpatanasin of UT Southwestern Medical Center directs the center’s section on hypertension.

Vongpatanasin noted that blood vessels are affected by sodium and potassium in opposite ways. Sodium makes arteries stiffer, while potassium generally relaxes the blood vessels.

“You get a twofer with a potassium-enriched salt substitute,” Jones said.

According to recent reports, A person who switches consumes less sodium and more potassium, he added. Both changes are considered healthy.

In a recent development, blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury, the units used in a reading such as 120 over 80. Jones noted that a blend with 25% potassium chloride lowers blood pressure by 5 to 7 points on average.

The top number is lowered by 8 to 10 points with most blood pressure drugs, he added.

Jones also explained the significance of such a drop for people with high blood pressure. Their risk of heart attack, heart failure, stroke, and kidney disease is reduced with every 10 points lost.

The reduction was estimated by Jones at about 15% to 20%.

In a recent development, the substitute was tested in a trial that was published in 2021 and conducted in 600 villages in rural China. The 20,995 participants had either survived a stroke or were at least 60 years old with high blood pressure.

The villages that received the potassium blend were selected at random and the remaining villages continued to use regular salt. One quarter of the blend consisted of potassium chloride.

The participants were followed for almost five years. About 29 strokes a year were recorded among every 1,000 people who cooked with the blend.

Roughly 34 strokes a year were recorded among every 1,000 people who used regular salt.

Deaths from any cause were also less frequent in the villages that used the blend. Blood pressure differed less than Jones’s average. The top number was about 3 points lower in villages using the blend.

Vongpatanasin and her colleagues examined how many people use these products. A national health survey of about 37,000 U.S. adults was analyzed for that purpose.

Sources indicate that in the survey years 2013 and 2014, 5.4% of adults remarked they used a salt substitute. No other survey round recorded a higher share. By 2017 to 2020, that figure was 2.5%.

Sources indicate that use was low throughout and later fell by more than half. A substitute was rarely used by patients being treated for high blood pressure, either. Fewer than 1 in 10 of them reported it.

Taste is one reason. Vongpatanasin noted that potassium chloride can taste bitter or briny. The effect is stronger in larger amounts and for people who prefer heavily salted food.

It has been revealed that she advised cooking with the substitute, along with other seasonings, instead of sprinkling it on cooked food. People become accustomed to the taste in about two weeks, Jones remarked.

According to recent reports, cost was also identified as a barrier in the 2025 guideline in which the World Health Organization suggested the switch. The guideline noted that the blends can cost more than regular salt and that public awareness is low.

A small consulting arrangement with the drugmaker AstraZeneca has been disclosed by Vongpatanasin.

She is also named as a co-inventor on a University of Texas patent for potassium magnesium citrate. No revenue has been generated by that patent to date.

Only a small part of dietary sodium is changed when a household switches completely to a substitute.

Roughly 11% of the sodium eaten by Americans is added during cooking or at the table. That estimate was reported by the FDA.

In a recent development, average intake in the United States has been put at about 3,400 milligrams a day by the same agency. About 2,300 milligrams of sodium are contained in one teaspoon of table salt.

Federal dietary advice sets that amount as the daily limit, and the 2025 heart guideline aims for less than 1,500.

The recommendation of the WHO applies only to salt that people add themselves.

This limit was explained by Rain Yamamoto, a scientist in the nutrition and food safety department of the agency.

The advice is most relevant in countries where most salt is consumed through home cooking, Yamamoto remarked. The United States does not belong to that group of countries.

“Standards of identity” are maintained by the FDA for foods such as bread, sour cream, and mayonnaise.

Industry observers note that the ingredients that a product needs before it can carry such a name are listed in each standard. Salt was allowed or required under 139 of those standards while a substitute was not permitted.

In October, the agency issued a final rule that lifted the restriction on substitutes in all 139 standards. Some or all of the salt in those foods may be replaced when the rule takes effect in December.

The affected foods include mayonnaise, salad dressing, many cheeses, canned vegetables, canned fish, bread, and pasta.

Potassium-enriched salt is not suitable for every patient. People with chronic kidney disease, especially end-stage disease, should not use potassium-based substitutes.

Other types of substitute such as herb blends can still be used by those patients.

In a recent development, blood potassium can also be raised by several kinds of medicine. Some diuretics are included in that group and are commonly known as water pills.

Sources indicate that two common families of blood pressure drugs are included as well. These are the ACE inhibitors such as enalapril and the angiotensin receptor blockers such as losartan.

A doctor should be consulted first by patients on those drugs so that blood potassium can be monitored.

The WHO’s recommendation excludes pregnant women and children because evidence in these groups is limited.

Serious events linked to high blood potassium occurred at similar rates in both groups.

However, the trial had excluded people with serious kidney disease and people who were taking potassium supplements. Blood potassium was also not tested routinely during the trial.

No fresh labeling requirements were added by the FDA rule, which makes those exclusions relevant to packaged food.

A required warning about high potassium on those foods was declined by the agency. Potassium chloride will still be listed by name among the ingredients.

Use of a substitute is allowed by the FDA rule but no manufacturer is obliged to change a recipe.

No minimum level of replacement was set and no penalties were listed for companies that keep regular salt.

The rule leaves the choice of substitute to manufacturers.

In a recent development, potassium chloride is mentioned in the rule as one example beside yeast extracts, MSG, and amino acids. Sodium in bread or cheese could therefore be lowered by a manufacturer with no potassium added.

Sources indicate that A related question was left open by the 2021 trial in China. The blend was used for home cooking in that trial and people who ate most meals elsewhere had been excluded.

Packaged food that already contains the blend was not examined in that trial.

According to recent reports, concern about the rest of the diet was expressed by Sotiria Everett, who is a dietitian at Stony Brook University. Little effect is expected from cooking with a substitute if deli meats, cheese, and bacon are still eaten, she remarked.

A fruit or vegetable at every meal was recommended by Everett because potassium intake is then increased naturally.

Industry observers note that the rule was published on October 13 and takes effect 60 days later in December. A report on progress toward the voluntary sodium targets of the FDA is also expected later in 2026.

The decision to use potassium salt in pursuit of those targets will be made by each manufacturer.

The full report was published in the journal JAMA.

America’s biggest data centers use nearly as much electricity as an entire state

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A study estimates that 403 major U.S.
  • It has been revealed that every backed-up photo, every chatbot answer and every streamed show lives somewhere called the cloud, which sounds like nowhere at all.
  • Industry observers note that at the high end of the estimate, 403 of the largest U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A study estimates that 403 major U.S. data centers used 82 terawatt-hours of electricity in a year, with natural gas and coal supplying more than half.

It has been revealed that every backed-up photo, every chatbot answer and every streamed show lives somewhere called the cloud, which sounds like nowhere at all. It is a set of windowless warehouses.

Industry observers note that at the high end of the estimate, 403 of the largest U.S. data centers together used nearly as much electricity in a year as Indiana uses statewide.

More than half of that electricity came from burning gas and coal.

A team led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative mapped 403 of these buildings, known as hyperscale data centers.

The researchers then estimated what each one drew from the grid between May 2024 and April 2025.

The totals are estimates built from each building’s electrical capacity, not meter readings.

“Data centers are growing incredibly fast, driven largely by AI, and decisions about where to build them and how to power them are being made right now,” said lead author Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics.

“But there’s very little facility-level information about their environmental footprint.”.

“Our study helps fill that gap,” Guidi added.

Sources indicate that hyperscale data centers are the largest class of data center, the kind that runs cloud services and trains big AI models. The buildings in the sample had an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.

Industry observers note that the team started with 675 candidate sites from a commercial database and kept the 403 it could confirm. Each address was matched to a rooftop and its footprint checked against OpenStreetMap.

Then the researchers looked at satellite and aerial images for the signs of a data center: big uniform roofs, cooling equipment and a substation next door.

It has been revealed that virginia had 142 of the 403, more than any other state. Oregon had 56 and Ohio 38.

No data center runs at its full rated capacity every hour, and the companies don’t publish their real loads. So the team multiplied each facility’s capacity by the hours in a year and by a load factor.

The researchers ran four versions of that factor, from a light load to one meant to bracket heavy AI training.

Across the four versions, the 403 facilities used an estimated 68 to 99 terawatt-hours of electricity over the year. The central estimate is about 82 terawatt-hours, or roughly 1.8% of all the electricity the country used.

In a recent development, indiana, Michigan and Tennessee each use about 100 terawatt-hours a year. So at the high end these warehouses matched a whole state, and even the central estimate covers most of one state’s use.

The central figure is about 3.6 times a 2021 estimate of what hyperscale centers used in 2018. Projections of AI’s appetite for electricity look ahead; this study counts the buildings that exist now.

To work out where the electricity came from, and the power emissions behind it, the team assigned each data center to its regional grid operator.

The team then allocated the data centers’ electricity demand across power plants in each region based on how much electricity each plant generated.

The plant-by-plant generation and emissions figures came from the Environmental Protection Agency.

On that basis, 53.9% of the electricity came from fossil fuels: 38.2% from natural gas and 15.2% from coal.

Nuclear plants supplied 20.9%, and hydro, wind, solar, biomass and geothermal together supplied 25.3%. Nuclear and renewables together fell short of half.

According to recent reports, the result was about 25.7 million metric tons (28.3 million U.S. tons) of carbon dioxide under the central version, and 21 to 31 million metric tons across all four.

In a recent development, A 2021 study estimated that U.S. hyperscale data centers were responsible for greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to about 10.5 million metric tons of carbon dioxide in 2018.

Virginia alone accounted for about 21 terawatt-hours, roughly a quarter of the total. Oregon followed with about 11, Ohio with about 9 and Iowa with about 7.

Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa together made up more than half of the electricity use, so the industry is heavily concentrated.

Oregon’s data centers drew more electricity than Ohio’s. Yet Oregon’s were tied to about 1.3 million metric tons of carbon dioxide and Ohio’s to 2.9 million, because Oregon’s grid runs far cleaner.

The fuel mix behind each state’s grid decides the carbon.

Virginia’s data centers were tied to about 7 million metric tons, the most of any state.

It has been revealed that PJM, the grid operator serving Virginia, oversaw the region with the highest data center electricity demand. Its territory spans parts of 13 states and the District of Columbia.

There, about 60% of the attributed electricity came from fossil fuels and 33% from nuclear plants.

The method gives each data center the average fuel mix of its regional power grid. It doesn’t trace which plant physically fed which building.

In a recent development, it also doesn’t count the renewable power contracts some operators sign, unless that power demonstrates up in the regional mix. The authors wrote that the numbers describe the grid, not any organization’s performance.

Measured that way, the data centers’ electricity was slightly cleaner than the national average: about 314 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour against 348 for the country.

About 23% of the demand, though, sat in regions dirtier than that average.

Recent findings suggest that the data also can’t separate AI work from ordinary cloud computing inside a building. And the 272 candidate sites the team couldn’t verify were left out, so the totals likely run low for the industry as a whole.

Guidi stated the picture has already moved on.

“The data center boom hasn’t slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. Newly introduced facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow,” he remarked.

The researchers estimated electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions.

The team plans to examine the health effects next, according to study co-author Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative.

“The fossil fuel power plants in the regional electricity systems associated with this demand also release other pollutants, such as fine particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide, that are directly linked to heart and lung disease and premature death,” Dominici said.

The people who breathe those pollutants live near the power plants, which may be far from any data center.

Earth.com has covered the industry’s other local footprints, from heat zones around server farms to the one in four data centers in water-stressed regions.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Sustainability.

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that carpet cleaning is one of those chores that feels like a massive undertaking every time—not to mention, no one likes having to lug around a heavy carpet cleaner sloshing with water. The Bissell TurboClean Upright Carpet Cleaner is made for people like us, with a lightweight design and minimal learning curve.

Sources indicate that this machine is great for small spaces, and for those who prefer streamlined and simplified household appliances. Although it does have a smaller water tank capacity and lacks handheld attachments, it provides a powerful clean paired with easy maneuverability and fast drying time.

The compact design makes it easy both to use and to store. It’ll be sitting alongside your favorite dry vacuum as a trusted staple of your cleaning routine in no time, as I found to be the case for myself.

In a recent development, I set aside a weekend morning to test the TurboClean upright across a frequently used area of my main living space, spanning the pathway from the door to the garage through to the kitchen. The area includes some carpet that I've vacuumed frequently, but not deep-cleaned in years, as well as a low-pile area rug. I didn’t pretreat the area with dry vacuuming, but I checked for any larger pieces of debris that might clog up the cleaner.

It has been revealed that the cleaner was quick and easy to assemble, and filling the water tank was simple too. I followed the manufacturer’s instructions to add some of the included Bissell cleaning solution along with warm water. Afterward, I tackled my designated area of carpeting, followed by a section of the area rug.

It has been revealed that throughout the process, I monitored how well the cleaner performed in a few ways. I kept an eye on how long the water tank lasted before I had to empty the dirty water and refill the clean tank, as well as how many times I had to go over an area for a satisfactory clean. I also maneuvered the machine as close as possible to the baseboards and into corners to test movability and range. Finally, I checked how long it took for the carpet to dry afterward, as well as how easy it was to clean the machine when I wrapped it all up.

The first thing I noticed about the TurboClean Upright was its lightness. Weighing just under 13 pounds, it’s one of the lightest carpet cleaners I’ve tried. That light weight, combined with a compact base and smooth wheels, made it especially easy to move around, whether I was pulling it along straight pathways, turning corners, or navigating as close to the wall as I could get. Even with a full tank, I found it very manageable.

Recent findings suggest that that lightness, though, didn’t mean flimsiness or poor performance. On the contrary: it pulled up considerably more dirt than I expected, providing a deep, visible clean on a high-traffic area of light-colored carpet.

While I didn’t have any serious stains for it to handle, it did do a great job on visible spots of dirt or water-drop stains that had become dried-in. It worked equally well on the area rug, refreshing it without damaging the fibers or dulling the colors.

As a compact machine, the TurboClean Upright does have one of the hallmark downsides to its class: the need for frequent refills. The water tank has a capacity of just over half a gallon. As I worked through my test area, I had to stop, empty the dirty water tank, and refill the cleaner with fresh water and cleaning solution.

In a recent development, if you’re trying to spot-clean a few small patches, you can probably get away without a refill, but if you’re actually doing a whole room or more, you’ll need to do the empty-and-refill routine—probably multiple times. It’s also worth noting that the machine does not heat the water from within. It recommends adding warm water (no warmer than 140°F) to the clean tank with the solution.

Fortunately, the process of refilling and, later, disassembling and cleaning, is very easy. The tank and handle feel a little light to the touch, but they’re sturdier than they seem, and it’s easy to get a grip and handle the empty/refill cycle without making a mess. Disassembling the main parts (the upper tank and the two-part handle) is as easy as the push of a button. There’s really very little in the way of maintenance, which I appreciated.

If you plan on cleaning an area with a lot of debris (like pet hair), I would suggest vacuuming first. Otherwise, you do run the risk of particles getting tangled up around the cleaning brush, which can take a while to get cleared.

It has been revealed that for me, the biggest downside to this cleaner is its lack of any hand tools. Where most home carpet cleaners come with at least a handheld tool or a spot-cleaning tool of some kind, the basic model TurboClean Upright has none. While it’s still a light and small enough machine to maneuver around most spaces, the lack of extensions and tools does limit what it can do.

I was able to lower it enough to clean underneath a coffee table, and I could get fairly close to the wall, but not quite as deep into the corners. I wish there had been a stain tool, a pet tool, or even just a simple hand tool extension. Without those, the cleaner is unable to handle smaller crevices or upholstery.

According to recent reports, I didn’t have any deep, dark stains that needed removing, but if I did have those, it would have been nice to be able to really focus the cleaning power on those areas. As currently designed, the best I could do was simply run the full cleaner over the same spot repeatedly.

According to recent reports, all that being stated, the TurboClean Upright does come in a deluxe “Pet” model as well. That model does include a 7-foot extendible hose, a self-cleaning “tough stains” brush, and a spraying crevice tool. Those additions offer more flexibility to tackle small spots and get into crevices, improving the cleaner’s performance and versatility. And, of course, anyone with pets will definitely want to look into this upgrade to gain the extra cleaning power for pet stains and hair.

The TurboClean Upright comes with two trial-size Bissell cleaning formulas: the Pro Max Clean + Protect and the Pet Pro Oxy Urine Eliminator. I used the Pro Max solution for deep cleaning, adding it to the clean tank up to the indicated “formula” line. The instructions also indicate that users can add a dose of the “Oxy Boost” formula for a stronger cleaning reaction, but since I didn’t have that on hand, I skipped that step.

After multiple passes across my testing area, I really appreciated the strong suction power. Although there’s not a specific “quick dry” mode, the manual does suggest running “dry passes” across the wet areas to suction up as much of the residual water as possible. It only took between one and two hours for the test section to feel pretty much dry to the touch.

In a recent development, the Bissell TurboClean Upright is ideal for smaller spaces and intuitive operation, bringing plenty of cleaning power but keeping the machine itself relatively compact and lightweight. I was able to easily clean carpeting and an area rug, and I could move around corners easily.

The smaller size does mean a smaller tank (requiring more frequent stops to refill), and I wish the standard model included some attachment tools for greater versatility. Still, if you’re looking for a reliable cleaner for a smaller area that does the job well (and doesn’t leave your carpet sopping wet), this could be a great pick for you.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.
  • Sources indicate that the fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

Sources indicate that the fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

Sources indicate that that species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other newly introduced related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” claims Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Recent findings suggest that discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik states. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve latest traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

In a recent development, ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

Sources indicate that the two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

According to recent reports, and there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle states. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

It has been revealed that “Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

“After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said on Monday evening.

Asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”.

Industry observers note that though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I noted, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”.

Sources indicate that johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

It has been revealed that also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”.

Kennedy stated Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he mentioned, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”.

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”.

According to recent reports, but Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, stated she has seen such requests debuted in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides remarked that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the prepares and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

Recent findings suggest that that includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”.

In a recent development, republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott noted. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”.

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

In a recent development, an online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”.

Banks similarly noted Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”.

Recent findings suggest that one senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday noted the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Sources indicate that cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”.
