Breaking: The 8 Best Salt Spreaders for Getting Out Ahead of Winter Storms

📅 16 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2461 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Winter doesn’t have to be severe for ice to be a problem—even one small storm can leave a slippery layer of frozen water that causes a fall.
  • Snow melt, typically rock salt or calcium chloride, melts existing ice and prevents new ice from forming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Winter doesn’t have to be severe for ice to be a problem—even one small storm can leave a slippery layer of frozen water that causes a fall. But putting down a simple layer of snow melt can easily prevent any accidents. It can also reduce the amount of time you have to mess with shovels or snowblowers. But believe it or not, how you put it down matters, and the best salt spreaders are there to guide you.

Snow melt, typically rock salt or calcium chloride, melts existing ice and prevents new ice from forming. Using a salt spreader, which spins and sprays your snow melt all around, helps ensure you get a nice, even coat over any area you prep. Gardeners may recognize the salt spreader as a close cousin of the fertilizer spreader, but with a more robust construction to endure winter weather and the corrosive nature of salt.

It has been revealed that salt spreaders come in a wide array of sizes to suit different jobs, including small handheld spreaders for front stoops and short walkways, walk-behind models for a long driveway, and large tow-behind spreaders for prepping parking lots. Whether you need to de-ice a front walk or an entire parking lot, we can help you find the best salt spreader for your snow removal situation.

Industry observers note that tony Carrick tapped his experience covering landscaping, home improvement, gardening, and home security to find the salt spreaders worth the money. Reviews Editor David Dritsas—who covers landscaping, tools, and DIY, including outdoor tools like snow blowers and snow shovels—then updated these recommendations ahead of winter. They picked the best salt spreaders based on their experiences using various models to treat driveways and sidewalks around the home. They also researched industry standards, detailed specifications, and user recommendations from customer reviews.

According to recent reports, this salt spreader’s size, ability to control salt flow, and reasonable price tag make it a great all-around choice for salt spreading. With its 80-pound capacity, it can cover the average driveway, as well as sidewalks and walkways in a single load. It also comes well equipped to handle winter weather with large, pneumatic 12-inch wheels and a sturdy steel frame.

The spreader features a plastic spiked auger (though we prefer a metal spiked auger) that cuts through clumps of most deicing salts, preventing clogs. You should, however, avoid using rock salt, as it is larger and could get caught in the plastic construction.

We appreciate its three adjustable baffles, which allow you to reduce or expand its coverage area to prevent overspread onto the lawn and landscaping. This is a great mid-size salt spreader and a perfect fit for most homes.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking to get the most bang for your buck out of a spreader, then go with this model from Scotts. Not only can you spread salt with it, but you can also use it to seed and fertilize your lawn. Unlike most fertilizer spreaders, this model can spread ice melt. Additionally, it features rubber tires, unlike the plastic wheels found on other Scotts spreaders, allowing it to handle icy conditions.

There’s a dial that gives you precise control over how much salt, seed, or fertilizer you’re releasing with each step—this is common on fertilizer spreaders but not so much with salt spreaders. And since it has Scott’s EdgeGuard technology, you can treat walks and driveways without showering your grass and landscaping with salt.

This combination of features makes it a great jack-of-all-trades spreader for those who want one machine for all seasons.

This top-of-the-line spreader from EarthWay can handle large jobs, holding up to 100 pounds, with holes and an auger large enough to pass rock salt up to 3 inches in size, plus a very large, 15-foot spread width.

It’s a little bit heavier than other models on our list—30 pounds alone before you even add the salt—but it rolls on two large, knobby 13-inch pneumatic tires, which help you avoid slipping and sliding over icy terrain.

These features make this walk-behind model a good option for professionals or homeowners with large paved areas to prep.

In a recent development, there’s no sense investing in an expensive walk-behind salt spreader if you only have to clear a walkway or front stoop. This handheld model gets the job done and doesn’t cost much. Plus, you can use it in the warmer months to seed and fertilize small patches of lawn and landscaping beds.

There are separate spreader settings for seed, fertilizer, and ice melt, and it holds up to 2 pounds of product. It even has an ergonomic arm support that makes it relatively comfortable to hold while you’re spreading product. Sure, it would be easier to use if it were automatic, but we’ll take the low-cost manual option any day of the week.

If you only need a small spreader but don’t want to deal with a hand crank, this rechargeable electric model may work better for you. It runs on a rechargeable lithium-ion battery, and in addition to working with salt and de-icer, you can also use it for seeds and fertilizer.

It has been revealed that it has eight flow rate settings, allowing you to release as little or as much as you like, though levels 7 and 8 are intended for use with heavy salts. The speed is variable, and you can adjust the spread up to 127 degrees with a lever on the side. Narrowing the spread can help you be more precise and protect garden beds or lawns from getting salt burn.

The hopper is 2.7 liters, and the battery runs for up to two hours, making this motorized spreader more than up to the challenge of covering the driveways and sidewalks of most average homes. Since it's battery-powered and listed as not waterproof, it's recommended to clean it of any moisture when you're done using it.

Agri-Fab’s massive salt spreader offers one of the largest capacities of any non-professional-grade walk-behind model we’ve seen. Its massive hopper can hold a whopping 130 pounds of salt, which is enough to cover a long service road or an 80-car parking lot. It’s built to handle all that weight with a frame made from 1-inch-thick steel tubing. The large 12-inch pneumatic tires have heavy treads to prevent slipping on snow and ice.

Industry observers note that the heavy-duty design wouldn’t be complete without a stainless steel impeller to break up clogs. It also features a waterproof cover to keep the ice melt dry if you have to go out on a rainy day. This commercial-grade salt spreader is built for big jobs.

If you’ve got an ATV or lawn tractor and a lot of ground to cover, spare your back and mount this towable spreader. With its 185-pound capacity, a single load can cover up to an acre of soon-to-be-snowy ground.

Sources indicate that the universal hitch will work with all tractors, UTVs, and ATVs. The control rod extends far enough that you won’t have to get out of the driver’s seat to adjust the flow of salt. Its 15-inch pneumatic tires and thick-gauge steel frame keep it stable, even when pulled a little too fast. There’s also a hopper cover that keeps the salt from getting wet while working in rain or snow.

This is a great option if you have a long driveway or a large parking area to cover.

Due to its mountable design, this salt spreader gives you the capacity of a towable spreader, but won’t compromise the maneuverability of a four-wheeler. This semipro spreader can hold up to 15 gallons of ice melt, which means it’s really made for prepping long service roads, parking lots, and commercial spaces, rather than homes.

The ATVS15A spreader uses a plate and auger powered by a 23-volt motor to launch a 30-foot-wide swath of salt. The hopper has a lid that keeps your ice melt dry and prevents it from bouncing out of the top of the hopper.

Since you sit right in front of the spreader, accessing the on/off switch and gate controls is convenient from the driver’s seat. This is a solid commercial option for contractors who need to prep worksites, workers in small communities with service roads, and commercial areas that might be easier to reach on an ATV than a truck.

These are compact, watering can-sized basins with a handle and either a hand crank or a motorized trigger mechanism. Their compact size and light weight make spreading salt easy work, provided you only need to cover a small area. They can’t hold much salt and have a limited range, so they’re best reserved for small jobs like patio doorways, stoops, or a short front walkway.

This type of spreader sits on two wheels, with a large plastic basin and a spinning impeller at the base. As you push the spreader forward, the salt shoots out the front and both sides of the basin. These wheelbarrow-esque spreaders can hold a large amount of ice melt, so they’re the way to go for most homes with large patios, parking spaces, driveways, and sidewalks.

This is one of the largest options. If you’re responsible for clearing snow off a parking lot or a long driveway that’s more than a couple of hundred feet long, you may want to get a truly massive salt spreader that hitches to the back of an ATV or riding lawn mower.

According to recent reports, some spreaders offer even larger capacities that attach to the trailer hitch on a pickup truck or mount to the back of an ATV. Obviously, these spreaders can hold a much larger amount of salt than a walk-behind. It’s overkill for most homes, but small businesses or farms could use one to prep large parking lots, loading docks, and other large paved areas.

Industry observers note that the more ice melt your salt spreader can hold, the more ground you can cover before you need to stop for a refill. As a rule of thumb, you’ll need to spread about 3 pounds of snow melt for every 1,000 square feet of area. Though there is some variation from model to model, picking the right type of spreader is the first and most vital step.

Most handheld spreaders only hold enough salt to de-ice a short walk and a front stoop; walk-behind spreaders can hold about 65 to 130 pounds of ice; and towable spreaders often hold up to 185 pounds of salt.

Spread width measures how far your spreader will throw salt as you use it. Most spreaders have a range between 6 feet for walk-behind models and as far as 30 feet for larger towable spreaders.

In a recent development, while a wide spread can save you time, keep in mind that it may also lead you to spray salt onto your lawn and landscaping. Salt will dry out plants, so you want to avoid spraying green areas as much as possible. If you need to salt sidewalks and driveways that border grass and landscaped areas, look for adjustable spreaders with baffles so you can narrow your spread and avoid overspray.

You have a few options when it comes to ice melt. Calcium chloride is the best option. It melts ice even at extreme sub-zero temperatures, won’t harm your plants, and is less toxic than rock salt, but it’s also pricier.

Rock salt is the cheapest, but‌ it’s more toxic, won’t work in extreme cold, and can clog spreaders more easily. Magnesium chloride is the least toxic option and works at temperatures as low as 5 degrees Fahrenheit.

Whichever ice melt you choose, be sure to use it as directed, as all of the above can eat away at wood, steel, and concrete.

Recent findings suggest that while they operate similarly, we don’t recommend putting rock salt in a fertilizer/seed spreader. Dedicated salt spreaders store corrosive salt and endure icy winter conditions. Using a fertilizer spreader to spread salt once or twice won’t break it, but it won’t work as well and may shorten its lifespan in the long term.

Recent findings suggest that salt spreaders typically have hoppers made from thick, durable plastic that sit on heavy-gauge steel frames and feature pneumatic rubber wheels with heavy tread that can grip slick paved surfaces. They also come equipped with metal moving parts that are capable of chopping up hard salt without wearing down.

In a recent development, if you want one spreader to do double duty, it would probably make more sense to use a salt spreader to spread seed or fertilizer. That said, fertilizer/seed spreaders often provide more precise control of the spread direction and quantity, which comes in handy when you have specific patches to cover and you want to be precise. Keep in mind that adding too much fertilizer to a lawn can cause it to burn out.

Sources indicate that if you do put fertilizer in your salt spreader (or vice versa), make sure to clean out the salt thoroughly before placing any seed or fertilizer in the hopper. Any lingering salt in the mix will dry out the grass, damaging your lawn.

Bottom line: We would recommend buying two separate spreaders, despite their similarities.

Most residential-use salt spreaders can't handle rock salt, while many professional-level salt spreaders can. Check with the manufacturer to determine what types of de-icer are compatible with your salt spreader before loading it with rock salt, as it can damage the spreader’s impeller.

If rock salt isn’t compatible with your spreader, use a different type of ice melt, such as potassium chloride, magnesium chloride, or calcium chloride.

#42600. Unusual warmth has reached the seafloor off Canada’s Pacific coast – and scientists may know why

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (937 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Unusual warmth has reached the seafloor off Canada’s Pacific coast – and scientists may know why

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A seafloor sensor off Vancouver Island logged its highest temperature since monitoring began in 2009, and researchers say El Niño may be behind the spike.
  • El Niño is usually described as a warming of the surface waters in the tropical Pacific.
  • This fall, sensors off Canada’s west coast recorded unusually warm water hundreds of feet below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A seafloor sensor off Vancouver Island logged its highest temperature since monitoring began in 2009, and researchers say El Niño may be behind the spike.

El Niño is usually described as a warming of the surface waters in the tropical Pacific.

This fall, sensors off Canada’s west coast recorded unusually warm water hundreds of feet below the surface.

Industry observers note that one seafloor sensor logged its highest temperature since monitoring began there in 2009. The scientists who operate the sensor noted the warm pulse is consistent with a strong El Niño.

The sensors are operated by Ocean Networks Canada, an ocean-monitoring initiative of the University of Victoria.

The readings were declared by the organization itself this week. They have not yet been published as a study.

Industry observers note that the record was set at a site called Barkley Canyon Upper Slope, off Vancouver Island. A sensor rests on the seafloor there, about 1,300 feet (400 meters) down. That depth is roughly a quarter of a mile.

On November 8, the water at this site reached 46.8°F (8.21°C).

Jay Cullen is the interim president and chief executive of Ocean Networks Canada.

“We’re seeing significant warming not just at the surface, but hundreds of meters below it,” Cullen noted.

According to recent reports, the November 8 reading was 4.5°F (2.49°C) above the long-term average for the site. It was also 1.6°F (0.89°C) warmer than the previous record, which was set in 2019.

Industry observers note that the water has cooled since then, but normal temperatures have not returned. In mid-November, it was still about 2.9°F (1.6°C) warmer than average.

Warm water has been found at other sites too. The Barkley Canyon sensor is one part of a much larger network. Roughly 530 miles (850 kilometers) of seafloor cable connect its five main research sites.

One of those sites is Clayoquot Slope, which lies more than 3,900 feet (1,200 meters) down. Temperatures well above average are being recorded there as well.

Since late summer, sites between 1,300 and 4,100 feet (400 and 1,250 meters) deep have logged record seasonal temperatures.

Sources indicate that the deepest site is the exception. At Cascadia Basin, about 8,700 feet (2,650 meters) down, temperatures remain within their usual range.

Sources indicate that el Niño was declared by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration in June.

On November 12, the agency’s Climate Prediction Center said El Niño was still strengthening.

It has been revealed that A strong or very strong event was judged likely to continue into early 2027. The chance of that was put at more than 79%.

How can El Niño affect waters off Canada’s Pacific coast?

Steve Mihaly is a senior scientist at Ocean Networks Canada. According to Mihaly, the energy of a strong El Niño travels north from the equatorial Pacific.

It moves as waves that follow the coastline, and oceanographers call them coastal trapped waves.

Recent findings suggest that sea level has also been above normal since the warm water arrived. The rise was recorded by tide gauges at Bamfield and Tofino, two communities on Vancouver Island.

Pressure recorders on the seafloor picked it up as well. By mid-November, sea level was about 10 inches (25 centimeters) above normal. Local wind and atmospheric effects were accounted for first.

The scientists then attributed about 6 inches (15 centimeters) of the rise to the waves.

At Barkley Canyon Upper Slope, the water temperature began climbing sharply in late October and reached a record on November 8.

Mihaly mentioned northwest winds persisted into the fall, pushing warmer surface water offshore and drawing colder water upward.

This process, known as upwelling, helped mask the warming at depth.

A second network, called VENUS, is run by Ocean Networks Canada in the Salish Sea.

According to recent reports, these sheltered waters are shared by British Columbia and Washington State. The VENUS sensors reach depths of about 980 feet (300 meters).

Temperatures in the Strait of Georgia, which is part of that sea, have been above average throughout 2026.

Jordan Watson is the science director of Ocean Networks Canada.

Industry observers note that “Since the start of 2026, the VENUS observatory has shown temperatures consistently higher than we’ve previously observed,” Watson noted. “And this was before any El Niño effects started to appear.”.

Watson described the area as known for migrating salmon, spawning herring, and marine mammals.

Recent findings suggest that warming from El Niño could add to the already high temperatures there. That would put more stress on marine ecosystems, the organization stated.

In a recent development, so far, only temperatures and sea levels have been reported by the scientists. No effects on marine life have been reported yet.

The record is also a short one. Monitoring at Barkley Canyon began in 2009, so it covers less than two decades.

The scientists were not certain about the cause either. They noted the warming likely marks the arrival of El Niño’s effects on Canada’s Pacific coast.

Cullen noted that conditions will be monitored closely over the coming months.

A fresh tool is also being planned by Ocean Networks Canada and CIOOS Pacific, a regional ocean-data group. It will track ocean conditions across the region.

The seafloor data will be combined with measurements from other groups around the Salish Sea.

Fisheries and Oceans Canada and the University of Washington are among them. More details will be shared later this year, the partners said.

Live and long-term readings can be viewed on Ocean Networks Canada’s data dashboard.

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

In a recent development, this is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

“We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown announced his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” mentioned a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:.

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of Latest Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

It has been revealed that but they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Children have been making art with help from grown-ups for millennia.

It has been revealed that fragmented clay figurines dating as far back as 15,000 years ago, discovered in what is now Israel, preserve the fingerprints of both adults and young children. The finding suggests the grown-ups taught the kids how to shape and decorate clay, researchers report November 11 in PLOS One.

Industry observers note that children’s contributions to prehistoric art and culture aren’t well understood. Concrete evidence of their involvement has been hard to find, claims archaeologist Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

In recent decades, researchers have found a handful of objects made by children — including 200,000-year-old rock art bearing child-sized handprints in Tibet and 30,000-year-old clay sculptures pockmarked with child-sized fingerprints in Czech Republic.

Industry observers note that davin and colleagues hadn’t set out to find Stone Age children’s artwork. They were investigating whether the Natufian culture — a group of hunter-gatherers who formed some of the first permanent settlements in the Levant about 14,000 years ago — made clay art before the advent of agriculture in the region.

Recent findings suggest that the archaeologists came across the first set of fingerprints while sorting through 40 kilograms of clay collected at three Natufian sites, which range in age from 15,000 to 11,600 years old. Among tens of thousands of clay lumps, the team found some 150 fragments of sculptures, including 15 recognizable bird, gazelle and human figures. Around 60 of these pieces preserved fingerprints from where people had pinched or prodded the clay.

The distances between the fingerprints’ ridges, which are influenced by age and sex, suggest that most of the figurines were made by women and children — some younger than 10. Only a few sets of fingerprints belonged to men. And the torso of one tiny human statue had both adult and child fingerprints, hinting that an elder and child had passed it back and forth. Davin suspects that the adult actively taught a child how to work the clay.

It has been revealed that this evidence of intergenerational learning so far back in time is fascinating, claims archaeologist Steven Dorland of Grand Valley State University in Allendale, Mich. It demonstrates how much researchers can learn from broadening their focus beyond adult males, he says. Dorland has used pottery to understand social learning in Indigenous societies of the Great Lakes region. He has even studied children’s fingerprints on some of those artifacts.

The purpose of the Natufian figurines is unclear. Most of the statues are less than 2 centimeters long and don’t display signs of intense use, the team found, suggesting they weren’t treated as precious heirlooms.

Recent findings suggest that davin suspects the figurines may have represented stories, like how kids draw Disney characters today, he says. “Maybe the idea is that the role of children here is not necessarily to learn to make figurines, but more to learn the story behind them.”.

Europe’s Hera mission is ready to double down on asteroid science

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.
  • According to recent reports, on November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft is about to start a twofold mission to a twofold asteroid.

According to recent reports, on November 4, after more than two years trekking through space, the spacecraft finally came within 30 kilometers of space rocks named Didymos and Dimorphos. The encounter marks the first time scientists will explore a pair of asteroids navigating the solar system together. To date, spacecraft have stopped to investigate just seven other asteroids, every one of them a lonely speck in outer space.

Hera will spend the coming weeks approaching Didymos and Dimorphos and will release two small companion spacecraft in January for an even closer look.

Industry observers note that didymos, a mass of rocks about twice as wide as the Empire State Building is tall, and its small moonlet Dimorphos have had a rough time lately. In 2022, NASA slammed its Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft into Dimorphos, sending a plume of debris into space and shortening its orbit around Didymos by more than half an hour.

According to recent reports, the cosmic realignment wasn’t a mere lark. Such an impact is one of the few ways scientists can practice planetary defense, the field dedicated to searching for dangerous asteroids and developing ways to deal with them lest humans go the way of the dinosaurs. DART and Hera are a carefully coordinated pair, with Hera’s top priority being to investigate the aftermath of DART’s crash and inform future planetary defense efforts.

That process will also yield a treasure trove of observations asteroid scientists are determined to exploit.

It has been revealed that “Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” notes planetary scientist Jessica Sunshine of the University of Maryland, who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission. On the science side, she says, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”.

Sources indicate that DART purposefully targeted a binary system instead of a solo asteroid to make measuring the change in orbit it accomplished easier: Any difference would be much more obvious against the 12-hour baseline orbit of Dimorphos around Didymos than against the months- or yearslong orbit of an asteroid circling the sun. (Despite the difficulty, scientists were able to calculate that DART shortened the more-than-two-year orbit of the Didymos system around the sun by a fraction of a second.).

It has been revealed that hera’s observations will provide a crucial glimpse at binary asteroids generally, which astronomers believe account for some 15 percent of all asteroids. Scientists expect that most binary asteroids in the inner solar system, including the Didymos system, probably formed their moonlets from debris that sloughed off the larger object then clumped together in orbit.

Didymos spins so rapidly that its gravity may not be strong enough to hold all its rock together. As the asteroid spins, it may send boulders into space, where they could end up landing on Dimorphos, continuing that material transfer today. Scientists will comb through Hera’s imagery for signs of rocks moving across each object’s surface, as well as between the two objects.

Recent findings suggest that scientists expect that Dimorphos is a rubble pile composed of boulders and rocky debris. It’s similar in structure to other recent spacecraft targets Ryugu and Bennu, although those are both significantly larger. The boulder-strewn landscape DART saw as it sped toward Dimorphos aligns with this theory, but how deep the rubbly structure extends is a mystery. “We’ve never seen the interior of an asteroid before,” says planetary scientist Angela Stickle of the Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory.

It has been revealed that juventas, Hera’s companion cubesat about the size of a breadbox, will change that. It carries a first-of-its-kind radar instrument to investigate Dimorphos’ internal structure.

Sources indicate that juventas will also attempt to land on Dimorphos, allowing scientists to directly interact with the surface. That’s a particularly tantalizing endeavor given one of the biggest surprises of NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission. When that spacecraft grabbed a sample of Bennu, it accidentally sank some half a meter into the rubble as the asteroid unexpectedly gave way beneath it, even though the surface had looked perfectly sturdy.

According to recent reports, “Even though we had amazing images, the reaction was not what we expected,” indicates planetary scientist Patrick Michel of the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) of that experience. “There is still sort of a mismatch between what we see and what we feel.” He hopes that the Juventas landing will help scientists better connect appearance and reality on this front.

Although scientists will need to pick out the ways DART made Didymos and Dimorphos different from other binary asteroids, observations with Hera will offer new avenues for investigating more general questions in asteroid science.

For example, scientists know that before DART’s impact, Dimorphos always highlighted the same face to Didymos, just like our moon does to Earth. The collision probably changed that, sending Dimorphos tumbling — but there’s no way to know what state it’s in now because scientists have never seen this resetting process unfold. “Eventually, the system might stabilize, but we don’t know how long it takes,” states planetary scientist Eva Lilly of the Planetary Science Institute, who is not involved in either mission.

Industry observers note that similarly, scientists know that the rain of charged particles onto an asteroid’s surface darkens a thin layer of rock at the surface, but without the detailed understanding they’d like. At Dimorphos, they’ll be able to observe fresh rock uncovered by a known event, potentially offering clearer insight into the universal process.

Cosmic crash scene or not, asteroid scientists are never going to miss out on up-close views of two different space rocks.

Howler monkey droppings hold clues about the fragmented forests they live in

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In southern Mexico, the mix of gut bacteria in howler monkeys varied with forest patch size, the trees growing there, and how well the patches were connected.
  • Howler monkeys can survive in small patches of forest.
  • A study in southern Mexico found that the mix of bacteria in their guts varied with the size of those patches, the trees growing there, and how well the patches were connected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In southern Mexico, the mix of gut bacteria in howler monkeys varied with forest patch size, the trees growing there, and how well the patches were connected.

Howler monkeys can survive in small patches of forest.

A study in southern Mexico found that the mix of bacteria in their guts varied with the size of those patches, the trees growing there, and how well the patches were connected.

Researchers found these patterns in droppings from adult male mantled howler monkeys.

Repeating that sampling could help conservationists track changes over time without capturing the animals.

The study was led by Tabor Whitney while she was a doctoral student at Northwestern University. She worked with primate researchers at Universidad Veracruzana in Mexico.

The work was carried out in the Los Tuxtlas Biosphere Reserve in the state of Veracruz. About 60% of the original forest cover in the reserve has been lost. The remaining forest is broken into patches among pastures, farm fields, and towns.

The 10 study patches ranged from about 5 acres to nearly 500 acres (2 to 199 hectares). Farmland or pasture bordered every one of them.

Whitney and field assistants followed adult male howlers in October and November, during the 2022 rainy season. When a male defecated, the fresh droppings were collected from the ground with sterile sticks.

Industry observers note that the team tested the droppings for three things. The first was the bacteria in them. The second was the fatty acids that those bacteria produce. The third was the breakdown products of stress hormones.

According to recent reports, the trees in every patch were also measured. Across patches, average trunk width ranged from about 10 to 16 inches (25 to 42 centimeters).

Biologists call the community of microbes in an animal’s gut its microbiome.

“An awesome takeaway of the study is the knowledge the gut microbiome is the most sensitive to ecological change,” Whitney stated.

It has been revealed that gut bacteria were analyzed in 41 samples from 32 males. Monkeys from different patches carried different mixes of bacteria.

According to recent reports, these differences were linked to all four measures of a patch’s size and layout. Its area and its distance from other forest were among those measures. All seven measures of the trees growing in the patch were linked to the differences too.

Plant fiber is digested by some of the bacteria involved. One such group is Prevotella, and monkeys in larger patches carried more of it.

According to recent reports, A different group of bacteria was most common where trees were small. The same was true where few rows of trees linked a patch to other forest.

Only one forest measure predicted the diversity of bacteria carried by a monkey. That measure was trunk thickness. Less variety was found in monkeys from patches with thicker-trunked trees.

It has been revealed that the authors suggested that monkeys in mature forest may eat a narrower diet. Fewer kinds of microbes may be taken in as a result.

The team also tested distances to the nearest houses and roads. Neither distance predicted any of the three health measures in the main analysis.

Stress hormone levels were measured in 36 males. They didn’t differ clearly from patch to patch. One pattern, however, was the reverse of what the team had predicted.

Males in larger patches tended to have higher hormone levels, not lower ones.

Recent findings suggest that higher levels were also found in patches with more fig trees. Figs are a central part of the howler diet.

Recent findings suggest that the authors explained the result in social terms. Several howler groups are supported by larger patches. More than one group may be attracted to the same place by fig trees.

It has been revealed that hormone levels could be raised by competition during encounters with rival groups, not by food shortage. Ordinary demands such as reproduction and fighting infection are also known to raise these hormones.

A monkey with a high level is therefore not necessarily in trouble.

Plant fiber is fermented by gut bacteria, and small fatty acids are released in the process.

Those acids are used by the animal for energy. These acids also help maintain the gut lining and the immune system.

No difference between patches was found in the amounts of these acids. Instead, the team’s attention was drawn to the balance between propionate and butyrate, two of the acids.

Recent findings suggest that A surplus of propionate over butyrate has been proposed as a sign of an unbalanced gut. That pattern has been documented both in people and in wild primates that are short of food.

More propionate than butyrate was present in the droppings from all 10 patches.

In four of the 10 forest patches, the ratio of propionate to butyrate was about 2.6 or higher.

Human studies have linked that threshold to gut disorders. Whether it signals a health problem in howler monkeys remains unknown.

It has been revealed that the authors wrote that a reduction in butyrate-producing bacteria may be indicated by the pattern. The reduction may extend across the whole landscape.

The researchers also raised the possibility of long-term effects on the monkeys’ gut lining and immune function.

Howlers in southern Mexico suffered a mass die-off in 2024. Up to 31% of some local populations died from the combined effects of extreme heat, drought, and habitat degradation.

Baseline health records are needed if early warning signs of decline are to be detected, the authors wrote.

According to recent reports, two conservation priorities were recommended by the authors. Patches of mature, varied forest should be protected and enlarged. Rows of trees and wooded strips along rivers should keep those patches connected.

The researchers also suggested that a wider variety of trees be planted, including fruiting species. Howlers would then be able to move through the canopy in search of food and mates.

Permission from local landowners was needed before the team could reach the monkeys.

“Landowners we’ve spoken with are really open to these conversations,” Whitney said.

“They’ve said they love seeing the monkeys, and if they can help them travel on the trees, they’re very interested in it.”.

Industry observers note that she remarked the same sampling could be repeated every five or 10 years. Changes could then be compared over time, and the effect of conservation work could be checked.

According to recent reports, every sample came from an adult male. All of the samples were collected in a single rainy season.

Female and young howlers have different energy and hormone demands. The results therefore can’t be assumed to apply to them.

The gut bacteria samples were also limited and unevenly distributed across patches. Some patches supplied one sample, while others supplied as many as 12.

The team identified which bacteria were present. What those bacteria were doing inside the monkeys was not measured.

The study found links between forest features and gut bacteria.

Further research could test whether changes to the forest lead to changes in the monkeys’ gut bacteria.

The authors also noted that forests across Los Tuxtlas may be too uniformly degraded.

That could explain why the fatty acids varied so little. Comparisons with other landscapes are needed, they wrote.

Sources indicate that future research could pair repeated sampling with long-term records of the monkeys’ behavior. Such work could test whether these signals change as the forest does.

The team is now preparing a study comparing the gut bacteria of male and female howlers.

The full study was published in the journal Animal Conservation.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (980 w)

Wildfire smoke is making two kinds of air pollution spike together

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (980 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As wildfire smoke travels across the U.S., fine particle pollution and ground-level ozone are more often spiking on the same day.
  • According to recent reports, two air pollutants are reaching unusually high levels on the same days more often across the contiguous United States.
  • According to recent reports, the research comes from a team at the Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As wildfire smoke travels across the U.S., fine particle pollution and ground-level ozone are more often spiking on the same day.

According to recent reports, two air pollutants are reaching unusually high levels on the same days more often across the contiguous United States. A new study links that rise to wildfire smoke.

According to recent reports, the research comes from a team at the Penn State College of Earth and Mineral Sciences. Researchers in the Department of Geography looked at public data from 48 states.

They studied the co-occurrence of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and ground-level ozone.

PM2.5 includes microscopic soot, ash, and other inhalable particles.

Ground-level ozone forms when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight.

Intensified by wildfires, vehicle emissions, and other sources, the pollutants are often evaluated separately.

Exposure to both pollutants at once may increase risks to the heart and lungs.

Starting in 2011, wildfire smoke was more often present on days when both pollutants spiked across large parts of the country.

During many of these widespread pollution episodes, both PM2.5 and ground-level ozone exceeded U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) thresholds.

Sources indicate that the study did not evaluate individual health impacts. But researchers assessed high-level regional and national pollutant patterns known to affect health.

Increases in the combined pollutant levels appeared alongside steady growth in summertime wildfire smoke. They were most dramatic in the eastern half of the country.

The analysis incorporated observations from 2004 to 2023.

The researchers merged EPA monitoring data, satellite smoke mapping from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and a blend of weather information.

It has been revealed that “We’ve been experiencing many summertime instances when wildfire smoke from the western U.S. or Canada has traveled into large parts of the eastern U.S., especially the Northeast,” mentioned lead author Manzhu Yu from Penn State.

Researchers found growing odds of combined pollution hazards across the continental U.S.

In the West, the likelihood of both pollutants spiking on the same day during summer wildfire smoke events roughly doubled over the study period.

Those risks may move progressively eastward.

The paper’s overall findings may help public health researchers and clinicians study, evaluate, and prevent emerging health risks through a regional lens.

Yu stated she is especially interested in the eastern U.S. Its smoke comes from several sources, not only the large wildfires in the West.

Regional smoke sources include prescribed burns, such as those to clear acreage for agriculture or general land management. Local wildfires are another source.

The distinct smoke types occasionally overlap, deepening health concerns.

In a recent development, different smoke carries distinct components. These range from inorganic and organic carbon to heavy metals and influence PM2.5 co-occurrence with ozone.

“We are particularly curious about the links among smoke composition and cardiorespiratory ailments, which involve the heart, blood vessels, and lungs,” Yu mentioned.

A larger goal at Penn State is to understand future wildfire risks and impacts in the eastern U.S.

“I can’t say we’re excited about the work – it’s not good news,” said co-author Erica Smithwick from Penn State.

“People have underestimated the effect of wildfire smoke in this region. But we are pleased to see progress in mapping out and estimating risk factors because of the impact on human health.”.

The analysis should help local and regional decisionmakers plan for hazardous smoke conditions. That includes risk-reducing steps at public schools, in older buildings, and for people with medical vulnerabilities.

“In ongoing research elsewhere, we’re learning more about longer-term exposures to air pollution,”  Smithwick remarked.

“It may affect everything from acute stressors such as sore throats and eye irritation to longer-term effects like mental health and dementia.”.

“We’re hoping that evidence-based information about the increase in compound pollutant exposures will help prioritize decision-making around mitigation and resilience to those stressors.”.

In a recent development, air pollution from wildfires historically centered in the western U.S. But longer-range distribution of western and Canadian smoke from bigger fires is posing sharply higher co-occurrence risks.

That now includes the Midwest and Ohio Valley, in addition to the Northeast.

During the study period, researchers found 2012, 2018, 2021, and 2023 were peak years for co-occurrence of the pollutants nationally.

They also determined that widespread co-occurrence days became more frequent, persistent, and intense.

A widespread day is when both pollutants exceed local 90th percentiles over more than 10% of the country.

For each pollutant, the local 90th percentile is the concentration that about 90% of daily values in that area fall below.

Industry observers note that light to moderate smoke raises co-occurrence risks. It introduces particulate organic compounds and nitrogen oxides that promote ozone production.

At the same time, more dense smoke can limit ozone production by blocking sunlight.

It has been revealed that to predict the likelihood of combined pollution extremes, the researchers created a machine-learning model. They call it the Spatiotemporal Bayesian Neural Field.

Their model combines the effects of smoke, ground-level pollution, and weather patterns to establish risk.

Parts of the West have fire seasons more than a month longer than they were 35 years ago.

Estimated carbon emissions from forest fires grew 60% globally from 2001 to 2023, according to NASA.

Researchers attributed the changing fire conditions largely to global warming and a drier climate.

“We need to think about community awareness and community perception around smoke and have people be aware of the ecosystems they’re living in,” Smithwick said.

“There should be a general awareness of when not to burn a debris pile in your backyard, or when to be more careful with a campfire because of heightened risks.”.

“We want to work with municipalities and communities to think about the educational backbone of this work.”.

The study is published in the journal Environmental Science & Technology.

#42588. Industry News: What happened when scientists kept birds and bats away from cocoa trees?

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (837 w)

Industry News: What happened when scientists kept birds and bats away from cocoa trees?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (837 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An experiment on cocoa farms in the Peruvian Amazon reveals how nearby trees, birds, and bats can help protect the harvest.
  • In the Peruvian Amazon, the trees beyond a cocoa farm can help determine how much cocoa it produces.
  • Farms surrounded by forests, orchards, and other tree crops had some of the highest yields in a new study, and an experiment pointed to an unlikely pair of allies: birds and bats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An experiment on cocoa farms in the Peruvian Amazon reveals how nearby trees, birds, and bats can help protect the harvest.

In the Peruvian Amazon, the trees beyond a cocoa farm can help determine how much cocoa it produces.

Farms surrounded by forests, orchards, and other tree crops had some of the highest yields in a new study, and an experiment pointed to an unlikely pair of allies: birds and bats.

To find out how much those animals mattered, researchers put nets around some cocoa trees and left others open.

Where forests covered 30–35% of the surrounding landscape, the cocoa trees that birds and bats could reach produced nearly twice as much as the netted trees.

An international team led by the University of Vienna mapped the connections between shade trees, wildlife, and cocoa productivity across 28 organic agroforests in the northern Peruvian Amazon.

The researchers estimated that cocoa trees accessible to birds and bats would yield about 265 kilograms per hectare per year where trees covered roughly 20% of the surrounding landscape.

Where surrounding tree cover reached 70–80%, the estimated yield was nearly four times as high, at about 1,000 kilograms per hectare per year.

At 2023 cocoa prices, the researchers valued the extra cocoa associated with bird and bat activity at about US$1,640 per hectare per year.

It has been revealed that for smallholder farmers in a region where average incomes are modest, that’s not a rounding error. It’s the difference between scraping by and building something.

“Birds and bats can be powerful allies for cacao farmers, but only if the surrounding landscape provides enough habitat. If these landscapes become large monocultures, much of this natural pest-control benefit is lost,” said senior author Bea Maas from the University of Vienna.

The intuitive assumption – more shade trees, more biodiversity, better farm – doesn’t hold up cleanly.

Shade-tree cover benefitted wildlife, improved soils, and buffered temperature extremes. But very dense shade starved the cocoa of light and substantially cut yields.

On farms in tree-rich landscapes, a mix of tall and short shade trees helped support biodiversity.

Dense shade, meanwhile, reduced cocoa yields by limiting sunlight.

Sources indicate that “Our data show that cacao farms do not need uniform shade to support biodiversity. A mosaic of tall and short trees, tree clusters and open patches can create habitat for wildlife while maintaining production,” mentioned lead author Aycart-Lazo from the University of Vienna.

In a recent development, the researchers surveyed birds, bats, and arthropods. They measured cocoa yield, natural pest control, pollination rates, pest and disease incidence, soil fertility, and microclimate.

Then they used drone imagery and remote-sensing data to connect what was happening inside each farm to what the surrounding landscape looked like.

The finding that probably matters most for policy is this: what’s outside the farm fence may be more important than what’s inside it.

A farmer can do everything right on their own plot and still lose most of the pest-control benefit if the surrounding land has been stripped bare.

This is an uncomfortable truth for programs that focus exclusively on farm-level certification.

A certified organic plot in a deforested landscape doesn’t get the same ecosystem services as one embedded in a matrix of forests and orchards.

“Our results show that these benefits depend strongly on how trees are managed both within farms and across the surrounding landscape,” Aycart-Lazo stated.

The team proposes a landscape-level formula for the region: roughly 30–35% forest cover, another 40–45% in tree-based habitats like agroforests or orchards, and 20–30% in open areas for annual crops.

That mix, they argue, could create multifunctional landscapes that sustain both high biodiversity and strong cocoa production.

This is a recommendation though, not a decree. Different regions have different land pressures, different communities, and different histories.

According to recent reports, “This is not a one-size-fits-all blueprint. Landscape strategies need to be adapted to local land availability and developed together with local communities,” Ocampo-Ariza stated.

The study was conducted in one of the world’s most biodiverse regions. The specifics belong to the northern Peruvian Amazon.

But the underlying logic is portable. Wherever crops depend on natural pest control, the surrounding habitat either supports or undermines it.

It has been revealed that the study cuts against a stubborn narrative in tropical agriculture – that farmers must choose between productivity and conservation. The data from these 28 Peruvian farms suggest the opposite.

Biodiversity didn’t just coexist with cocoa production. It actively drove it.

The ecosystem services provided by wildlife – pest control above all – were the mechanism converting habitat into yield.

That doesn’t mean conservation is free. Managing a structurally varied canopy takes skill.

Maintaining landscape-level forest cover requires coordination across farms, communities, and governments. But the economic argument is now harder to wave away.

For cocoa growers, keeping forests nearby can help protect the harvest.

The study is published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.

One November storm changed how California’s Sierra Nevada looked from orbit

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An early storm brought nearly a foot of snow to Donner Pass, offering a first look at the snowpack that helps supply California with water.
  • Fresh snow stretches across California’s Sierra Nevada in a satellite image taken on the morning of November 14.
  • Around Lake Tahoe and farther south, white covers much of the high country.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An early storm brought nearly a foot of snow to Donner Pass, offering a first look at the snowpack that helps supply California with water.

Fresh snow stretches across California’s Sierra Nevada in a satellite image taken on the morning of November 14.

Around Lake Tahoe and farther south, white covers much of the high country.

Along part of the range’s western side, green slopes still show through, making it easy to see where the storm left its mark.

A Pacific storm swept through the previous day, bringing heavy rain to the Sacramento area and close to a foot of snow to some mountain locations.

A break between weather systems gave NASA’s Terra satellite a clear look at the mountains after one of the season’s first major snowfalls.

The instrument that captured the view, the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer, or MODIS, takes in long stretches of the mountain range at once.

From that vantage point, the snow that fell on individual peaks and mountain passes comes into view as a broad band of white.

NASA Earth Observatory paired the November 14 view with an image from two days earlier, when snow was largely confined to the highest ridges southeast of Lake Tahoe.

The earlier view gives a sense of how much changed in the time it took for one storm to cross California.

A separate regional analysis from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) estimated that snow covered about 43 percent of its Sierra Nevada analysis area on November 14.

According to recent reports, A month earlier, the estimate was less than 1 percent. The comparison indicates how quickly snow can spread across terrain that was largely bare in mid-October.

At Donner Pass, northwest of Lake Tahoe, the Central Sierra Snow Laboratory recorded nearly 12 inches of snow on November 13.

Officials closed Interstate 80 in both directions over Donner Summit that evening.

Farther south, Mammoth Mountain reported 9 to 13 inches of fresh snow. In Yosemite National Park, officials closed several roads ahead of the storm.

The reports from Donner Pass and Mammoth give a sense of how much snow fell at specific locations across the long stretch of mountains visible from above.

The storm also brought heavy rain to the Sacramento area, west of the Sierra Nevada.

Elevation helped determine what reached the ground. Where the air was warm enough, precipitation fell as rain.

Higher in the mountains, colder conditions allowed snow to accumulate.

The green slopes along the western side of the range are a reminder that a storm can bring very different weather to places only a short distance apart.

The broad cover visible on November 14 raises a question that matters well beyond the mountains.

How much water is in all that snow? Hydrologists answer it by measuring snow water equivalent, the depth of water that would remain if the snow at a given spot melted.

A foot of light, powdery snow can hold less water than a shallower layer of dense, wet snow.

California’s Department of Water Resources uses that measurement to help forecast how much water could flow out of the mountains as the snow melts.

Some of that runoff reaches major reservoirs in spring and early summer, helping supply water during the state’s dry months.

Timing matters because California receives much of its precipitation during the cooler part of the year.

Rain can reach streams and reservoirs soon after a storm.

Snow can stay in the mountains for months before melting, releasing some of that water later, when storms are less frequent.

The November storm arrived about six weeks into the water year, the 12-month period hydrologists use to track precipitation and runoff beginning October 1.

The Sierra Nevada snowpack generally peaks around April 1, leaving several months for fresh storms to add to it or for warm spells to melt some of what has already accumulated.

More snow was already in the forecast when NASA released the image on November 18.

The National Weather Service had issued a winter storm warning for parts of the Sierra Nevada through November 20, with around four feet of snow possible at some locations above 8,000 feet.

The November 14 image captures the mountains at the start of that longer process.

In a single day, snow spread across enough of the Sierra Nevada to change how the range looked from orbit.

Over the coming months, the same slopes will collect or lose snow with each shift in the weather.

By spring, what remains will help determine how much meltwater reaches California’s reservoirs as the state heads into its dry season.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison, using MODIS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE and GIBS/Worldview.

#42583. Industry News: Office light may throw off the body’s daily rhythm

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (917 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Office light may throw off the body’s daily rhythm

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a study of day-active rats, an hour of simulated daylight at noon helped restore activity rhythms weakened by fluorescent office lighting.
  • People spend about 90% of their time indoors, under ceiling lights that are a small fraction as bright as the sky outside.
  • In a rodent that keeps human hours, living under standard fluorescent office light weakened the animal’s daily rhythm of activity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a study of day-active rats, an hour of simulated daylight at noon helped restore activity rhythms weakened by fluorescent office lighting.

People spend about 90% of their time indoors, under ceiling lights that are a small fraction as bright as the sky outside. The body reads that light as a biological signal.

In a rodent that keeps human hours, living under standard fluorescent office light weakened the animal’s daily rhythm of activity.

An hour of simulated daylight at noon each day, roughly analogous to a lunchtime walk outdoors, partly restored the rats’ daily activity rhythm.

In a second experiment, more of the male rats that spent six weeks under fluorescent light showed diabetic-range blood sugar than rats under daylight-strength light.

A smaller share of sperm were moving in the fluorescent-light group, about 19% compared with 45% under simulated daylight.

The study is small, with eight animals in the first experiment and 20 in the second, and all of them were male.

According to recent reports, lily Yan, a professor in the Department of Psychology at Michigan State University, led the work. The lead author is Antony Bum Kim of the Department of Architecture at the University of California, Berkeley.

“It is a biological signal that influences circadian organization and, potentially, a range of downstream health outcomes,” Yan said of light.

The body’s internal clock helps regulate daily patterns, known as circadian rhythms, in sleep, appetite, and much else.

Nearly every lab rodent is awake at night, which makes it a poor stand-in for a person whose body clock runs on daylight.

The Nile grass rat, a small African rodent, is active in the daytime, and Yan’s lab has used it for years to study how light affects the brain.

According to recent reports, over each cage, the team installed a programmable light that can imitate the color mix of many sources. Its daylight setting ran at about 5,600 lux, roughly the level that building designers treat as true daylight.

The office setting imitated a standard fluorescent tube at about 150 lux, the brightness of a typical indoor workspace.

Sources indicate that eight male grass rats lived under four lighting schedules in turn, two weeks each. Sensors logged their movement day and night.

Sources indicate that the first schedule was steady daylight from dawn to dusk. The second was daylight that brightened to the same midday peak and faded again, which delivered about half the total light.

Sources indicate that the third was fluorescent office light all day. The fourth was office light with one hour of full daylight at noon.

The rats were most active, and most sharply divided between a busy day and a quiet night, under steady daylight.

Under fluorescent light their activity was lower and their rhythm flatter, with its peak shifted later in the day.

The ramped daylight did not match the steady version even though it reached the same peak.

The authors wrote that the total amount of light over the day, more than its brightest moment, seems to set the strength of the rhythm.

Adding the noon hour of daylight to the office schedule raised the strength of the rhythm again, though only partly.

All eight animals showed a burst of activity during that hour. The authors called it a partial rescue.

A separate group of 20 male grass rats lived for six weeks under either steady daylight or fluorescent light, 10 in each group.

The rats’ body weight, belly fat, and average blood sugar did not differ between the groups.

But five of the 20 animals had blood sugar in a range the lab treats as diabetic, and four of the five had lived under fluorescent light.

Recent findings suggest that in a follow-up with a different way of drawing blood, the pattern held. Four of eight rats under fluorescent light crossed that line, compared with one of seven under daylight.

According to recent reports, the two groups produced the same number of sperm. Under daylight, about 45% of those sperm were moving. Under fluorescent light, about 19% were.

“Factors affecting health are not limited to drugs, diet and exercise,” Kim said. “The light environments we create in our homes, schools and workplaces are also biological exposures.”.

Ten animals per group is a small sample. More rats under fluorescent light crossed the study’s threshold for diabetic-range blood sugar, while average blood sugar was similar in the two groups.

The authors also wrote that blood drawn after euthanasia can read differently, which is why they ran the follow-up.

Every animal was male, so the study states nothing about females. And a grass rat under a programmable lamp is not an office worker with windows, a commute, and a phone.

The authors wrote that the findings support daylight deficiency as a risk factor for diabetes in this animal.

The sperm result is new, they wrote, since earlier work on light and sperm looked at day length rather than light quality.

What remains untested is whether the same shifts happen in people. The authors wrote that the next step is for other groups to repeat the work in grass rats or other day-active animals.

The next question is whether an hour of brighter light at midday could help people who work far from a window maintain a stronger daily rhythm.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Biological Rhythms.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Recent findings suggest that neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

The study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, states neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

Recent findings suggest that although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, says cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

Recent findings suggest that “You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman indicates. The latest study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

Recent findings suggest that the amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their upcoming role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao claims.

Although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team showed that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are currently no broadly effective treatments.

In a recent development, the hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao states. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao claims.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Selective breeding could help Australia’s southern corroboree frog survive longer after exposure to the deadly chytrid fungus.
  • A breeding technique from agriculture might help one of Australia’s most threatened frogs.
  • Researchers found that southern corroboree frogs can inherit traits that help them survive longer after exposure to a deadly fungus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Selective breeding could help Australia’s southern corroboree frog survive longer after exposure to the deadly chytrid fungus.

A breeding technique from agriculture might help one of Australia’s most threatened frogs.

Researchers found that southern corroboree frogs can inherit traits that help them survive longer after exposure to a deadly fungus. That means selective breeding could make the species more resilient.

Industry observers note that the frog is functionally extinct in the wild. The culprit is chytridiomycosis, an infectious disease caused by the amphibian chytrid fungus.

Industry observers note that captive breeding has kept the species alive. But returning frogs to the wild is hard because the fungus persists in the environment.

Lead author Mikaeylah Davidson completed the work as part of her PhD at the University of Melbourne.

The study tested whether genomic selection could guide conservation breeding for the frog.

Davidson and her colleagues combined laboratory experiments with genome-wide genetic information. That included a custom genotyping array built for the frog.

Industry observers note that the team found that southern corroboree frogs differ in how long they survive after exposure to chytrid fungus. Some of that variation is inherited.

“Using genomic data, we were able to show that survival following chytrid infection is a heritable trait, meaning some of the differences in survival are due to genetic differences that can be passed on to the next generation,” Davidson noted.

“This means there is genetic variation we could potentially use to improve survival through selective breeding.”.

“Excitingly, this approach is a potential way to move beyond simply keeping endangered frogs alive in captivity, towards actively improving their ability to cope with the threats preventing their recovery in the wild.”.

Modeling suggested genomic information could guide breeding decisions.

It could potentially increase average survival time after exposure to chytrid fungus by around nine percent in the next generation.

The model projected that gain while accounting for inbreeding and genetic diversity.

Sources indicate that an established captive breeding program offered a chance to test the idea in practice. Zoos Victoria and the Taronga Conservation Society support that program through partnerships.

Industry observers note that the research suggests improved disease resilience doesn’t need to come at the expense of genetic diversity. That is especially significant for small, critically endangered populations.

In such groups, maintaining diversity and limiting inbreeding are central to long-term population health and evolutionary potential.

Senior author Lee Skerratt from the University of Melbourne argued the approach may also have potential for other threatened wildlife affected by persistent disease.

That is particularly true for species already managed through captive breeding.

“Amphibians are an crucial focus, with hundreds of species now maintained in captivity for conservation as chytrid fungus continues to threaten populations globally,” he mentioned.

“Genomic selection could help conservation breeding programs move beyond preventing extinction by moving animals into captivity towards actively supporting animals’ ability to survive threats in the wild.”.

This work builds on six years of effort.

According to recent reports, first, researchers developed the genomic tools and disease datasets needed to explore newly introduced strategies for the frog. They then combined a newly mapped genome and a custom genotyping array with extensive disease-resilience data.

That let them investigate selective breeding as a proactive approach to species recovery.

The next stage is to improve and validate the predictions.

Recent findings suggest that the team will use genomic information from more of the breeding population. They will also explore other genetic approaches to improve disease resistance.

Researchers will also test whether the predicted improvements show up in later generations. And critically, they will check whether greater survival in the lab translates into better outcomes in the wild.

Recent findings suggest that amphibians are in deep trouble worldwide. The chytrid fungus has caused catastrophic declines and extinctions.

More than 200 threatened frog species are now kept in captivity. These colonies have prevented immediate extinctions.

But they are temporary refuges, meant to hold the line until threats can be mitigated.

Recent findings suggest that selective breeding offers a different path. Instead of just keeping animals alive, it can improve their ability to cope. That could raise the odds of successful reintroduction.

In a recent development, while genomic selection has transformed plant and animal breeding, it has rarely been applied to wildlife. The main barriers have been missing datasets and a lack of structured breeding programs.

This frog had both, which made it an ideal test case.

Recent findings suggest that the species produces fewer than 30 eggs per year and reaches sexual maturity at 2 to 5 years of age. Those traits slow generational turnover.

The trait is also polygenic. No single gene has a large effect. Resistance is shaped by many loci, each contributing a little.

Because many genes contribute to survival, the team used genomic selection, which draws on information from across the genome.

According to recent reports, and the modelling covers only part of the breeding population. Future work could capture more genetic variation.

The team proposes a phased rollout.

First, refine the breeding value predictions with more parental genotyping. Second, test realized responses in controlled and semi-natural conditions. Third, run multi-generational selective breeding alongside ongoing diversity management.

Data from each phase would feed back into the program. That supports adaptive management and continuous improvement.

For now, the result is a proof of concept. It shows that captive populations can become more than passive safeguards. For a frog on the brink, that shift could matter a great deal.

The study is published in the journal npj Biodiversity.
