💡 Key Takeaways
  • Heat pumps could reshape the power grid more than climate change, pushing the worst demand spikes in cold regions into winter by 2060.
  • Ask when the power grid has its hardest day and most people picture a heat wave, with every air conditioner in town running at once.
  • Across much of the northern United States, that day may soon be a cold winter night instead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Heat pumps could reshape the power grid more than climate change, pushing the worst demand spikes in cold regions into winter by 2060.

Ask when the power grid has its hardest day and most people picture a heat wave, with every air conditioner in town running at once.

Across much of the northern United States, that day may soon be a cold winter night instead.

Latest modeling finds that as homes swap gas furnaces for heat pumps, the worst spikes in electricity demand in cold regions could grow by half to nearly double by 2060.

With today’s heating and cooling equipment, warming alone changes extreme peaks by less than 10% in either direction.

The model projects much larger increases in cold regions as buildings switch to electric heating.

Mai Shi, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Michigan‘s School for Environment and Sustainability, led the work with colleagues at Michigan, MIT and Cornell University.

In a recent development, their projections cover 183 counties through 2060 and hold the number of buildings fixed. Every change they report comes from weather and equipment, not from new construction or population growth.

“We focused on the extreme peak demands because we want to keep our power systems reliable,” Shi said.

Industry observers note that “If the system works for moderate conditions but fails in extremes, it doesn’t work. That’s not how we build the power grid. We need to blueprint for extremes.”.

Industry observers note that an electric heat pump can both heat and cool a building. When it replaces a gas furnace, heating shifts onto the power grid. The standard heat pump in the study lost heating capacity as outdoor temperatures fell.

The standard unit in the study keeps only half of its rated heating capacity at 5°F (-15°C).

In the team’s model, heat pumps and insulation spread through buildings at the pace home air conditioning spread across the country, about 10% a year.

With that pace of adoption and today’s weather, the most extreme peaks grow by 60% to 104% by 2060 across the six cold regions.

Those are New England, New York, the Midwest, the Mid-Atlantic, the Northwest and the Great Plains. The season changes too.

At the start of the projections, more than 95% of those regions’ yearly peaks fall in summer.

Recent findings suggest that by 2060, more than 95% fall in winter. Insulation lowers demand, but in cold regions it can’t cancel out the furnaces being replaced.

Run the same buildings through a warming climate with today’s equipment and the changes are smaller.

In a recent development, extreme peaks rise 3% to 9% in every region but the Northwest, as extreme heat pushes up cooling demand. In the Northwest, winter heating already sets the peak, and a milder winter trims it by 3%.

Put the two drivers together and they don’t simply add up. Warmer winters offset part of the heat pump demand, cutting the growth in cold-region extremes by up to 18% compared with technology alone.

The net result in those regions is still a 48% to 93% increase through 2060. That is up to roughly 10 times what warming alone would do. Warming also delays the switch to winter peaking rather than stopping it.

Researchers call the spread of a technology through homes tech diffusion.

“Tech diffusion may have a larger impact than climate change on peak demand in a lot of regions,” stated Shi, who is also a member of the university’s Center for Sustainable Systems.

In the projections for California and Texas, the peak stays in summer. Heat pumps and insulation make cooling more efficient there, so the technology lowers extreme peaks instead of raising them.

With warming included, those two regions’ extremes end up 1% to 9% lower than they would be under climate change alone.

The Southwest and Southeast are in between. Technology alone pushes their extremes up 17% and 11%, because about 60% of their yearly peaks move to winter while the rest stay in summer.

Recent findings suggest that A winter peak on a cold night can run higher than a summer one. Warming lowers those winter extremes by 4% to 6%.

In Texas, faster adoption lowers the peak further. Under climate change alone, the largest peak between 2020 and 2060 is 12% above today’s.

With the fastest spread of heat pumps and insulation, that increase shrinks to 5%.

The team trained 209,352 machine learning models on simulated hourly heating and cooling use for 362,227 homes and commercial buildings across 183 counties.

The counties were chosen so that each state’s mix of weather zones matched the real one.

The researchers used 100 simulations from four climate models and three emissions scenarios to project how future weather could affect electricity demand for heating and cooling.

It has been revealed that adoption speed came from history. The researchers looked at how fast 18 past technologies spread, from vacuum cleaners at about 2% a year to cell phones at about 36%. Home air conditioning, at 10%, was their main case.

The researchers used the 95th percentile of projected annual peaks to estimate extreme demand. Only about one in 20 of those peaks exceeds that level.

Sources indicate that in the projections, peaks change little through the early 2030s and the weather is nearly the whole source of uncertainty. In cold regions, that changes in the late 2030s and the 2040s.

Heat pump adoption reaches the steep part of its curve and winter peaks grow quickly. From one climate run to the next, it becomes uncertain whether a year’s peak falls in summer or winter.

Sources indicate that the spread of possible peaks in those regions widens to three or four times its 2020 level by the 2050s. By then, winter peaking is established in most of them.

For grid planners, the source of uncertainty moves with that transition. By the 2050s, how fast people adopt the technology is the largest single factor in Newly introduced England and New York, at 65% to 75% of the total.

Climate still drives 85% to 99% in the Southeast, the Northwest and California.

Michael Craig is the study’s senior author and an associate professor at Michigan.

“Climate change still matters a lot. If I’m thinking about my power system and what I should worry about, climate change is still an notable source of risk and uncertainty,” Craig said.

Industry observers note that the team also tested a heat pump that keeps 90% of its heating capacity at 5°F instead of 50%. With it, extreme peaks come out 5% to 40% lower, with the biggest savings in cold regions.

It has been revealed that the projections hold the equipment’s performance fixed over 40 years, so they don’t include heat pumps improving, or smart thermostats and thermal storage moving demand off the worst hours. They cover heating and cooling only.

Electric vehicle charging isn’t in them, and neither are data centers.

One recent tally of utility forecasts attributes roughly half of the projected growth in U.S. peak load through 2030 to data centers.

Industry observers note that humidity isn’t in the model either, only temperature. And it assumes heat pumps spread at the same pace everywhere, when energy prices, housing and policy will set different speeds in different states.

How fast adoption will actually run in each region is the open question. Shi stated that number, unlike the weather, is one that local rules and incentives can steer.

The authors wrote that the next step is building those regional differences into the projections, so that each region’s planners see the projection that applies to them.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Patients taking weight-loss drugs may unknowingly eat too little, missing key nutrients and receiving limited dietary support.
  • Appetite is reduced by weight-loss drugs such as Wegovy and Mounjaro, so a drop in food intake is expected.
  • According to recent reports, what some patients may not know is how little they end up eating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Patients taking weight-loss drugs may unknowingly eat too little, missing key nutrients and receiving limited dietary support.

Appetite is reduced by weight-loss drugs such as Wegovy and Mounjaro, so a drop in food intake is expected.

According to recent reports, what some patients may not know is how little they end up eating. Their intake of several nutrients may also be too low.

A small study at one English medical practice recorded intakes below 800 calories a day in three of 14 patients.

Too little fiber and vitamin D was obtained from food by most of the group. Protein intake, in contrast, was adequate in nearly every participant.

A possible gap in care is suggested by the findings. Little structured follow-up or dietary guidance was reported by many participants after the drugs were started.

The project was run by Dhanush Ammineni and Milou Ottolini, medical students at the University of Oxford. They worked with Dr. Ellen Fallows at Brackley Medical Centre, a family practice in Northamptonshire, England.

It has been revealed that only 14 volunteers took part, and no more than two days of meals were analyzed for each. The project therefore cannot show how common the problem is. Nor can it show that the drugs were the cause.

A text message was sent by the practice to 97 eligible patients on its register.

Recent findings suggest that all of them had been prescribed one of these weight-loss drugs within the past year. The project was completed by 14 people: 11 women and three men, aged 27 to 73.

According to recent reports, tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro, was taken by twelve of them. Ten paid for their prescriptions privately.

The other four received them through the National Health Service (NHS), Britain’s public health system.

Since the start of treatment, the participants had lost between 6.6 and 75 pounds (3 and 34 kilograms).

Sources indicate that meals were recorded by each person in an online food diary called myfood24. Participants were asked to choose days they considered typical.

It has been revealed that up to two recorded days from each person were analyzed by the team. Intake of 28 nutrients was then compared with the UK’s recommended daily amounts.

An intake below two-thirds of a recommended amount was counted as a shortfall.

Each participant also took part in a 20-minute phone interview about life on the drug.

Fewer than 1,231 calories a day were eaten by half of the participants. Individual intakes ranged from 541 to 2,312 calories.

It has been revealed that weight loss on these drugs depends partly on a lower calorie intake. The concern is how low some intakes were. The food was also being chosen by the patients themselves.

UK health guidance covers meal-replacement diets of 800 to 1,200 calories a day.

That guidance claims such diets should be used only with specialist support and nutritionally complete products. No such oversight was available to the three participants with the lowest intakes.

According to recent reports, the lowest intake in the group was 541 calories a day, averaged by one woman. She fell short on all six nutrients the team focused on.

About a quarter of an ounce (7.8 grams) of fruit a day was recorded in her diary.

The six nutrients were fiber, iron, vitamin D, potassium, protein, and magnesium.

Less than two-thirds of the recommended fiber was obtained by twelve of the 14 participants. Eleven fell below that mark for vitamin D from food. Seven fell below it for iron.

It has been revealed that protein was the exception. Too little was eaten by only one participant. Half the group ate more than one and a half times the recommended amount.

It has been revealed that A possible reason was suggested by the interviews. Snacks had been cut out and portions had become smaller, participants said. Main meals that included protein were still being eaten.

Sources indicate that at least three of the six nutrients fell short in eight participants. Most of those eight spoke of cooking at home or of choosing food with their health in mind.

The researchers attributed the shortfalls mainly to how little food was eaten overall.

In a recent development, low intake was not the full explanation, however. Four nutrients were still short in one woman whose diary averaged 1,421 calories a day.

In a recent development, the quality of the food may matter as well. A second woman ate 677 calories a day and got 84% of them from ultra-processed foods. Five of the six nutrients fell short in her diet.

It has been revealed that the vitamin D figures have to be read with caution, since the body also produces the vitamin in sunlit skin. Production of that kind is not captured by a food diary.

Industry observers note that two participants remarked they were shocked at how little they were eating. This had not been realized until the diary was filled in.

Industry observers note that the researchers suggested that reduced appetite may lead people to under-eat without recognizing it. Under-eating of this kind would not be detected unless diet were monitored in some way.

Benefits were also described. Many participants mentioned they felt more in control of their eating. Food could be enjoyed without guilt.

Recent findings suggest that some of them also reported that pain had eased and that they could move about more freely. In many interviews the medication was spoken of as a turning point.

The interviews brought out drawbacks as well. Because of nausea or diarrhea, some participants had stopped eating in company.

It has been revealed that others were afraid of regaining weight once the drug was stopped. The long-term cost of the medication was a further worry.

A lack of structured follow-up was consistently described by participants.

Some participants stated they managed symptoms such as dizziness and low blood pressure on their own or sought advice from online peer groups.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers set this against the care given around weight-loss surgery. Screening for vitamin and mineral deficiencies is routine before such operations. Afterward, patients remain under the care of a dietitian.

“No drug-specific nutritional monitoring framework exists,” the researchers wrote.

UK dietary advice is based on the Eatwell Guide, a general healthy-eating guide. It was not designed for people taking these drugs.

An earlier analysis covered 461,382 adults newly prescribed GLP-1 drugs, the group that includes Wegovy.

In a recent development, A nutritional deficiency had been diagnosed in nearly 13% of them within six months. By 12 months, the share was more than 22%.

Sources indicate that the food diary was completed without help by eight of the 14 participants. In the researchers’ view, a diary of this kind might offer busy clinics a practical means of spotting nutritional risk.

It has yet to be tested whether patients’ health would improve as a result.

What participants ate before treatment began was never recorded.

It has been revealed that for that reason the diaries cannot tell the drugs apart from earlier eating habits as a cause. Something the project did not measure could also be responsible.

The project depended on meals reported by the participants themselves, and laboratory tests were not part of it. What people ate is described by the results, but a diagnosed deficiency cannot be inferred from them.

The volunteers also differed from typical patients. Each had chosen to take part, and women made up most of the group. Most prescriptions were private, and the practice is located in a relatively affluent area.

Fear that the medication would be withdrawn reportedly kept some patients from joining.

The volunteers were motivated and lived in a relatively affluent area. For that reason, the researchers suggested that the risk among patients more widely may be underestimated.

A larger study was called for by the team. It would cover several practices and include both NHS and private patients.

Three separate days of food records would be collected from each person. By their calculations, about 120 participants would be enough to estimate how common each shortfall is.

Larger studies would also need to determine whether the shortfalls affect patients’ health.

The full study was published in the journal BMJ Nutrition, Prevention & Health.

#42577. Why the 2021 heat dome killed some mussels and spared others

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (762 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Why the 2021 heat dome killed some mussels and spared others

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (762 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome, mussels just a few feet apart on the same rocky shore faced very different odds of survival.
  • During the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome, a mussel’s survival came down to two things: its size and its location on the shoreline.
  • The heatwave brought 100-degree weather to a region used to highs in the mid-70s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome, mussels just a few feet apart on the same rocky shore faced very different odds of survival.

During the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome, a mussel’s survival came down to two things: its size and its location on the shoreline.

The heatwave brought 100-degree weather to a region used to highs in the mid-70s. Many marine organisms withered.

According to recent reports, but the mussels at Cattle Point on San Juan Island fared relatively well. Researchers built a physics-based model to predict survival from mass and heat transfer data.

“We found this survival pattern that favored small mussels high on the shore and large mussels lower on the shore,” said lead author Jack Litle from the University of Washington (UW).

Although the experts looked only at mussels, the model can apply to other shellfish elsewhere.

Sources indicate that the carpet of mussels covering the rocky promontory varies in size. Smaller mussels cluster higher up the shore, while the beefier ones sit 10 to 15 feet lower.

Before the heatwave, researchers had been collecting temperature data using biomimetic “robomussels” for decades.

Former UW graduate student Brian Helmuth developed the approach. The study’s senior author, Emily Carrington, has managed the robomussels for the past 10 years.

A small thermometer embedded in black epoxy continuously records the robomussel’s temperature.

It has been revealed that litle approached Carrington, a professor of biology at UW and his advisor, about studying the effect of extreme heat on mussels. She suggested Cattle Point, where the robomussels were already spread out.

Carrington also suggested they look at size as well as survival since she thought older, often larger mussels might tolerate heat better than young ones.

The team returned to the site one, two, and three weeks after the heatwave began and counted the dead mussels.

When the researchers analyzed the data, the results seemed underwhelming.

Overall, mortality was low and the size pattern was the opposite of what they expected.

The researchers expected most of the dead mussels high on the shore to be small and most of those lower down to be large.

The mussels that died up high were bigger than average, while those that died down low were smaller.

“I can just so clearly remember where Jack and I were standing when the first data graphs popped on the screen – it was one of those rare ‘aha moments,'” Carrington said.

Sources indicate that “We immediately began thinking about how rates of heating depend on body size. Jack got to work developing the heat budget model to show how the temperature effects of body size change with habitat.”.

Sources indicate that the explanation comes down to tides and cooling. Mussels higher on the shore get sun for nearly twice as long as those lower down.

Mussels can cool in two ways. They can “sweat” out seawater or they can rely on the wind.

In a recent development, larger mussels hold more seawater, which stretches out the window for evaporative cooling. Smaller mussels have more surface area relative to volume, which makes them better wind coolers.

The mussels that died high on the shore likely ran out of water for evaporative cooling. They were also too major for efficient wind cooling.

Those that died lower down were too small to hold enough water for extended evaporative cooling.

The model could be applied to other coastal areas with tides.

Oyster growers keep oysters low on the shore to fatten up, then they move them higher to strengthen their shells. This study could tell them how big the shells can get before heat mortality risk rises.

In the future, a similar approach could shed light on other evaporative coolers too.

“Evaporative cooling is not just a shellfish thing – amphibians, birds, and mammals do something very similar,” Litle stated.

“The biology is different, but the same physical principles apply. This same sort of thinking could be extended to different taxonomic groups.”.

This study shows that predicting who survives a heatwave from traits alone can mislead.

Recent findings suggest that body size interacts with microhabitat at the meter scale. That interaction shapes which cooling strategy is available. And it flips the direction of selection from one spot on the shore to the next.

Small mussels fared better high on the shore, while large mussels fared better lower down.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences.

#42574. Earth’s early crust left a fingerprint in rocks for a billion years, then it vanished

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (950 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Earth’s early crust left a fingerprint in rocks for a billion years, then it vanished

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lead in ancient rocks may help pinpoint when modern plate tectonics took hold and began reshaping how Earth recycles its crust.
  • Earth’s surface is made of plates that slide, collide, and sink back into the planet, and it’s tempting to assume it has always worked that way.
  • The signature comes from a pool of crust that formed roughly 4 billion years ago and kept getting remelted in place for more than a billion years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lead in ancient rocks may help pinpoint when modern plate tectonics took hold and began reshaping how Earth recycles its crust.

Earth’s surface is made of plates that slide, collide, and sink back into the planet, and it’s tempting to assume it has always worked that way. Rocks older than about 2.6 billion years carry a chemical signature that indicates otherwise.

The signature comes from a pool of crust that formed roughly 4 billion years ago and kept getting remelted in place for more than a billion years.

Recent findings suggest that between about 2.75 and 2.63 billion years ago, the pattern changes sharply. One source’s signature vanishes from the record, and the other turns up only rarely after that.

The researchers interpret the shift as a possible sign that modern plate tectonics was taking hold and reshaping how Earth recycled its crust.

The study is an interpretation of a global compilation of lead measurements, and the authors call their explanation a testable hypothesis rather than a settled fact.

Janne Liebmann of Curtin University in Perth, Australia, led the work with colleagues at Curtin’s School of Earth and Planetary Sciences and Queen’s University in Canada.

“Fresh crust often forms by melting older rock, leaving behind a distinctive chemical fingerprint,” Liebmann remarked.

The fingerprint is carried by lead. Uranium and thorium decay into three different forms of lead at three different rates. So the mix of lead in a rock records how much uranium and thorium its source held, and for how long.

Some minerals, including feldspar and certain sulphides, take in lead as they crystallize but almost no uranium or thorium. Their lead mix is fixed at the moment they form, which makes them a record of the magma they grew from.

In a recent development, the team compiled published lead measurements on such minerals from rocks whose ages were known independently. They added eight newly introduced feldspar analyses from China, West Africa, and Finland.

After discarding samples whose lead had been disturbed, 1,235 remained, with ages from 3.8 billion years to the present.

In a recent development, in rocks older than about 2.6 billion years, the lead points to two sources that split from the mantle between 4.0 and 3.7 billion years ago. One was rich in uranium relative to lead, the other poor.

Both show up in rocks from ancient continental cores around the world.

For those signatures to develop, the two sources had to stay chemically isolated for at least a billion years.

The authors’ explanation is a primitive crust split into an upper layer and a lower layer, each with its own uranium budget, that magmas kept tapping without destroying.

Most of the old rocks in the dataset are granites, which can form when existing crust melts. That fits the idea that early Earth repeatedly reworked its crust in place.

After about 2.6 billion years ago, the lead in new rocks clusters near the average for the whole planet. The spread in the inferred uranium budgets of their sources roughly halves.

A statistical test for abrupt changes, repeated 300 times on reshuffled versions of the data, kept finding the same break between 2.75 and 2.63 billion years ago.

The break held in the full dataset and in two subsets the team checked separately. Australian samples make up 71% of the compilation, so the authors treated the 358 non-Australian samples as an independent test. The break appeared there too.

The uranium-rich source never reappears. The uranium-poor one surfaces only four times afterward, in granites from Russia and Australia between 1.6 billion and 400 million years ago.

Liebmann’s team wrote that the old sources were either destroyed, most likely by being dragged back into the mantle, or cut off from the places where newly introduced crust was made.

Both fit a planet that had begun moving crust around and recycling it, with magma production shifting from the interiors of plates to their edges.

Other changes geologists have documented in rocks of that age line up with the break. Continents were becoming thicker and richer in silica. Buried rocks began recording sharper contrasts in temperature. And what may have been the first supercontinent was assembling.

“It marks the transition from an early Earth where ancient crust could be repeatedly melted and reworked in place, to a system capable of moving and recycling crust on a much larger scale,” noted co-author Chris Kirkland of Curtin.

Kirkland said the finding helps explain when Earth developed the global system of moving plates that distinguishes it from Venus and Mars.

Lead isotopes record that the old sources stopped feeding fresh magma. They don’t by themselves show plates sinking.

The team wrote that direct evidence for global subduction at that time is limited, and that its model is a framework still to be tested.

The dataset also leans on Australia, where recent mapping projects have produced far more lead measurements than elsewhere.

The non-Australian check helps, but a more even global sample would test the result harder.

In a recent development, one detail may prove useful. The rare reappearances of the uranium-poor source suggest pieces of that ancient lower crust still survive under some continents.

If so, they could account for part of a long-standing puzzle. Surface rocks on average hold more uranium-derived lead than the whole Earth should, which implies a hidden, uranium-poor reservoir somewhere below.

The team’s data are available through the EarthBank platform, where other researchers could test the break against new samples as they are measured.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society A.

#42573. The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

The ‘hell chicken’ dinosaur was a real terror — to fruit

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (455 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • It has been revealed that more than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit.
  • It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that more than 65 million years ago, a small, beaked dinosaur dubbed the “hell chicken” was a real terror – to fruit. Reconstruction of its beak and jaw suggest it mashed up fruit much like modern parrots.

It’s the first evidence of non-avian dinosaurs evolving specialized adaptations for eating fruit, and comes at a time when flowering plants were coming into their own, researchers report October 10 in Nature Communications.

In 2011, a fossil collector found much of the fossilized skeleton of an odd theropod dinosaur in eastern Montana and brought to the attention of David Evans, a paleontologist at the Royal Ontario Museum in Canada. Over the next several years, fossil collectors and paleontologists working in Montana and North and South Dakota unearthed four more partial skeletons.

Recent findings suggest that the dinosaur belonged to a particularly birdlike subgroup of beaked theropods called oviraptorosaurs that lived during the Cretaceous Period. This species probably weighed around 12 kilograms — about the size of a turkey.

Evans and Greg Funston — a paleontologist at Stony Brook University in New York — and their colleagues named it Infernogallus jamesi, or ‘hell chicken,’ after its discovery in the Hell Creek geological formation and its overall poultrylike appearance.

It has been revealed that when the researchers studied Infernogallus’s skull and reconstructed the musculature, they discovered that it was no ordinary theropod. The construction of its jaw joints, muscles and palate suggest that it moved its jaw forward and back when eating rather than up and down like its chomping relatives.

According to recent reports, this chewing style is unique among non-avian dinosaurs but is strikingly similar to that of fruit-eating parrots. Funston and his colleagues think Infernogallus had adapted to a fruit-rich diet, deftly stripping the flesh from large seeds using its tongue and sliding jaw motions.

These fruit-munching adaptations were surprising, Funston claims. “But the more we delved into it, the more sense it made,” he says. “All the different lines of evidence seemed to converge on this one answer.”.

Angiosperms — plants that produce flowers and fruits — were rapidly diversifying throughout the Cretaceous. Mounting evidence suggests that angiosperms were coevolving with Cretaceous animals, and that dinosaurs may have been eating their fruits. Infernogallus adds to that emerging picture. It’s possible that other ‘hell chicken’ relatives or other dinosaur groups were habitual fruit eaters too, Funston says.

“[The discovery] suggests that our picture of dinosaur ecology right before the Cretaceous extinction has been missing major puzzle pieces, and that dinosaurs were more diverse than we thought.”.

#42572. When AI runs the lab, who checks the results?

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (906 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

When AI runs the lab, who checks the results?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A review across 11 fields examines how scientists test AI-generated results as machines take on more of the work of proposing and running experiments.
  • It’s easy to picture AI in science as a very fast assistant: feed it the data and it finds the pattern.
  • Some AI systems now take on several steps in the research process, from reading papers and proposing hypotheses to directing robots in the lab and adjusting experiments based on the results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A review across 11 fields examines how scientists test AI-generated results as machines take on more of the work of proposing and running experiments.

It’s easy to picture AI in science as a very fast assistant: feed it the data and it finds the pattern. A review by researchers at 94 institutions calls that picture out of date.

Some AI systems now take on several steps in the research process, from reading papers and proposing hypotheses to directing robots in the lab and adjusting experiments based on the results.

Sources indicate that the authors ask how much of what comes out of that loop can be trusted. They rank the field’s claims by how well each has been tested in the real world.

The review is a survey of published work across 11 fields, not a newly introduced experiment.

The lead authors include Yongjun Xu of the Institute of Computing Technology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and Heyang Li of the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Co-authors come from institutions including the University of Queensland and Berlin’s Hertie School.

Sources indicate that the authors’ own 2021 review, in the same journal, described AI as a powerful tool for analyzing data. AlphaFold, which predicts a protein’s shape from its sequence, was the model case.

That program answered one question that had resisted decades of work and left the rest of the job to people.

Five years on, the review describes systems built from six modules that feed each other.

One reads papers, one analyzes data, one proposes hypotheses, one runs experiments, one writes the report, and one adjusts the whole process based on what failed.

Large language models supply the knowledge and reasoning, software agents sequence the work, and robots supply the hands.

Some groups, the authors wrote, are already testing whether AI can take part in peer review itself.

It has been revealed that the clearest example comes from materials science. An autonomous laboratory called A-Lab was handed 58 target compounds.

Drawing synthesis recipes from the literature and adjusting when a route failed, it made 41 of them in 17 days.

The review treats materials science as the field where the loop is most complete, with generative models proposing fresh crystals and robotic platforms making and testing them.

Other fields are further behind. In medicine, the authors flagged limited prospective validation and the risk of fabricated outputs.

In geoscience, models trained on past conditions struggle when the conditions themselves shift.

Sources indicate that the review’s most practical contribution is a grading scheme. For each field, the authors coded the level of validation behind AI results on a scale from A to D.

An A means a method has been experimentally validated or is already deployed in real workflows. A B means a prototype tested in a controlled, closed-loop setting.

In a recent development, A C means the result rests on benchmarks, simulations, or retrospective tests. A D means the work is still conceptual.

The point, the authors wrote, is that a high score on a benchmark is not the same as a discovery.

Closing what they call the reality gap between benchmark success and real-world use is, in their words, a top priority.

Three constraints recur across every field in the review. Standardized, high-quality data remain scarce.

Deep networks still trade interpretability for accuracy, so a model can predict a molecule’s behavior without explaining it.

And generative models can produce outputs that look plausible while violating physical laws, which the authors tie to the lack of explicit physical constraints in current architectures.

According to recent reports, A fourth limit is human. The review cites earlier warnings that AI’s fluency can create what one group called “illusions of understanding,” with scientists mistaking output for insight and converging on the same few methods.

The authors also put a price on scale. Global data centers used about 415 terawatt-hours of electricity during 2024.

The review projects that figure roughly doubling by 2030, an increase about equal to Japan’s current annual consumption.

For science, the authors wrote, the cost of discovery is becoming tied to electricity prices and hardware supply.

According to recent reports, in the United States, about 56% of data center electricity comes from fossil fuels. The authors put the resulting emissions at more than 105 million tons of carbon dioxide a year.

Training a single large model, they wrote, can cost from thousands to hundreds of millions of dollars, which risks a “computational divide” between well-funded labs and everyone else.

A review maps what has been published, and the authors are candid that maturity is uneven and that the grades are theirs. The open question for any one field is the A-to-D test itself: has anyone checked the machine’s result against the world?

Sources indicate that the authors expect the next decade to be the test. Governments in the United States, Britain, the European Union, and China have all rolled out AI-for-science strategies.

The review’s case is that the advantage will go to whoever best combines data, computing, and people, not to the biggest budget.

Industry observers note that the authors’ closing line is a limit as much as a forecast. AI, they wrote, will serve as a cognitive copilot rather than a replacement for scientists.

The review was published in the journal The Innovation.

#42571. Córdoba’s famous orange trees face a test in one of Spain’s hottest cities

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (987 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Córdoba’s famous orange trees face a test in one of Spain’s hottest cities

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Olive and holm oak leaves kept working at temperatures that damaged orange and tipu, a 17-species test finds, a guide to heat-tolerant trees.
  • Orange trees line the streets and plazas of Córdoba, in southern Spain, and a tree from a warm climate seems like a safe bet for a hot city.
  • In a test of 17 common street and park trees in Córdoba, the orange was among the first to fail in the heat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Olive and holm oak leaves kept working at temperatures that damaged orange and tipu, a 17-species test finds, a guide to heat-tolerant trees.

Orange trees line the streets and plazas of Córdoba, in southern Spain, and a tree from a warm climate seems like a safe bet for a hot city.

In a test of 17 common street and park trees in Córdoba, the orange was among the first to fail in the heat.

In a recent development, the orange tree’s leaves had lost 90% of their photosynthetic function by the time they reached 123°F (50.6°C). Olive leaves held on to 141°F (60.6°C), and holm oak kept working longer than any other species at the halfway mark.

Native Mediterranean and temperate trees tolerated more heat than exotic species from the subtropics, the study found.

The trees were sampled during one week in one city, so the rankings are a starting point rather than a verdict.

Sonia Vega-Rosete and Cristina Bastias of the University of Córdoba ran the test.

Córdoba’s summers already pass 104°F (40°C) on more than 15 days in some months, according to records from AEMET, Spain’s weather agency, and the count is rising.

In a recent development, street trees cool a city with shade and with the water their leaves release. If heat damages the leaves, both services shrink.

The researchers picked 17 species that are common in Córdoba and span a range of origins. The native Mediterranean trees included olive, holm oak, cork oak and carob.

Industry observers note that ash, white poplar and elm stood in for native temperate trees. The exotics from the subtropics included orange, jacaranda, chinaberry, tipu and catalpa.

In the last week of June 2025, the team cut one sun-exposed branch from each of five mature trees per species, all growing in irrigated city parks.

Back in the lab, they punched leaf discs about 0.6 inches (1.5 centimeters) across and sealed them in bags.

The bags went into a water bath for 30 minutes at each of 11 temperatures, from 77°F to 140°F (25°C to 60°C), six discs per temperature.

Afterward the team measured how well each disc’s light-harvesting machinery still worked.

From those readings, they fitted a curve for each species and read off three thresholds.

The first was the temperature where damage began, and the other two were where half and 90% of function was gone.

In a recent development, every species held up to about 108°F (42.5°C). Above that, the damage threshold ranged from 108°F for tipu to 125°F (51.5°C) for holm oak.

It has been revealed that the halfway point separated the groups most clearly. Native species lost half their function at an average of about 125°F (51.5°C), exotics at about 121°F (49.6°C).

The gap between the two groups was unlikely to be chance.

For 90% loss, the averages were about 135°F (57.2°C) for natives and 130°F (54.4°C) for exotics.

Grouped by climate of origin, Mediterranean and temperate trees reached about 136°F and 134°F (57.6°C and 56.4°C) before losing 90% of function, and subtropical trees about 128°F (53.5°C).

In a recent development, whether a tree keeps its leaves in winter made no difference. Evergreen and deciduous species were spread across the rankings.

“This allowed us to identify the temperature thresholds at which the photosynthetic performance of these species begins to be impaired, which could compromise their ability to ‘cool their surroundings,'” Vega-Rosete stated.

Sources indicate that the orange tree, chinaberry, catalpa and tipu are planted across Córdoba’s parks and streets, often for their looks or their history there. All four were among the least heat-tolerant trees.

In a recent development, the authors offer one explanation. A subtropical climate pairs warmth with humidity and plenty of water, and Córdoba supplies the warmth without the other two.

To measure that gap, the team mapped each species’ home climate from occurrence records in GBIF and other databases, matched to climate data from WorldClim.

For the subtropical species, the farther Córdoba’s climate was from the climate of their native range, the lower the temperature at which leaf damage began. Native species showed no such drop.

Holm oak, whose native range includes places as hot as Córdoba, had the highest damage threshold of all.

In a recent development, leaf temperatures matter here. The authors note that leaves can run 14°F to 18°F (8°C to 10°C) hotter than the air around them, and up to 36°F (20°C) hotter in full sun.

A 104°F afternoon can put a leaf past the damage threshold of several of these trees.

Industry observers note that the heat-tolerant trees shared a build. Their wood was denser, their leaves were thicker, and each leaf packed more dry matter into its area.

Species with heavier leaves per unit area lost half their function at higher temperatures, and species with denser wood resisted the onset of damage longer.

Such traits were most pronounced in the native Mediterranean evergreens.

The subtropical exotics, and a few temperate trees such as white poplar and black locust, had the opposite build: bigger leaves with more nitrogen, geared to fast growth.

All of the trees grew in watered parks, so the thresholds may differ for trees on dry streets or in other cities.

The leaves came from a single week of a hot summer. The five trees of each species were pooled, so the test gives one curve per species rather than a range.

In a recent development, the thresholds also capture only one part of how a tree copes with heat. Heat-shock proteins and other chemical defenses weren’t part of the study.

The authors wrote that the same test needs to run in other cities, climates, seasons and years, and on more species, before the rankings can guide planting broadly.

The full study was published in the journal Urban Forestry & Urban Greening.

StarDream Cruises has signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with LOTI to bring Chinese fashion and design to a wider regional audience.

Starting in 2027, the Genting Dream will get a dedicated fashion retail space, which will feature a collection of fashion and lifestyle pieces and exclusive merchandise available only onboard.

The collaboration will also bring fashion reveals and designer showcases to the ship, opening up latest opportunities for Chinese designers and original brands to introduce their work to consumers across Southeast Asia, according to a statement.

StarDream Cruises President Michael Goh and LOTI Co-Founder Pan YuanYua signed the agreement in Singapore on November 13.

“Cruising is about creating memorable experiences, and we are always looking at latest ways to bring fresh and exciting lifestyle offerings onboard for our guests,” said Goh.

Recent findings suggest that “Through our collaboration with LOTI, we look forward to bringing a newly introduced fashion experience to Genting Dream, from exclusive merchandise and curated collections to designer showcases at sea. Beyond enhancing the onboard experience, this partnership also creates an exciting platform for Chinese creativity to connect with a wider audience across the region.”.

The collaboration brings together travel and fashion, creating new ways for guests to discover and engage with creativity throughout their holiday.

“LOTI has always been committed to bringing original Chinese design to the global stage. Through this collaboration with Dream Cruises’ Genting Dream, we are taking the fashion runway to the sea,” noted Yuanyuan.

“Leveraging the unique advantage of a cruise voyage that connects destinations across Southeast Asia, we have created an immersive maritime fashion space that integrates retail, fashion showcases, and exclusive products, allowing guests from around the world to experience the charm of Chinese design while on holiday.”.

The Genting Dream operates  two-, three- and five-night cruises year-round from Singapore and Malaysia, taking guests to destinations across Southeast Asia, including Kuala Lumpur, Melaka, Penang and Redang Island in Malaysia; Phuket, Bangkok and Koh Samui in Thailand; and Bali in Indonesia.

The 2016-built vessel went into drydock in Singapore at the start of September, welcoming guests back on September 25, 2026.

Exercise may have an overlooked social benefit beyond boosting your mood

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mice with running wheels fought less over food and warmth, suggesting that exercise can influence their social behavior.
  • Recent findings suggest that exercise is usually recommended for the heart, the lungs, and a better mood.
  • Less fighting over food and a warm resting place was observed in mouse pairs housed with a working running wheel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mice with running wheels fought less over food and warmth, suggesting that exercise can influence their social behavior.

Recent findings suggest that exercise is usually recommended for the heart, the lungs, and a better mood. In mice, a new study suggests that it may also alter how animals treat one another.

Less fighting over food and a warm resting place was observed in mouse pairs housed with a working running wheel.

Pairs whose wheel had been locked fought more often. Greater activity was also recorded in brain areas tied to social behavior among the mice that ran.

In a recent development, the work was led by Liz Kirby of Ohio State University. She is an associate professor of behavioral neuroscience in the Department of Psychology.

Recent findings suggest that the findings come from mice and were presented at a scientific meeting. They have not yet appeared in a journal.

According to recent reports, “Mice are known to be naturally social. They like hanging out with other mice, just like humans like hanging out with other humans,” Kirby said.

“They also exercise naturally. If you give them a running wheel, they run about six miles a night, voluntarily.”.

Mice were housed in pairs for six weeks by Kirby’s team. Each pair consisted of two males or two females.

It has been revealed that A running wheel was available to some pairs at any hour of the day or night. Other pairs were given a wheel that could not turn.

The same object was therefore present in every cage, yet only one group could run on it.

In a recent development, each pair was then given something to compete for. A tasty treat was used in one test. In another, the prize was a warm resting spot with room for only one mouse.

In a recent development, the researchers recorded behaviors linked to competitive fighting. These included attempts to steal the food or to push a cage mate off the warm spot.

According to Kirby, a food pellet was shared more readily by the mice with working wheels. Mice with locked wheels were not as good at sharing it.

According to recent reports, “They would rip it from each other’s paws and run away with it in a cage and chase each other down. Generally very rude behavior when it comes to mealtime,” Kirby mentioned.

A follow-up experiment limited some mice to scheduled wheel sessions. These sessions lasted six hours a day and were held five days a week. Kirby called them visiting the gym.

The same tests were carried out after six weeks on that schedule. Kirby said that living with a wheel and visiting the gym both seemed to reduce fighting over limited resources.

Constant access to a wheel therefore did not appear necessary for the mice to fight less.

Will Butke is a doctoral student in Kirby’s lab and the lead author of the study. The effects of running inside the brain were also examined by him and his colleagues.

A technique that marks recently active brain cells was used. Some regions linked to social behavior were more active in the mice that ran. Other regions remained unchanged.

“This points toward the idea that this isn’t just a brain-wide increase in activation, but instead that the activation is specifically in certain subregions of the brain,” Butke said.

According to recent reports, these measurements indicate which areas were more active in the running mice. They cannot show whether that activity explains the reduced fighting.

Clubs where people exercise together have grown quickly. The fitness app Strava reported that new clubs on its platform nearly quadrupled in 2025.

The total was put at 1 million clubs by Strava. Hiking clubs grew fastest and were followed by running clubs.

Meanwhile, loneliness has worried health officials.

Falling rates of social connection were described as “an urgent public health concern” in a 2023 advisory. It was issued by U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy.

According to Butke, research on what happens in the brain when people exercise socially is limited.

“People like to run in groups or exercise together – not only because you get to have a person you can rely upon, but also it gets you into a social context where you can de-stress,” he said.

Sources indicate that mice and people are difficult to compare directly. Even so, Kirby said the work suggests that exercise has a direct social benefit, since competitive fighting was reduced.

“This adds to the list of potential benefits you could be getting by exercising,” Kirby noted.

“It’s not just going to make your heart healthier, and it’s not just going to reduce your risk for cancer, obesity and stroke, but it also might help strengthen your social ties.”.

According to recent reports, A poster is an early step, and a full paper has not yet been released. The number of mice tested and the brain regions that changed would be detailed in that paper.

It has been revealed that all of the mice lived in pairs, so the results describe exercise with a companion nearby. The behavior of a mouse that runs alone remains a separate question.

Future research could test whether exercise changes how people share and compete, as it did in these mice.

The work was presented on November 18 as a poster at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for upcoming member orientation on Monday.
  • What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?
  • As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for upcoming member orientation on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?

As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”.

In a recent development, trainings and guest speakers aren’t everyone’s idea of a fun time, but Democrats are feeling good about this year’s new member orientation. Giddy, even.

The incoming freshmen will pose for a class photo on the House steps. They’ll test their luck in a lottery to see who lands the best office space. And everywhere they look, they see signs of the blue wave that swept over the country.

Industry observers note that “I think — well, I hope — that we will be doing a lot of exceeding expectations in this caucus. The American people deserve it and expect it,” stated Rep.-elect Sam Forstag, D-Mont., as he headed to lunch after an orientation session on Monday.

It has been revealed that forstag is the first Democratic congressman from Montana in 30 years, succeeding retiring GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke. A former smokejumper who parachuted into remote forests to put out wildfires, Forstag won by more than 3 points in a district President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that “I think there’s a lot of folks who didn’t expect us to,” he remarked of his win. “Nobody knew who we were this past December when I was still working at the smoke jumper base in Missoula.”.

Democrats are still digesting their larger-than-expected wins, which saw them flip more than 40 House seats and oust a number of high-profile incumbents, including National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, R-N.C.

Sources indicate that “It’s like drinking out of a firehose,” mentioned Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke, D-Wis., who unseated incumbent GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd District.

Cooke and her opponent clashed during the campaign over his use of AI-generated ads that she described as deepfakes. Now, they have to work together to make sure the transition goes smoothly.

Sources indicate that “The congressman remarked that he’s willing to be helpful in that transition. I think it’s important that we make sure that the casework is transferred over, that constituent service is a priority, and that nothing falls through the cracks for people,” she said.

The 120th Congress will be full of history-makers, and a record-breaking number of women are set to serve in the House.

It has been revealed that “This is a Congress with the most women ever to be a part of this chamber,” Cooke said. “And a lot of [Democrats], frankly, from the Midwest, and so I’m excited to build that sort of power from the Midwest to make sure that our interests are represented.”.

The math isn’t lost on Republicans navigating a freshman class where they have fewer peers than they hoped.

“I thought that it would probably go a little bit different. I think a lot of people did, but it is what it is. You work with what we have,” mentioned Rep.-elect Mark Lamb, R-Ariz.

Sources indicate that but just like high school, everyone’s trying to make friends. As incoming members filed into the Capitol Visitor Center on Monday morning, Rep.-elect Cait Conley, D-N.Y., introduced herself to Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, R-Fla.

Meanwhile, Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., who describes herself as a “proud democratic socialist,” walked by chatting with Del.-elect Robert White, who will become only the third person in the modern era to hold the title of D.C.’s nonvoting delegate.

“I’m sitting next to a teacher right now; I’m sitting next to the mayor of Scranton … good, nice people,” mentioned Rep.-elect Zack Mullock, D-N.J., who said he was surprised by how many “regular people” he was meeting among the incoming class.

Rep.-elect Brad Lander, D-N.Y., who ousted fellow Democrat Dan Goldman in a Brooklyn-based primary before cruising to victory in the general election, was also making friends.

“I was hanging out with Donavan McKinney yesterday in orientation, and I’m just really excited to meet all the amazing people. Micah Lasher, we were hanging out last night. Jacqui Irwin, so we’re just trying to get to know each other,” he noted.

Recent findings suggest that after arriving on Sunday with suitcases in hand, the future freshmen got a chance to set foot inside the House chamber later that day. Lander said he’d been there before to see Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, a friend of his, get sworn in four years ago. But Sunday was his first time on the floor itself.

“It’s obviously a lot different when it’s you,” he said.

Koh agreed, saying “everyone in that room, Republican or Democrat, had a lot of reverence for where they were.”.

“I think it was just a good reminder about how despite all the division, that’s what we’re going to focus on — trying to figure out how to get things done for the American people,” he stated.

Members-elect were trying their best to navigate their new workplace on Monday, many of them donning backpacks as they came to terms with the realities of their new job.

“We just have to get back to class,” mentioned Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, R-Ky., to a crowd of reporters trying to flag him down as he left orientation to use the restroom.

They’d have Italian food for lunch, after a session in the CVC auditorium where many of the future members typed notes on their laptops.

Sources indicate that “They’ve got a packed agenda for us all week, really helping us figure out how to get started. Build our team, set course, understand where the bathrooms are — large and small. We got a lot to learn,” Lander stated.

#42565. Locusts may help scientists detect hard-to-treat lung infections

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1259 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Locusts may help scientists detect hard-to-treat lung infections

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1259 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In lab tests, locusts could smell the difference between bacterial biofilms and free-floating bacteria, a finding that could inform future breath tests.
  • Bacteria become much harder to kill once they attach to a surface and build a slimy protective layer.
  • Sources indicate that these colonies are called biofilms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In lab tests, locusts could smell the difference between bacterial biofilms and free-floating bacteria, a finding that could inform future breath tests.

Bacteria become much harder to kill once they attach to a surface and build a slimy protective layer.

Sources indicate that these colonies are called biofilms. No test can currently detect them in a patient’s lungs without an invasive procedure.

A locust’s sense of smell might help one day.

In lab tests, researchers used signals from locust brains to tell biofilms apart from free-floating bacteria of the same species by smell.

The clearest signal appeared about a second after the odor reached the locusts’ antennae.

Debajit Saha and Jonathan Hardy were the senior authors of the study. Both are associate professors at Michigan State University (MSU). Michael Parnas was the first author.

Recent findings suggest that saha works in the College of Engineering. Hardy is based in the Department of Microbiology, Genetics and Immunology. Both researchers also belong to MSU’s Institute for Quantitative Health Science and Engineering.

Only bacterial cultures grown in flasks were used. Breath samples and patients were not tested.

Saha noted that before the experiments, it was not clear that an odor alone could show how bacteria were growing.

“Seeing such a high level of discrimination was therefore quite surprising,” Saha said.

According to recent reports, A biofilm forms when bacteria settle on a solid surface. A sticky coating is then built around the whole colony.

Recent findings suggest that inside that coating, bacteria can be up to 1,000 times more resistant to antibiotics than free-floating bacteria. The authors gave that figure in the paper.

It has been revealed that some bacteria deep in the colony have a slower metabolism. Those cells can survive treatment, and the biofilm is rebuilt afterward.

In a recent development, biofilms account for about 80% of bacterial infections in people, according to earlier research cited in the paper. Wounds, implants and the lungs can all be affected.

Industry observers note that an infection is usually identified by growing a sample in a laboratory. That process takes a few days. Faster tests exist, but they cannot separate a biofilm from free-floating bacteria.

Industry observers note that bacteria also release chemicals into the air as they grow. Together, those airborne chemicals form an odor. An odor can be sampled from outside the body.

Locusts smell with their antennae. More than 100,000 odor-sensing nerve cells are found on each antenna.

In a recent development, the signals from those cells all pass through about 800 output neurons. These neurons are located in one small smell-processing region of the brain.

Sources indicate that for the experiment, the brain was surgically exposed in six living locusts. Each insect was held still, and an electrode was placed in that region.

Recent findings suggest that the team then blew air from five flasks across the antennae. Four flasks contained bacteria. The fifth contained only the broth in which the bacteria had been grown.

Recent findings suggest that two species were used, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. Each species was grown in two ways, as a biofilm and as a free-floating culture.

Sources indicate that each odor was delivered for four seconds and repeated five times, with one minute between deliveries. The activity of 32 neurons was isolated from the recordings.

In a recent development, the locusts had not been trained on these odors. Insect brains have been used this way by Saha’s lab before. In earlier work, recordings were taken from locusts and honeybees exposed to the odors of human cancer cells.

In a recent development, trained dogs can also detect some diseases by smell. However, a test based on an animal’s behavior gives only a yes or a no, the authors wrote.

Recent findings suggest that A computer program compared the firing pattern from each trial with the patterns from the other trials. The closest match was then selected.

Recent findings suggest that when all five odors were included, 22 of 25 trials were matched to the correct flask. That is an accuracy of 88%. Guessing would be right only 20% of the time.

Both biofilms were identified in every trial.

In a recent development, one of the five free-floating Staphylococcus trials was mistaken for the Staphylococcus biofilm. The plain broth was also mistaken for a Staphylococcus odor twice.

According to recent reports, in this analysis, every biofilm was caught by the program. One free-floating sample was wrongly flagged as a biofilm, however.

The researchers reported accuracy of up to 96% when individual biofilm and free-floating odors were classified.

In a recent development, the largest differences in firing patterns were seen between the two species. Biofilm and free-floating cultures of the same species produced more similar patterns. Even so, they were still separated by the recordings.

It has been revealed that saha noted bacteria release a different mix of airborne chemicals when their growth state changes. These subtle changes can be picked up by the insects.

In a recent development, before the odor arrived, the program performed no better than guessing. Accuracy rose quickly once the odor was delivered.

The team then tested how little brain activity was needed. A half-second slice of the recording was enough for 91% accuracy. That slice was centered about one second after the odor arrived.

A quarter-second slice from the same moment gave 82% accuracy. A laboratory culture, by comparison, takes days.

Recent findings suggest that the 32 neurons represent about 4% of the roughly 800 output neurons in the smell-processing region. The biofilm analysis was also repeated on random subsets of the 32.

Performance improved as more neurons were included.

Only one laboratory strain of each species was used. Human breath is more complicated. It also carries chemicals from food, medications and the surrounding air.

Recent findings suggest that several other limits were listed by the authors. The number of bacteria could not be kept exactly equal in the biofilm and free-floating flasks. That difference alone could change an odor.

All 32 neurons were pooled from six insects. The study therefore does not show a single locust doing the job.

Sources indicate that the recordings stayed strong for about four hours after surgery. How long a locust lasts as a sensor depends on its health and the surgeon’s skill, the authors wrote.

Drug-resistant strains such as MRSA were not tested either. The team expects those strains to be harder to distinguish from ordinary Staphylococcus.

No one has yet tested whether a locust brain can pick a biofilm’s odor out of human breath.

Sources indicate that breath studies are the next step, the authors wrote. Hardy stated the team is interested in testing breath samples from children with cystic fibrosis. Persistent lung infections that involve biofilms can develop in these children.

Pseudomonas is a major cause of lung infections in people with the disease, according to the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation.

Custom electrodes are also being developed so that enough data can be collected from a single locust.

In a recent development, in the long term, the researchers want to build a portable sensor. It would connect a living locust’s smell system to small electronics and artificial intelligence.

In a recent development, more bacterial species and samples from patients will be needed in future work. The results will also have to be compared with the laboratory methods already used in hospitals.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Biology.

#42564. Eagles may hunt baboons as heavy as some early human relatives

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1293 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Eagles may hunt baboons as heavy as some early human relatives

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1293 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Punctured baboon skulls found beneath cliffs in Chad suggest Verreaux’s eagles may hunt larger primates than scientists once thought possible.
  • Sources indicate that eagles are known to kill monkeys.
  • That view is now challenged by skulls of adult male olive baboons found below desert cliffs in the Sahara.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Punctured baboon skulls found beneath cliffs in Chad suggest Verreaux’s eagles may hunt larger primates than scientists once thought possible.

Sources indicate that eagles are known to kill monkeys. A full-grown male baboon, however, has long been considered too heavy for any bird to take.

That view is now challenged by skulls of adult male olive baboons found below desert cliffs in the Sahara. The damage on them suggests that Verreaux’s eagles can kill such animals anyway.

In a recent development, A hole was punched through the bone of the eye socket in each skull. It is the kind of wound that an eagle’s talon leaves. One of the baboons weighed an estimated 48 pounds (21.8 kg).

If the researchers are right, an eagle can kill prey as heavy as some early human relatives.

It has been revealed that the study was led by Catherine Hobaiter of the University of St Andrews. She worked with colleagues at Dartmouth College, the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, and African Parks.

No one on the team saw an eagle attack a baboon. The case rests on bones.

Sources indicate that three sites on the Ennedi Plateau were visited by the team in February and March 2025. The plateau is a sandstone landscape in northeastern Chad.

Among the fallen rock below its cliffs, the skulls of two adult male baboons were found at two different sites.

Neither puncture showed signs of healing, so the damage could have occurred around the time of death or afterward.

“We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them,” Hobaiter said.

“Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”.

The right shoulder blade of the first male had been punctured and scraped as well. Eagles leave that pattern when they open a body to reach the heart and lungs.

The team also needed to know how heavy the baboons were. The ball at the top of each thigh bone was therefore measured in scaled photographs.

An established formula for monkeys converts that width into an estimate of body weight.

In a recent development, both thigh bones were found with the first punctured skull. From them, the team estimated that male’s weight at about 48 pounds (21.8 kg).

These weights matter because of a rule of thumb in research on primates and their predators. Primates under 29 pounds (13 kg) are known eagle prey. No heavier primate has ever been confirmed as an eagle’s kill.

Recent findings suggest that primates between 29 and 44 pounds (13 and 20 kg) are treated as vulnerable in theory. Anything heavier is assumed to be safe from birds.

A third punctured skull was recovered on a return trip in June 2026, along with part of the skeleton. This male weighed an estimated 58 pounds (26.2 kg), and both of his shoulder blades had been scraped.

He was at least twice as heavy as any primate confirmed as eagle prey.

In all, thigh bones were collected from nine baboons. Eight were adult males with an average estimated weight of 49 pounds (22.2 kg).

A hole in a baboon’s skull does not have to come from an eagle. Other causes were therefore considered by the team.

A gunshot would be expected to do much more damage to the skull, and none was found. Male baboons also kill each other with their canine teeth. Such fights tend to leave crushed bone and extra tooth gouges, yet the skulls had neither.

Verreaux’s eagles are known to dive at baboons that come near their nests. No nest was found above or near the skulls, however.

One possibility was harder to dismiss. Verreaux’s eagles sometimes eat dead animals. The scraped shoulder blade could be explained by an eagle pulling apart a carcass.

The authors wrote that this cannot be definitively ruled out. Two reasons to doubt it were given.

First, the skull punctures are far more severe than the shallow pits seen in an earlier experiment. In that experiment, a golden eagle had gripped a dead monkey.

Industry observers note that second, nearly all the bones came from adult males. An eagle that feeds on carcasses would be expected to eat a dead baboon of either sex.

“At first, the idea of eagles hunting adult male baboons seemed to exist on the thin edge of possibility, until it didn’t,” mentioned Nathaniel Dominy of Dartmouth, the study’s senior author.

According to recent reports, an eagle does not have to lift its prey to kill it. Golden eagles land on the back of a hoofed animal and hold on until it collapses. Similar methods are used by Verreaux’s eagles.

In a recent development, verreaux’s eagles also hunt in pairs. The prey is startled by one bird, and the other attacks from below to force it off the cliff.

The grip of a Verreaux’s eagle can span up to 16 inches (40 cm). That is more than twice the width of an adult male baboon’s skull.

Sources indicate that the Ennedi baboons appear to spend much of the day on vertical cliff faces. Some are as tall as 490 feet (150 meters).

Water and palm fruit are found on the canyon floor, but it offers little shade or shelter.

Sources indicate that when young baboons are threatened by an eagle, the males bark and lunge at it. The team suggested that this could make males more likely to be killed on a cliff.

On June 19, 2026, the researchers watched a pair of Verreaux’s eagles.

The birds flew along a cliff where baboons were resting. Several baboons gave alarm calls, and those in exposed spots dropped quickly to shelter.

“We’d seen them very relaxed around other big birds of prey, but as soon as the Verreaux came into view they alarm called and dropped down to safety,” Hobaiter mentioned.

The argument reaches past baboons because of a famous fossil. In 1995, researchers argued that the Taung Child had been killed by an eagle.

The Taung Child was a young early human relative.

It has been revealed that the punctures in the Ennedi skulls resemble the damage to that fossil’s eye socket. The Taung Child, however, weighed an estimated 22 to 26 pounds (10 to 12 kg) at most.

That weight falls inside the accepted limit for eagle prey.

Sources indicate that research on what hunted larger early human relatives has focused on mammals, especially massive cats. Hobaiter’s team argued that eagles deserve attention too.

If eagles can kill adult baboons this large, the authors argue that some early human relatives may also have been vulnerable.

Monkeys defend themselves differently against eagles than against cats, and males often step in during eagle attacks.

Industry observers note that several traits could have been shaped by pressure from eagles, the authors wrote. These include the size difference between males and females, cooperation among males, and infant care.

That part of the argument was called speculative by the authors.

Three punctured skulls point to possible eagle attacks, and baboons sounded alarm calls when a pair of Verreaux’s eagles flew past.

The researchers have yet to see one of these eagles attack an adult baboon.

Nearly all the bones came from adult males, and the authors called that pattern puzzling.

3D scans of the bones have been posted in public archives by the researchers, where others can examine the punctures.

Future fieldwork at Ennedi could show whether eagles kill adult male baboons there, and how often.

The full study was published in the journal American Journal of Biological Anthropology.

#42563. Breaking: In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck
